Question: Does it bother atheists that people believe in God?
Answer: It does bother me that people believe in gods, but the extent to which it bothers me depends very much on the specifics of how the person acts. Look, most of my friends are Christians. And for the most part, we only discuss religion a bit, and have a live and let live attitude. As long as people are reasonable and tolerant, religion isn't the type of thing that gets me up in arms. But even then, it still bothers me some. I mean, I think back to when I was still a Christian, and all the cognitive dissonance I experienced, the fear of Hell (especially for others besides myself), the Catholic guilt, the wrestling with secular ethics vs. Biblical rules, etc. It may have taken me a few years to get to this point, but I'm happier now as an atheist than I was as a Christian, and I'd like for others to have that. But, I also don't want to be that guy that's always arguing and being pushy about beliefs. So here's a list of examples stepping through different types of believers and how I feel about them. Type of Believer: Tolerant believer who keeps their religion private and doesn't impose on others My Feelings: This bothers me on the same level as people who believe in urban legends, or who root for different sports teams from me. They're wrong about the nature of reality, and I would like to help them see the world more clearly, and recognize that the Steelers are the one true... sorry - wrong topic Level of Opposition: Good natured discussions over beer (though I hardly ever bring it up, waiting for others to broach the subject) Type of Believer: Somewhat tolerant believer, but who lets their religious beliefs influence the way they vote (particularly if they vote against women's rights or LGBT rights, or think global warming can't be real because God wouldn't let it happen) My Feelings: Well, now your religious beliefs aren't as private anymore, since they're having real world effects. So, now I do feel more justified in trying to get you to change your mind. Level of Opposition: More heated discussions over beer, Possible end of friendship depending on how they treat individuals Type of Believer: Door to door proselytizers My Feelings: Hoo boy. I love debate, and I have strong opinions on religion, and you actually came to my house with the purpose of talking about religion, so here we go. Level of Opposition: Debate for as long as they're willing to stay at my house Type of Believer: Parents who withhold real medical treatment from children in favor of faith healing My Feelings: I don't personally know anyone like this, but I know they're out there. The case of Makayla Sault was a heartbreaking, recent example. Children shouldn't have to suffer or die for the religious beliefs of their parents. Level of Opposition: Push for laws to outlaw this type of child abuse Type of Believer: Intolerant believer, who lets their religious beliefs influence the way they vote and how they treat individuals (particularly women, the LGBT community, and people outside their faith) My Feelings: Yeah, now they're definitely into the strong negative effects of religion, and I don't just feel justified to try to change their minds, but see it as a moral duty to society. Level of Opposition: Strong debate, definitely not going to be friends Type of Believer: Preachers/Leaders of Creationist/Evangelical/Fundamentalist Groups My Feelings: You're not just misleading yourself, but misleading all the people who follow you. And these brands of religion are usually the more close-minded branches that lead to negative effects, so I'm definitely going to speak up. Level of Opposition: Pointed blog entries and Quora answers Type of Believer: Intolerant Religious Politicians My Feelings: We have a First Amendment for a reason. Government and religion aren't supposed to be intertwined. It really, really bothers me when politicians pass religiously based laws, or give preferential treatment to certain religious institutions. Level of Opposition: Pointed blog entries and Quora answers, Vote for opponent So, that's how I feel about it. We live in a free, multicultural society, where people have the right to believe anything they want. As long as religious people are tolerant of others and don't use religion as a reason to discriminate or make bad decisions, the most they'll have to fear from me is talking about religion over a beer every once in a while. However, if a person's religious beliefs are having harmful, real-world consequences, then I'm going to speak up.

Question: Did Kamala Harris lose the atheist vote when she said "God bless America"?
Answer: If saying 'God bless America' lost you the atheist vote, we atheists would scarcely have anybody to vote for in any election, all the way down to city politics. I mean, sure, in a perfect world, I'd prefer a candidate who was also an atheist*, or at least someone who kept their religion and politics separate. But the reality is that the U.S. is still too overtly religious, and so candidates have to pander at least a bit to Christianity if they want to win. So, in the real world, where no candidate is going to be a perfect, 100% match to everything you'd want, you have to compromise and pick the candidate with the qualities, and especially the policies, that you like the most (or, more cynically, dislike the least). And when the opposition is Trump, that's not a hard choice at all. *Not that a candidate being an atheist would get anything like automatic support from me, either. It's their public policies that are the biggest consideration, while their private religious beliefs are way down the list (though if they start to push their religious beliefs into their public policies, then it’s no longer a mere private belief and does become an issue).

Question: How can one respond to the argument that the existence of monkeys disproves the theory of evolution?
Answer: I see a lot of answers here proposing ridicule and laughter, which I think are missing a great opportunity to make somebody one of today's "lucky 10,000". ABOVE SOURCE: XKCD - Ten Thousand Anybody asking this question quite obviously didn't have the best science education growing up, so this is your chance to share the excitement of understanding a topic as enthralling as universal common descent. Anyway, as far as this particular question goes, it's been asked so many times that there are countless responses. Perhaps my favorite is to ask, if I'm descended from Germans, why are there still Germans? I think it hits on several key points in one example. First, it's obvious that I'm not descended from any living Germans. You have to go back several generations to find my most recent German ancestry. So, modern day Germans and I share a common ancestor. I'm not descended from modern day Germans. Quite literally, modern day Germans are my distant cousins, and modern day monkeys are my even more distant cousins. Related to that, the German culture of my ancestors back in Germany wasn't the same as modern day German culture. Once my family split away from our German relatives, my family's culture developed independently here in the U.S., while my cousins’ culture developed differently in Germany. Likewise, when we say that humans are descended from monkeys, those ancient species of monkeys weren't the same as modern day species of monkeys. We took one evolutionary path, and they took another. Further, this analogy shows that there's not necessarily a single ideal form that culture will develop towards, or by analogy, any single ideal form that animals will evolve towards. I'm sure American and German patriots will argue over which country is better (I actually do have very good German friends, and yes, we do argue about this good naturedly over beers), but both nations exist and are fairly successful. Looking back to the animal kingdom, there are lots of food sources, lifestyles, and niches for animals to survive in, including monkeys. Species will diversify to take advantage of all this variety of niches. There's no reason to suspect that other monkeys or apes would evolve to be more like people when they're already finding success in their own different ways. (There's also the competitive exclusion principle that predicts that no two species in the same environment will occupy the same niche.) Anyway, the next time somebody asks you that question, don't laugh at them or ridicule them. That's simply a surefire way to shut down any learning opportunity. Instead, take it as a teaching moment, and share a bit of the excitement of this topic.

Question: How many Flat-Earthers are there in the United States?
Answer: Skimming through the other answers, it seems that many people doubt that there are significant numbers of people who believe in the flat earth nonsense at all. They chalk it up to trolling or just trying to get a rise out of people. A couple of the answers I read from Quorans who I follow put their estimates at just a few hundred to a few thousand true believers. But I suspect the number is actually much higher. Let me tell a story about a different conspiracy theory. I've told it on Quora before, but I think it's relevant here. So, I'm an aerospace engineer, and especially in my day to day interactions with colleagues, I'm used to interacting with college educated professionals. So while I know that there are people out there who doubt the moon landings, I don't interact with any of those conspiracy theorists on a daily basis, and I just chalked them up to a tiny lunatic fringe. Well, about a year or so ago, I was at a party that was a different group than my professional colleagues. Somehow we got onto the topic of the moon landings, and not a single other person in the discussion was certain we’d been to the moon. The most was one person who said they believe it probably happened, but they’d seen some things online that raised some questions for them. Most of the others ranged from doubtful, to outright rejection. They weren't trolling me to try to get a rise out of me. They were very sincere in their doubts. The point of that anecdote is that you can't generalize to the entire population based just on your own peer group. If you're well educated, it may seem super obvious to you that the Earth is round, and you may doubt that anybody could sincerely doubt that fact. But not everyone is well educated. When people say they think the Earth may be flat, many of them really do mean it. So what do polls say? Well, here are the results of one (with a few other conspiracy theories thrown in as a bonus): ABOVE SOURCE: Conspiracy vs. Science: A Survey of U.S. Public Beliefs According to that, around 10% of Americans think the Earth is flat, with another 10% being unsure. In a nation of 330 million, 10% is 33 million. If that percentage seems too high to you, consider another poll that got repeated every couple years for around 3 decades, measuring Americans' understanding of super basic science*: ABOVE SOURCE: Science and Engineering Indicators 2016 These results go back to the 1980s, before being an online troll was cool. The one that always gets me is the question about whether the Earth goes around the Sun or vice versa. Only 3/4 of Americans got that right every year it was asked, meaning that around a quarter of Americans got it wrong. And only around half knew that it takes a year for the Earth to go around the Sun. So if people going back 30 years can get such basic facts wrong, well, I'm not shocked that 10% of Americans, 33 million of us, might actually believe in a flat Earth. * If you're not from the U.S., don't get all snobbish about our ignorance. Most countries do about as poorly. In fact, only 66% of people in the European Union correctly answered the question about the Earth orbiting the Sun.

Question: 👋 Hello. Although I have many reservations about the New Testament, I wonder why so many people put pen to paper about the life of Jesus. What inspired them to write about his life. Surely there is a 'Kernel ' of truth contained within them?
Answer: I guess there are two shades of meaning to this question. Why did people write about Jesus at all (which I'll cover first). And why did so many people write about him in particular, to the relative exclusion of similar cult leaders at the time (which I'll get to a bit later). Broadly speaking, people were motivated to write about Jesus for the same reasons that they write about anybody. I've discussed a more modern day cult leader here on Quora before, Sathya Sai Baba*. He just died relatively recently in 2011, and you can find a ton of stuff written about him by his followers, from an official biography, to innumerable online essays by rank and file followers. You can even find answers by many of his followers right here on Quora (just type his name into the Quora search bar). Whatever you might think of his own motivations (e.g. were his 'miracles' intentional sleight of hand deception), he struck a chord with people and was able to parlay that into fame and a successful movement in his lifetime. Will Sai Baba's cult survive for centuries like Jesus's did? Who knows? Some sects seem to die out with the death of their leader, while others seem to resonate even afterwards. There are plenty of examples of this persistence, from major religions right down to smaller sects – Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Zoroastrianism, Mormons, Seventh-day Adventists, Rastafarianism, Scientology, etc. I don't think there's really any way of knowing why Jesus's cult became so hugely popular compared to all the other similar cults in that time and place. Heck, history has relegated John the Baptist to basically supporting cast in the Jesus story, despite being a leader of a religious movement in his own right.** There have actually been studies on smaller scale versions of this. Back in 2003, some researchers created a music download website that they could control to run experiments. They tested a specific set of songs across multiple groups. None of the groups could see what songs the other groups had downloaded or how the other groups rated all of the songs. So in each group, there was equal opportunity for any song to go 'viral'. And what they found that was it was probabilistic and random at the same time (stochastic). Some songs tended to end up in the top downloads more often, while other songs tended to remain relegated to the bottom, but the specific songs that became the most popular varied from group to group with no way to definitively predict it ahead of time. It seemed to come down to random chance and extreme sensitivity to initial conditions. Here’s a pop-sci article discussing the study, and the actual research report: So, there probably was something to Jesus's message about loving your neighbor, caring for the poor, and not being judgmental that resonated with people. But why that particular cult ended up becoming a major world religion as opposed to the similar cults is probably down to chance. Had history played out a bit differently, billions of people might now be worshipping John the Baptist, wearing necklaces with dinner platters instead of crucifixes. * That previous answer about Sathya Sai Baba can be found here: ** It’s interested to read Josephus’s mention of John the Baptist, where he describes John the Baptist as an important figure in his own right, not some second fiddle to Jesus like in the Gospels:

Question: According to the Bible, the earth is only 6000 years old. How does it explain the 4.49-billion-year gap between that and the actual age of the earth?
Answer: Whenever questions like this pop up, poor Archbishop James Ussher is sure to unfairly come under fire for supposedly inventing the roughly 6000 year old age of the Earth out of some misconceived eccentric interpretation of the Bible. But really, that was a fairly mainstream view of the Bible at the time. While no passage in the Bible gives an explicit date for creation, if you take certain passages at more or less face value, you can come up with a reasonable estimate. Plenty of other scholars besides Ussher came up with their own estimates, and they all clustered around the same ages – either around 5500 BC if using the Septuagint as your basis for scripture (i.e. the Greek Old Testament), or around 4000 BC if using the Masoretic Text (i.e. the authoritative Hebrew version). Wikipedia lists many of these other scholars in its article on Dating creation, and it includes such well known names as Clement of Alexandria, Eusebius of Caesarea, Hillel, Johannes Kepler (yes, that Kepler), and Martin Luther, among many more. You can get a good part of the estimate pretty easily yourself by looking at just a handful of passages: The first two list genealogies from Adam down to Abraham, including the ages of how old the men were when their sons were born. The third states that Abraham was 75 years old when he left Haran for Egypt. The four is an explicit statement of the time the Israelites spent in Egypt before the Exodus, and the fifth is an explicit statement of the time passed from the Exodus until Solomon’s Temple. And that right there is enough to get you from creation to the Bronze Age in roughly 3000 years. Sure, there are a couple ages in there that are slightly ambiguous (particularly Noah and Terah), and also a bit of ambiguity about how long it took Abraham to travel from Haran to Egypt, but you're only looking at a few years of ambiguity there, nothing major. After that is where things get more intricate. You have to scour through the reigns of a bunch of kings of Judah and piece together that history (particularly from Judges, Kings, and Chronicles). And of course, that's exactly what Ussher (and all those other scholars) did, totaling up to around 430 years. That gets you to the accession of the Babylonian king Amel-Marduk, which from other historical sources was known to have taken in place in 562 BC. So, take the 3000 years from Adam to Solomon's temple, the 424 years of kings reigning in Judah, and 562 BC as a reference point, and you end up with a date for creation right around 4000 BC (4004 BC per Ussher). Now, I'm not a believer in the Bible, myself, so I take all this with a grain of salt since I don't think the Bible is a reliable source of history (particularly the older books like Genesis). But for those folks who do take the Bible seriously, this all seems perfectly reasonable. If you want to argue that the Bible doesn't indicate that creation took place in roughly 4000 BC, which of those portions are you willing to say is wrong? The reigns of rulers in Judah? The Exodus story? The otherwise boring and tedious recitation of fathers begetting sons? Given the mainstream view in Ussher's time of trusting the Bible to be historically accurate, I think he made a pretty good go of it. He just made the mistake of using an unreliable reference. (In fact, it’s precisely because he was so diligent and meticulous in his efforts that his particular estimate became one of the most respected in his time, and why it’s still remembered today.) As far as the OP's question about reconciling this age with the more accurate 4.5 billion year age of the Earth, I think the simple answer is that the Bible was a compilation from a more primitive people who simply didn't yet know any better. They certainly weren't dumb. It just takes time for humanity as a whole to build up our knowledge, generation by generation. As the saying goes, we only know as much as we do today thanks to standing on the shoulders of giants. Related:

Question: Why do we call apes ‘monkey’ but not ‘human’?
Answer: This is why technical fields have jargon, to allow for precise, unambiguous definitions, as opposed to normal language, where the meaning of words is a little fuzzier and dependent on individual usage. To introduce some of that technical jargon, different categories of organisms can be either monophyletic, paraphyletic, or polyphyletic. ABOVE SOURCE: Monophyletic, Polyphyletic, & Paraphyletc Taxa (rearranged by me) Monophyletic groups are organisms that all share a common ancestor, and every descendant of that ancestor is also within that group. One example would be mammals. From the very first mammal that evolved, all of its descendants are also mammals. Paraphyletic groups still all share a common ancestor that's considered a part of that group, but among the descendants of that ancestor, some lineage has evolved enough in a different manner that it's considered to no longer be a part of the group. A good example of this is fish. All fish share a common ancestor that's also a fish, but one lineage among its descendants became specialized for life on land, and those animals (tetrapods) are considered different enough to no longer be called fish. ABOVE SOURCE: Surprising new research: We're more like primitive fishes than once believed Polyphyletic groups are groupings that don't necessarily have any particularly recent common ancestry at all. These kinds of groupings can come about for a variety of reasons, such as ‘wastebasket taxons’, where organisms just get thrown in there because they don't fit anywhere else, or examples of convergent evolution, where disparate lineages have developed similar adaptations. A good example of the latter is trees. Perennial plants with an elongated trunk supporting branches or leaves have evolved numerous times in many disparate lineages of plants (e.g. an oak tree is more closely related to a daisy than to a pine tree). So that brings us to monkeys and apes. 'Monkey' and 'ape' are not technical scientific terms, but everyday language. The scientific term, simians or Simiiformes, is precise, and does include all monkeys and apes as a monophyletic group. But what counts as a monkey in everyday language doesn't have a precise definition. Some people consider monkeys to be a paraphyletic group, composed of only the old world monkeys and new world monkeys, but with the apes being different enough to not count as monkeys. Other people (myself included – eventually) think that monkeys should be a monophyletic group, and that apes should just be one branch of specialized monkeys. And then, rather obviously, humans are just one species within those groups. ABOVE SOURCE: Glossary: Primates (with some additions by me) So, as far as everyday language, humans are definitely a kind of ape, but whether you want to also count us as a type of monkey depends on your semantics. But in scientific terms, we definitely are a kind of simian or Simiiforme.

Question: Is it considered rude to be served on paper plates and plastic utensils at a dinner party?
Answer: It depends on the formality of the party and the number of guests. But even then, there are other options besides paper plates. If it's hot dogs and hamburgers from the grill, paper plates are fine. If it's prime rib, roasted potatoes, and grilled asparagus, you'll probably want to serve those on something nicer. If it's a small enough dinner party to where you own enough plates to cover it, go with real plates with real silverware. But if the party gets bigger than that, then it's just a practical matter that you have to do something else. We do this every Christmas and Thanksgiving with my wife's family. She has a pretty big extended family, so these are meals for several dozen people. But we still don't go with paper plates. We try to compromise with 'nice' disposable dinnerware. Something like this, which is actually plastic plates, plastic utensils, and a plastic wine glass: ABOVE SOURCE: Sam's Club But some other family events get hosted by family members not quite as concerned about 'formality'. So then it might be paper plates and regular plastic utensils. And, well, taking the time and spending the money to provide a meal for the whole family is generous enough. Rude would be turning up your nose at that meal because the dinnerware wasn't fancy enough. Basically, if you're doing the hosting yourself, try to use dinnerware that matches the formality of the meal, even if it's disposable. If you're attending an event that somebody else is hosting, appreciate the generosity even if it is paper plates.

Question: Can a Republican ever win the presidency again without some kind of a reset?
Answer: Anyone remember headlines like these from 2008, when Obama had a strong victory and Democrats won a majority in the House and a supermajority in the Senate? Well, it only took until 2010 for the Republicans to win back control of the House, which they held onto for 8 more years until the 2018 election. And while Obama did manage to win re-election in 2012, I think we all remember what happened in 2016. And even in 2020, Trump only lost thanks to about 40 thousand voters in 3 key swing states. Even this year, 538 is currently giving Trump a 40% chance of winning the election, which is barely worse than a coin toss. That's just the nature of our two party system and polarized politics. The Democratic and Republican candidates will always get roughly half the vote. And with the way the electoral college currently biases the results towards rural states that tend to favor Republicans, presidential elections in particular will remain competitive, even when Democrats might have a nationwide advantage in raw numbers. So yes, the Republicans still have a very good chance of winning the presidency even maintaining their current strategies. They have a very good chance of winning this year. So don't get complacent like 2016, thinking a Democratic victory is a sure thing. Everybody needs to get out and vote to make sure their voice is heard.

Question: Will America ever eventually switch to the metric system of measurement for all applications?
Answer: Eh. Maybe eventually. It seems like we're already slowly transitioning that way. There are certain measurements where metric has been used in the U.S. pretty much my whole life – the sciences (especially at universities), electrical power, measuring volumes of beverages (750 ml, 2 liter bottles, etc.). And there are some where I've seen the switch in my lifetime – particularly U.S. automakers – I only need my 'standard' sockets for classic cars, these days. But there are plenty of areas of society that haven't made the switch, and some of those seem like there's a lot of momentum resisting any change. My own field of aerospace engineering is one. With the high levels of regulation involved, including in the supply chains and standardized hardware, it's not easy for any single company to make the jump to metric on their own. Construction seems like another that will be hard to switch, especially since you still have to support maintenance on existing buildings. We're going to need 2x4s, 3/4" water supply lines, and 4"x10" air vents for a while. In fact, talking to a German friend of mine, even Germany still uses inch based measurements for plumbing for backwards compatibility. But I suspect that the U.S. will probably get there eventually, even if it takes a while. Americans are comfortable enough with metric in our lives where it does exist, so there's little incentive to switch those measurements back to USCS. And there is at least some incentive for international commerce and compatibility to switch to metric in the holdouts. In other words, I only see future changes going in one direction – from USCS to metric. So, like I said, it may take a while, but I suspect the eventual end state is complete metrification (or, at least as complete as European countries are today*). *In addition to my friend's comment about Germany using inches for plumbing, there are plenty of not actual metric units that get used in otherwise metric countries, especially when time is involved in those units – things like km/hr (instead of m/s) or kWh (instead of Joules).

Question: Which movie would have been five minutes long if its characters had just been sensible in the first place?
Answer: The low brow guilty pleasure of Dude, Where’s My Car? The entire plot of the movie is driven by the characters not having been sensible the night before, leading to all types of outlandish and bizarre scenarios. Had they just been sensible, they wouldn’t have had any adventures at all. I’ve probably seen this movie more times than any other movie. It’s not that I liked it that much to sit down and watch it start to finish over and over. It’s that right after I graduated from college, one of my roommates figured out how to hack one of the satellite TV services. It was a kludge of a system with a wire running out of the card slot of the satellite receiver and down to a PC set up next to the TV – very nerdy. But for a while there, we got every single channel that the service provided, including pay-per-view. And Dude, Where’s My Car just happened to be playing around the clock on several of the PPV channels at the time. So whenever we had some down time and just wanted to pop something on the TV (especially as this was a couple decades before streaming), and considering that we were a group of guys in our early 20s, this movie was our go-to. So, I’d get 20 minutes here, 20 minutes there, all combining to essentially multiple viewings. Trying to watch it again recently, I can’t say I’m exactly proud of my extensive knowledge of this movie, but it is what it is.

Question: Do you eat the same cake every year for your birthday?
Answer: Yup. Every year that I can remember, as long as I've been alive – wacky cake. ABOVE SOURCE: Wacky Cake - Bake. Eat. Repeat. It was tradition in my family growing up. Everybody else in the family had wacky cake for their birthdays, too. It's a family recipe going back at least to my grandmother. What makes the cake 'wacky' is that it doesn't use any eggs, butter, or milk in the recipe. And the leavening comes from baking powder and vinegar, giving the cake a unique flavor (and a delicious flavor at that – it wouldn’t have become a tradition if the entire family didn’t love it). It was purportedly invented, or at least became popular, during the Great Depression thanks to its lack of hard to find (at the time) ingredients. And although I'm not sure vegan was even a term back when I was growing up, this cake is, in fact, vegan (you just have to be careful about your icing if that’s what you’re going for). I'm not sure I can recall ever seeing wacky cake for sale at a grocery store or a bakery, so it's strictly a homemade dessert, and my wife and daughter have indulged me by baking it for me every year. I suspect I'll keep the tradition going for a while longer. As an aside, if you think it's boring to have the same thing every year, there's still 364 days out of the year to try other desserts, which I do (though truth be told, if a restaurant has crème brûlée on the menu, it's hard to pass it up to try something else). Question: Do you think there is a unique atheist approach to morality, or do atheists simply adhere to the same moral code as everyone else?
Answer: I'd actually put it the other way around. I think that religious folks, despite often paying lip service to their religion or taking a few superficial rules from their scriptures, actually develop their moral code the same way as everyone else. Do you really need the Bible telling you that murder is wrong to avoid wanting to kill people? I don't mean in a 'ha-ha' hyperbolic sort of way, but the thought of literally taking somebody's life and living with that on your conscience. For most people, being averse to murder is just a part of human nature, independent of whatever religion they were raised in or lack thereof. On the other hand, do you agree that it's immoral to sell your daughter into slavery? Or simply to own slaves in general? Probably, even though the Bible says those things are perfectly fine. It merely sets some rules around those practices to keep them from becoming excessively bad, but even the New Testament has a passage instructing slaves to be loyal to their masters - 1 Peter 2:18. So, where do people get morality? It's a combination of innate instincts and human nature in things like empathy and fairness, built upon by social mores that we learn as we grow up, and perhaps even a bit of philosophy for the people who think about it a lot. If you're raised in a religious community, you may acquire the specific social mores of that community, but it's still the same general process as folks outside that community.

Question: If Christianity is wrong, then why do people believe in it?
Answer: Before getting into the why, let's get a little perspective. Here is the breakdown of global religious affiliation: SOURCE: The Changing Global Religious Landscape That's a lot of diversity of religions, and none of them are believed by a majority of the world's population. And since many of these religions are mutually contradictory, it stands to reason that most of them are wrong. So, your question isn't just applicable to Christianity. It's applicable to all religions. Why do people believe them, when logically, most of them must be wrong? A big reason is the cognitive bias that Deborah Kelemen has coined 'promiscuous teleology', which is a tendency to see purpose and intention even when it's not really there. Here's an explanation from one paper on the topic, Teleology and the intentions of supernatural agents: Given that according to PT [promiscuous teleology], teleological reasoning develops from an early understanding of intentionality which is then overextended (Kelemen, 1999a), the notion of agency is central to teleology. This is because the only things capable of having intentions are things with minds, and the only things with minds are agents. In this view, just as “chairs are for sitting on” is true only if an agent intends the chair to serve this function, the statement “clouds rain so that plants can grow” is based in the misbelief that plants growing is the intended function of the cloud raining. The difference between these two teleological explanations is that whereas the former implies the intentions of a natural agent (a human), the latter seems to imply the intentions of a supernatural agent. And here's the abstract from a different paper, Promiscuous Teleology: From Childhood Through Adulthood and from West to East: From infancy we continually try to make sense of what goes on around us. One strategy in making sense of things is to look for how things might be purposeful or designed. So useful is this strategy that sometimes it gets overused—what Deborah Keleman calls promiscuous teleology . This chapter reviews research with children and adults across cultures—including recent work in China —that demonstrates that promiscuous teleology is a conceptual default that all peoples share but that may be tamped down through enculturation. Kelemen argues that this teleological reasoning makes certain religious ideas about supernatural agents’ activity in creating or ordering the world largely intuitive. Or to summarize all that, our tendency to see agency everywhere makes us prone to supernatural explanations. Now, there are further questions as to why we might have evolved this cognitive bias in the first place. As I noted in another answer, "There are various explanations for why we might have evolved this bias – from being social animals and having to understand intentions of our fellow humans, to being prodigious tool makers and having an instinctual sense of 'function' for items. And there's no reason the explanations need to be mutually exclusive. (And even all that is assuming it's an adaptive trait, and not just a spandrel of San Marco.)" Add in how children credulously accept lessons from their parents (and understandably so – there's too much knowledge to pass down any other way), and culture, and how these stories morph and change over the generations, and you've got the perfect recipe for a large diversity of supernatural stories to explain various aspects of our world. Christianity just happens to be one of these myths among many.

Question: Why is the Francesinha the world's best sandwich?
Answer: This question contains a fallacy, and so it can’t be answered as asked. Now, I’d never heard of the Francesinha before coming across this question. So if you’re like me and had similarly never heard of it, here’s what this dish looks like: And admittedly, that does look pretty darn good. But I’m also not going to call it a sandwich. Sandwiches are meant to be eaten with your hands. That’s kind of the whole point from the very earliest times when the Earl of Sandwich invented them. If you need a knife and a fork to eat a food, that’s not a sandwich. I mean, you could put your bacon in between your French toast, but that wouldn’t make it a sandwich. So however good a Francesinha might taste, it can’t take the title for world’s best sandwich*. So what is the best sandwich? Man, there are just way too many choices to narrow it down to one. You’ve got everything from hoagies to BLTs to Reubens to club sandwiches to Bánh mì to panini to tortas to cheesesteaks to Primanti’s and on and on and on. Heck, on a cold day after playing out in the snow, a simple grilled cheese with a bowl of tomato soup can’t be beat. ABOVE: Philly Hoagie SOURCE: The 14 Best Hoagies In Philadelphia - Philadelphia - The Infatuation ABOVE: My favorite torta place from El Paso SOURCE: rainbow fountain tortas - Google Search ABOVE: A Pittsburgh staple from Primanti Brothers SOURCE: Primanti Brothers - Pittsburgh, PA | Review & What to Eat So I’m not even going to try to pick a single best sandwich. There are just too many delicious options available. *Even going with the Sandwich Alignment Chart, the only way a Francesinha could qualify as a sandwich is in the bottom right hand corner with Radical Sandwich Anarchy, since you have an egg and sauce as the outermost ingredients. ETA: After a discussion in the comments, if you really wanted to make an actual sandwich out of a Francesinha, you could take the base sandwich at the core of the dish, put the cheese and egg inside the bread (or leave the egg off if you don’t like it), and then put the tomato and beer sauce in a container on the side to dip your sandwich into (kind of like a French dip). Question: ‘After-birth abortion’: Are they serious?
Answer: Well, if you look at the actual situations where this is being discussed rather than just fear mongering about imaginary situations, then yes. Nobody wants to kill a healthy late term fetus or newborn. No woman goes through 9 months of pregnancy just to decide at the last minute that she's changed her mind. And certainly no doctor would kill a healthy newborn baby after the entire process of labor or a Caesarean delivery. But not all fetuses and newborns are healthy. Hopefully, with good pre-natal care, any major complications will be detected early. But not everybody has access to the best pre-natal care, and even then, some complications simply don't get detected until late into the pregnancy. And some of these complications are euphemistically referred to as "incompatible with life". In other words, they're complications so severe that the baby won't survive even with the best medical treatment available. Trying to treat these conditions will only delay the inevitable and prolong the suffering. So, the question becomes, what truly is the most humane and merciful course of action in these cases? Prolonging suffering, or doing what you can to ease the pain and try to end the suffering as soon as possible? In another recent answer, Jeff Lewis's answer to Democrats support post-birth abortion, but isn’t abortion after birth just murder?, I discussed a study that polled "physicians and paramedical professionals involved in late TOP [termination of pregnancy] decision‐making in all eight centers with a Neonatal Intensive Care Unit in Flanders, Belgium (N = 117)". As I pointed out in that answer, "These aren't folks for whom this question is a mere hypothetical. They have to see the consequences and suffering of the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit on a daily basis." And such health care professionals were overwhelmingly in favor of "actively terminat[ing] life" for newborns with serious enough conditions. And while the support for feticide wasn't quite so overwhelming, a majority still supported feticide over palliative care in serious enough cases. So yes, sometimes the humane and merciful choice is to end a poor newborn's suffering. It's a tragedy, and would be absolutely gut wrenching to the parents (and the doctors – they're humans, too). But the alternative is just forcing the newborn to suffer longer before still eventually dying. Seriously, these are profound and extremely serious situations that some families find themselves in. Let's not take away the merciful options in an already shitty situation just so we can shout some slogans to win political points. ETA: After some feedback in the comments, I want to be very clear on this. I'm talking about newborns with severe complications and no chance of recovery. The question is what’s best for these babies, which has to be looked at on a case by case basis. Is there any quality of life at all, or just suffering? Palliative care and hospice are already available for newborns with severe complications, ranging from not attempting to treat the condition, to withholding nutrition. And quite obviously, such infants will die. But with their condition, they would have died anyway. It certainly can't be considered more humane to prolong their suffering. And that leads into the debate raised in this question, although the OP seemed disingenuous in how they framed it, of whether active feticide is an appropriate approach for these babies, or if the current standard of palliative care is sufficient (and I really, really hope you're not against palliative care – who would actually push for making babies suffer even more). As I said in my prior answer, "I understand people's hesitancy to enable doctor's to actively end the life of patients as opposed to mere palliative care, especially in the case of patients who are too young to voice their own desires." So the question comes down to balancing the best interests of babies with such severe complications vs. how comfortable we are with intentionally taking steps to end a life. Minimizing the suffering for these babies as much as possible would require active feticide. Palliative care allows people to have an easier conscience, but forces the babies to suffer a bit longer. Active attempts to treat such conditions would prolong the suffering the longest. And as I pointed out in my answer, these aren't just hypotheticals. There are real, non-thought experiment babies suffering in NICUs right now, with parents agonizing over their decisions.

Question: What accidents or incidents have you personally had with deep fryers?
Answer: Back when I was in high school, I got a job at KFC. There was a certain minimum level for the shortening in the pressure fryers, but they never actually gave us any formal training on proper technique to add more. The method I developed for myself was to cut off a chunk of shortening (it was solid at room temperature), then stab that chunk with the knife, and lower it down into the fryer. That seemed better to me than just throwing the chunk in there and having the hot grease splash. Well, one day, I had a just gotten a big chunk of shortening over the fryer when it fell off of the knife, and sent a huge splash of grease up at my head. I managed to turn to the side and close my eyes, but the grease got half of my face. I immediately went to the sink in the kitchen, and began running cold water over my face. The manager didn't seem to quite know what to do, and couldn't get a hold of my parents, so eventually, somebody gave me a ride home. When I did get home, my parents were out in the yard working (why they never heard the phone – this was a bit before cell phones), and were quite surprised to see me, especially with half my face burnt. So they immediately threw me into the car and drove me to the ER. The ER took me in right away (no waiting around like when you've merely got the sniffles), took me straight to a room, and then promptly treated me with nothing fancier than cold washcloths. Really, that was the only treatment – a basin of ice water with a few washcloths soaking in it, that my mom would swap out when the one on my face started to warm up too much. After a couple hours to draw out as much heat as possible, they sent me on my way with referrals for follow ups. Over the next few days, my face started to look bad. Luckily, it was mostly 'just' second degree burns. But once those blisters started popping and oozing puss all over my face, I was not a pretty sight. One of those referrals was a plastic surgeon, but the only real treatment I needed was bacitracin to prevent infection. All this happened just a couple weeks before graduation. Any open wounds had mostly healed in time, but the skin was still pretty tender, and I was supposed to keep out of the sun. So, I went everywhere with a wide brimmed hat, and avoided sitting out under the sun for all of the graduation rehearsals. I also avoided shaving, so I had that just wrong 17 year old level of stubble – more scruffy than rugged. A couple friends and I had also planned a cross country road trip right after graduation, which meant upgrading our provisional drivers licenses to full licenses, so we wouldn't have any restrictions driving during the trip. Oh man was that a horrible drivers license photo, between the scruff, red face, and completely unkempt hair once I took off the wide brimmed hat. Whenever anybody complained about a bad drivers license photo, I always had them beat (and they always agreed). Thankfully, I only developed a few minor scars, that weren't even that obvious when I was clean shaven, but are now completely hidden by my (adult) beard. Anyway, I was more careful adding shortening after that. I even got workman’s comp out of it.

Question: What's your go-to healthy snack when cravings hit?
Answer: Single serve bags of potato chips: Because let's be frank. When it's an honest to goodness craving, rabbit food just isn't going to cut it. I see a bunch of other answers here trying to promote 'healthy' snacks, and while all those would be fine under normal circumstances when you’re merely peckish, they're just not going to satisfy a craving the same way junk food will. And I've tried. You eat the healthy alternative, and you're not satiated. You just want more. And if you eat enough until you're full, you've just eaten more calories without actually satisfying the craving. But a single serve bag of potato chips is only 1 oz of food, and only 160 calories. Sure, it's not the best thing to eat all the time. But every once in a while? That's not going to kill you. And it will actually satisfy your craving with all that starchy, greasy, salty goodness. And the fact that it's in a single serving bag makes portion control that much easier. With a full size bag, it's easy to just keep going back for one more chip, one more chip, one more chip, until eventually you've eaten a lot more than you should have. But if you know the one small bag is all you get, you eat your one serving and stop. The whole point is that a healthy diet is all about balance and moderation. And abstinence will just lead to worse cravings, or even falling off the healthy diet altogether. No single food in moderation is going to be all that bad for you. Just make sure to balance it out with enough other types of food to have a healthy diet overall. On days when the cravings aren't quite so bad to give in to potato chips, my next go-tos are pickles and olives (or olive salad on crackers). You still get enough saltiness to help satisfy the craving (and the olive oil from the olives), but not too terrible on the calories. After that is probably pita chips. Still starchy and salty, but not quite as greasy as the chips.

Question: Is it common for American people to say "I've met him one time" or "I've met him once"?
Answer: I don’t think there’s much difference in usage between “one time” or “once”. The bigger question is whether someone would use present perfect tense as you have here (“I’ve met…”) vs. simple past tense (“I met…”). This is just me giving my opinion as a plain old American, not a linguist, but I went over a few scenarios in my head, and the more I thought about it, the more complicated it got. But the main thing seems to be whether you’re referring to a specific event in the past, or just a general state of things. And using either term, “once” or “one time” tends to imply a specific event, so you’d be more likely to use the simple perfect tense, “I met.” But even then, there’s nuance. For example: Have you met John? Yeah. I met him once. You probably have the meeting in mind, so simple past tense seems most appropriate. You could say “I’ve met him once”, but that’s implicitly emphasizing the “once”, implying that it wasn’t twice or three times or some other number. If you don’t quite recall exactly when you met somebody, you’d probably use the present perfect tense to indicate the general state of a non-specific meeting having taken place. Though since this is no longer in reference to a specific event, you’d probably be more likely to use “before” instead of “once”. Have you met John? Yeah. I’ve met him before. - Have you met John? Yeah. I think I’ve met him before. You could use “once” instead of “before”, and it wouldn’t sound awful. It’s just not quite as natural. And just for good measure, here are a few more examples. These first two are in reference to specific events, so you use the simple past tense: That guy over there is John. Yeah. I already met him earlier tonight. - That guy over there is John. Yeah. I already met him at the last party. While this next one is in reference to a general state, so you use present perfect: That guy over the is John. Yeah. We’ve already met. Anyway, using either “one time” or “once” isn’t a big deal, nor is the present perfect tense vs. the simple perfect tense. But to sound the most natural (at least in the dialect I grew up speaking), in general, use “once” or “one time” in combination with the simple past tense when you’re referring to a specific event. Use the present perfect and a different modifier like “before” when you’re referring to a non-specific state.

Question: Evolution survival of the fittest, and organism get better adapted to their environment. Then how do we say that humans evolved, as humans are less fit to the than other animals. Humans need to protect themselves from the environment artificially?
Answer: 'Artificial' is an (ahem) artificial distinction. When we humans adjust our environments or make tools, we call it artificial. But when other animals do it, we call it natural. But from a beaver's point of view, if they were smart enough to think such things, they might consider their dams and lodges to be artificial, while other animals' constructions would be 'natural', seeing the huts of those weird hairless apes not much differently than they'd see a bee hive or a bird's nest. ABOVE: Beaver Lodge SOURCE: Beaver lodge ABOVE: Polar Bear Den SOURCE: Polar Bear Dens - Churchill Polar Bears ABOVE: Castings of ant colonies SOURCE: A Review of Ant Nests and Their Implications for Architecture I don't know of any animals that do anything quite like human clothing, but you do get critters like hermit crabs that do something somewhat similar, wearing shells to protect their bodies. ABOVE: A hermit crab in a glass shell SOURCE: Hermit Crab Shells made of Blown Glass And tool use in animals has become so well documented that it really isn't all that shocking, anymore. ABOVE: A chimp using a stick as a tool to catch ants SOURCE: Chimpanzee - Intelligence, Tool Use, Social Behavior Yes. Humans take all these things to an extreme not seen in other animals. But, especially with the smarter animals that aren't acting on mere instinct, it's more of a difference in magnitude than a difference in kind. And some animal is bound to be the 'most' anything, anyway. Just like cheetahs are the fastest runners, and free-tailed bats are the fastest flyers*, we humans are the most prolific tool users. That's simply the niche we evolved into. *Peregrine falcons may fall the fastest on a regular basis, but then even I could be the fastest if I just jumped out of a plane from high enough. Free-tailed bats are the fastest measured so far in level flight. Of course, a few birds like swifts are also pretty fast – getting reliable measurements is the challenge.

Question: Why are first class passengers boarded first? Since their seat is guaranteed, I thought they would want to board last and not have to sit there as everyone loaded past them.
Answer: I've only been upgraded to first class a handful of times, and usually fly coach, but I still prefer to get onto the plane as early as possible. The main reason is simply peace of mind. I can quit paying attention to the boarding process and that looming sensation of having an unfinished task and just settle in. From then on, I can just relax and take a nap, read a book, watch a movie, or anything else I want to do. And once my head is buried in the book, I don’t notice the people filing past, anyway. On top of that, you've got the additional peace of mind of knowing that there will be space to stow your luggage in an overhead bin and not get stuck doing a valet checked bag, and then get stuck waiting around for the bag after the flight. And the few times I have flown first class, they'll even bring you a drink as soon as you sit down (gin & tonic is my go to in first class – it just feels a touch more appropriate than a beer). I'm not sure what a guaranteed seat has to do with it. All of the seats are already guaranteed, and the airlines I fly on have assigned seating, so I know what seat I'm going to get before I even arrive at the airport. But yeah. The main thing is just peace of mind to get settled in early. And since it doesn't cost the airline anything at all to adjust boarding priority, they offer that as a perk to higher paying / loyal customers*. *And yeah, those loyalty programs do make a difference. Living near DFW, I fly mostly American, and so have a decent priority status. Last time I flew a different airline, I was one of the last people on the plane, and I did get worried about fitting my luggage on board. So, as long as the company is paying for my travel, I try to stick to American to get my perks.

Question: Why did Tim Walz put female tampons and pads in the boys washroom?
Answer: I have to say, this is one of the stranger tempests in a teapot I've seen in a while. The reality seems like such a mundane law (albeit very beneficial) that I’m surprised it’s managed to draw this much attention. But while most of the manufactured controversy came out of the right-wing, some left-wing responses have also been a bit more rationalization after the fact rather than what the law originally intended, and based more around conjecture than what's actually going on in Minnesota (i.e. it didn't have anything to do with logistics). So first – the civics lessons. Tim Walz didn't write this law. He didn't campaign on it or provide a draft for the legislature to act on. The law was originally sponsored by Sandra Feist in the Minnesota House, in a standalone bill, HF 44 , and then got included in the much larger Education Finance Bill, HF 2497. After going through the full process in the Minnesota House and Senate, the Education Finance Bill was eventually approved by majorities in both chambers, and so Tim Walz signed it into law. But this whole initiative of providing menstrual products to student was never something that Walz himself led. The main purpose of the law originally proposed by Feist is to provide menstrual products to students. This isn't some revolutionary idea new to Minnesota. There are similar laws on the books in 28 states and D.C. to address what some describe as "period poverty". According to Period Products in Schools, 1 in 4 students struggle to afford such products. And one study of a program in NYC found a 2.4% increase in attendance when free period products were offered to students. As one of the students who testified in the Minnesota House during a hearing on the legislation put it, "We cannot learn while we are leaking" (source: Minnesota may soon OK free menstrual products in schools. These teens led the way). ABOVE SOURCE: Period Products in Schools - Alliance for Period Supplies If you want to read the law for yourself, go to the full text of HF2497. It's easy to find the relevant portions. Just do a search for 'menstrual'. Here's the main portion: ARTICLE 1 GENERAL EDUCATION Section 1. [121A.212] ACCESS TO MENSTRUAL PRODUCTS. A school district or charter school must provide students with access to menstrual products at no charge. The products must be available to all menstruating students in restrooms regularly used by students in grades 4 to 12 according to a plan developed by the school district. For purposes of this section, "menstrual products" means pads, tampons, or other similar products used in connection with the menstrual cycle. There's another passage specifying that the budget for this will be "$2 times the adjusted pupil units of the school district for the school year", and another passage including these menstrual products in a list of allowed purposes for "Total operating capital revenue". Note that there's no mandate that tampons have to be supplied in the boys restroom. However, the language was gender neutral, allowing for discretion at the local levels for schools to implement this law. And that gender neutral language was on purpose. According to Feist, the sponsor of the original bill: While the vast majority of the period products will be used in the girls’ bathrooms, the decision was made to structure the bill as gender-inclusive in order to ensure that trans and nonbinary students who menstruate would have equal access to the products they need. SOURCE: Yes, Tim Walz signed a law requiring Minnesota public schools to provide free tampons in school bathrooms Also, as noted in the article, Why Republicans are calling Walz 'Tampon Tim' — and why Democrats embrace it, there was opposition to this gender inclusivity when "Some Minnesota Republicans initially tried to limit the initiative to female-assigned and gender-neutral bathrooms, but were unsuccessful." However, it's interesting to note that the Republican who proposed that amendment did go on to support the final bill, as he felt the overall issue was important, and not worth killing over that compromise. It’s also worth pointing out that schools are free to come up with their own plans to implement the law. According to an editorial from the Minnesota based Star Tribune, A reality check on the ‘Tampon Tim’ meme: At Anoka-Hennepin, the state’s largest school district, the free products are not found in traditional male-only bathrooms, a spokesman said. But they are provided for free to all in “nongendered bathrooms,” girls’ bathrooms or from health staffers. I can't say that absolutely no schools in Minnesota have provided tampons in the boys room, but if the largest school district in the state isn't doing so, it's obviously not a requirement of the law, so long as transgender students can still receive menstrual products if they need them. So basically, Tim Walz signed a large law that had a bunch of different sections dealing with multiple aspects of education funding. Among these was a requirement to provide tampons to students for free, which seems utterly reasonable to me. The language was made specifically gender neutral, allowing individual schools to implement the law as they saw fit, so long as they were still complying and supporting all students who needed menstrual products, which also seems pretty reasonable to me. And just to be clear, the law doesn't actually force schools to provide tampons in the boys room, and as proven in practice, at least one school district cited in the news hasn't.

Question: Is English considered a foreign language to the US? Why can't most Americans speak English fluently or even close? As someone who has been learning English for about 3 months, I probably speak much better English than most Americans. Why?
Answer: I'm going to focus on this part of your question: As someone who has been learning English for about 3 months, I probably speak much better English than most Americans. No, you don't. I studied Spanish pretty extensively in high school and college, to the point of being only 2 classes away from a Spanish minor*. I could speak fairly fluently. Then, after I graduated, I met the woman who was to become my wife, who happens to be Mexican with a large Mexican family (all living in the U.S.). I could catch them making grammatical 'errors' that weren't 'proper' Spanish**, and I could definitely spell Spanish words better than them (they mostly grew up in the U.S., so didn't have much formal education in Spanish). But my way of speaking Spanish was much more academic and stuffy, and just didn't flow the same way. Nobody would have confused me as speaking better Spanish than native speakers who had been speaking it their entire lives. Going the other way, I once made a business trip to China, and during the one day we set aside for sight seeing, I was approached by an old Chinese guy who wanted to speak to me in English, who turned out to be a retired English teacher. In other words, he was such an expert in the English language among the Chinese that he was teaching others how to speak English. But his English wasn't exactly the best. Don't get me wrong, his English was far better than my non-existent skills in Chinese, but it seemed obvious that he'd probably never been outside China and gotten to practice with actual native speakers. Even a lifetime of academic study isn't enough to make someone speak as well as a native speaker. Now, I really suspect you're a troll and not somebody who just began studying English 3 months ago. But people who aren't native speakers have to study a long, long, long time to become as proficient at the language as native speakers. And it really requires immersion in the culture, hearing the language day in and day out to pick up all the nuances and informalities that you simply can't completely learn any other way. On the off chance that you really are new to studying English, learn a bit of humility like I did when I met my wife’s family. Academic English is not the way real people speak, and it’s going to take a lot more than three months of studying in a school environment before you sound natural. *The reason I didn't just tack on two more classes was because I was already taking one Spanish class my final semester, and another two would have given me a very full load. So, instead, I tacked on a semester of Italian to learn a bit more of a different language. I figured the actual skill would serve me better than an additional piece of paper. **I put grammatical 'errors' in scare quotes, because I've come around to the idea of grammar being descriptive, not prescriptive. Who gets to decide what's proper and what's not. Where do they get off thinking they have that authority? Language has been around for far longer than scholars to study it, and people did just fine.

Question: Democrats support post-birth abortion, but isn’t abortion after birth just murder?
Answer: What I think is enlightening is the opinion of medical professionals who actually have to deal with such situations on a regular basis. Here's a study from just a few years ago: This poll "was conducted among all physicians and paramedical professionals involved in late TOP [termination of pregnancy] decision‐making in all eight centers with a Neonatal Intensive Care Unit in Flanders, Belgium (N = 117)". These aren't folks for whom this question is a mere hypothetical. They have to see the consequences and suffering of the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit on a daily basis. When posed with the statement, "For newborn children presenting a serious condition it is, in certain cases, acceptable to actively terminate life", a full 89.1% of all such health care professionals agreed, rising to 93.6% among the physicians. On a separate but related statement over methods, "Feticide is to be preferred to palliative care", majorities still favored the active approach – 57.8% of all health care professionals, 53.2% of the physicians. I understand people's hesitancy to enable doctor's to actively end the life of patients as opposed to mere palliative care, especially in the case of patients who are too young to voice their own desires. But extending a baby's life in certain serious cases isn't mercy or caring. It's only prolonging their suffering while delaying the inevitable. FWIW, most people in the general public, Democrats and Republicans, Pro-Choice and Anti-Choice, don't hold the same views as the medical professionals. The vast majority of the general public is opposed to late term abortions, and the idea of feticide is so taboo that you don't even find polls that ask about it.

Question: Is reheating leftovers in a microwave good or bad?
Answer: It depends on the food and your own taste buds. For me, they're fine for 'wet' foods, like mashed potatoes, macaroni and cheese, soups, etc. They're not so great for foods that need a crunchy or dry texture, like the breading on fried chicken, or the crust of a pizza. Microwaves tend to make such foods soggy, and, in my opinion, worse than just eating those foods cold. If you feel the need to reheat foods like that, you're better off using an oven, convection oven, or stovetop. If you're somehow worried about health risks because microwaves emit electromagnetic radiation, just remember that a light bulb also emits electromagnetic radiation. Microwaves are just a longer wavelength than visible light, which works out better for penetrating a bit more beneath the surface of food to excite the water molecules to heat them up. But a sufficiently powerful light bulb (or better yet, a heat lamp) will also heat up food just from visible light. Microwaves are no more dangerous to your food than shining a flashlight onto it or eating food in broad daylight. ABOVE: Microwaves are actually lower energy waves than visible light. It's the other end of the electromagnetic spectrum, with x-rays and gamma rays, where you have to worry about ionizing radiation SOURCE: Electromagnetic Spectrum - Introduction So, for the right kinds of food, microwaves do just fine for re-heating.

Question: When and how were you first introduced to the concepts of intelligent design and creationism? What was your initial reaction to these ideas?
Answer: I actually can pinpoint this, because I was (thankfully) raised in a reasonably well educated and scientifically literate family, while going to a mainstream Catholic church that didn't really discuss issues of basic science, so evolution was just taken for granted for pretty much all of my childhood. If you want to put it in a less positive light, you might say I was a bit sheltered. My very first inkling that there were such people came in my high school biology class. We were getting ready to start the unit on evolution, when the kid sitting next to me leaned over to ask if I actually believed in evolution. I was taken a bit off guard. That's kind of like asking if you actually believe the world is a globe. But of course, I answered yes. He responded that he didn't, because there were "too many holes" (and yes, I still remember those exact words, because it really was surprising for me at the time to hear someone doubt accepted mainstream science). Anyway, we didn't really discuss it again after that. I just assumed he hadn't watched as many nature documentaries as I had, and that after everything we learned in class and how obvious evolution seemed, surely all his 'holes' must have been filled in. Fast forward several more years to my first job out of college. This was a white collar office job full of other college educated professionals. Around the water cooler one day, one guy mentioned that he thought the Earth was only a few thousand years old. A few of us started laughing thinking that he was joking, because we'd never heard anybody say anything that outlandish about the age of the Earth before. But no, he informed us. He was quite sincere, and there were actually a lot of other folks who believed the same thing he did. He told us to go look up "young Earth" on the Internet (this was back in the early 2000s, so Internet was a thing by then, if not quite as mature as today). So during my lunch break that day, I did. And I was quite surprised at the extent of information I found about Young Earth Creationism. But I still didn't dig too deep, just yet. I thought of the belief as a bit eccentric, kind of like folks who believed they could invent perpetual motion machines, but I didn't comprehend just how widespread it was. Less than a year later, I moved down to a small town in Texas for a new job. As you might expect, creationism was quite a bit more prominent there than inside the D.C. beltway. This was also around the time that Intelligent Design was hitting its peak popularity, with the landmark Kitzmiller decision set to take place in 2005. That's when I really began to pay attention and look into the statistics. And I must say, I really was shocked that nearly half of Americans rejected evolution in favor of creationism. ABOVE: A slim majority of Americans accept evolution (33% + 22%), and the numbers are slowly improving, but the number who reject evolution is still shockingly high SOURCE: Evolution, Creationism, Intelligent Design So, my first minor introductions to creationism came in my high school biology class, and then water cooler talk at my first real job, but it was the move to Texas coinciding with the rising popularity of Intelligent Design that truly got me caught up in the evolution vs. creationism culture wars. And given the religious side of the debate, it also prompted me to dig deeper into my own religious beliefs, which is actually one of the early factors that set me on the path to atheism (though certainly not the only one). Anyway, I really do find evolution quite fascinating, and I'm not sure I would have delved into it quite as deeply if not for the religious controversy. So I suppose that in a way, I have creationists to thank for motivating me to learn as much about evolution as I have (and further, for helping to nudge me towards atheism, which as I’ve said before here on Quora, I find much more fulfilling than Christianity).

Question: Do we actually need to learn about Math at school? Don’t calculators already exist? In my honest opinion, I feel like years of our lives could’ve already been saved if we just used a damn calculator.
Answer: As I like to somewhat jokingly say, I'm good at math, but not so great with numbers. Calculators handle arithmetic, which is just about the very lowest level of math. You should have mastered that by elementary school and moved on to more advanced math by middle school. At the very least, you should have studied algebra, geometry, and trigonometry by the time you graduated from high school. And even that's barely scratching the surface of the topics you can study in math. As an engineer, I'm nowhere near on par with actual mathematicians, but even I got into topics like calculus, differential equations, and complex numbers. It's kind of like studying language arts. You should have gotten the basics of penmanship and basic literacy in elementary school to form a minimal foundation. Then you move on to more advanced topics as you get older, until eventually you're writing essays and research papers, where you barely even think about the fact that you need to know how to spell or form basic sentences. Such basic tasks are taken for granted. The basic tasks of arithmetic that calculators can handle are the equivalent of being able to write out a sentence. Sure, we've got calculators and Excel for the grunt-work of churning numbers. But you still need an education in math to understand all the concepts behind it to make sense of what your spreadsheet is telling you (and even to build your spreadsheets in the first place). I will grant you something, though. Since calculators and computers are so ubiquitous these days, there isn’t really the need to spend so much time on arithmetic. You still need to understand it at a basic level, but this should free up teachers to start getting into the more advanced and fun topics earlier, so that students can be exposed to more math in the time available in school.

Question: When will kitchens become obsolete? I read an article about how builders are now building new homes without kitchens because cooking is becoming a thing of the past. Most people just order delivery for every meal, so why waste space on a kitchen?
Answer: My wife and I have been casually looking at new houses in expectation of an upcoming move. And in the U.S., at least, the idea of kitchens disappearing couldn't be further from the truth. Kitchens in new houses are far grander than the houses when I was growing up in the '80s & '90s. Back then, kitchens were still mainly about cooking, isolated from the rest of the house, with maybe some space for a small table for the family to eat around. And while the running joke even back then was that everybody always congregated in the kitchen, kitchens simply weren't big enough to accommodate big groups. For example, here's the kitchen in my grandparent's old house, built in the '50s (with an obvious face lift since then, but still the same layout). Even in that small space, they raised a family with 4 kids, and my grandmother made plenty of holiday meals. Only back when my grandparents lived there, they even had a kitchen table stuffed in there where the butcher block rolling island is now. Obviously, that's not a kitchen that can handle a big crowd. ABOVE SOURCE: realtor.com (which is awesome for finding pictures of homes you remember from your childhood that are no longer in the family) With present day lifestyles, kitchens have become hubs of social activity. The typical layout is to have a combined open area for the kitchen, informal dining area, and family room, so that the kitchen isn't isolated from the rest of the house. It's also typical for the kitchen to have a large island or bar top, so that people can sit around the outskirts of the kitchen socializing. Here's one example from a brand new house in the Dallas-Fort Worth area. Notice how the kitchen is open to the family room, and the large island and chairs for people who want to hang out at the kitchen. Admittedly, this house is pretty big, but the open concept is typical in most new houses. Sure, if I do a google search for "new houses built without kitchen", I see plenty of articles discussing this idea. But these articles seem to focus on the novelty of the idea, and how the idea of a kitchen-less house seems almost shocking. And the reason it seems so shocking is because most of us really do want kitchens. Even if Americans are eating out or ordering in more than we used to, it's not every single meal. You still need to at least be able to fry an egg for a weekend breakfast, make a sandwich for a lunch, or even just reheat leftovers for a late night snack. Even if a handful of builders are experimenting with eliminating kitchens, I doubt it's a trend that's going to catch on. If the DFW housing market is anything to go by, kitchens are just getting fancier and fancier.

Question: If the weight of a body in water is 12N and weight of liquid displaced by the body is 8N, then what is the weights of that object in air?
Answer: This is a bit of a trick question. To overcomplicate it a bit, here are free body diagrams comparing when the object is underwater vs. above water (with the force arrows obviously not drawn to scale): Weight is the same in each case. And of course that has to be the case, since weight is defined as W=mg. As long as the mass didn’t change, and you’re conducting these experiments from roughly the same location on Earth (so that g doesn’t change), the weight won’t change, either. Sure, if you wanted to be very precise about the net force, you could calculate the exact buoyancy force (hint: you should know or at least be able to look up the densities of water and air). But given that water is roughly 800 times denser than air, you know that the buoyancy force from air is going to be pretty negligible. Weight doesn’t change even when other forces are acting on an object. Buoyancy may change the net force, but not the weight.

Question: Hypothetically, let's say there is a world where Christianity is backed by mountains of evidence and all the stories of the Bible are verifiable and proven, would you still follow the teachings of Christianity or choose to live your own life?

Just to go with one example, are we going with the God of Exodus 20:5-6, who threatens "punishing children for the iniquity of parents to the third and the fourth generation," or the God of Ezekiel 18:19-20, who says that "A child shall not suffer for the iniquity of a parent nor a parent suffer for the iniquity of a child; the righteousness of the righteous shall be their own, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be their own"? Because the former seems quite barbaric and not at all worthy of worship. The latter at least seems fair. Still, though, the overall portrayal of God in the Bible is not particularly flattering. You've got the massacre of Noah's Flood with its drowning of infants and children, the horrific treatment of Egyptian commoners and their slaves in the Exodus story (Jeff Lewis's answer to Can you cite the verses of some morality flaws in the Bible?), and then the whole fiery furnace of Hell for the grave sin of doubt. And that's just scratching the surface. So, given all the contradictions within the Bible, even as a hypothetical, you can't imagine a scenario where all of it was proven true. But even going with the overall general portrayal of God in the Bible, he's not a being deserving of worship.
