Question: Why is childhood considered the best time in life if you couldn't drink beer, alcohol, had no money and intimacy with women?
Answer: I don't agree with the premise. Being an adult is better than being a child. Don't get me wrong. I had a great childhood. But you just don't have the agency, capabilities, or skills as a child that you do as an adult. For example, one of my favorite toys as a kid was Legos. I never followed any kits or instructions, but just built whatever I could imagine. But at the end of the day, my creations were still just toys, with very little practical utility. But now as an adult, I'm an honest to goodness engineer. I have the knowledge and skills to design complex machinery, and (through my job, at least) the connections and resources to have those designs turned into reality, far exceeding anything I could have built out of Legos as a kid. Even at home, I have a variety of hand tools and power tools and the experience and skills using them to do all manner of projects that I couldn't have accomplished as a kid with construction paper and scissors. I actually just helped my daughter renovate an entire house, including framing, wiring, plumbing, etc. Finishing a home renovation is much more fulfilling than arts and crafts time. There's also my understanding of the world in general. I read a lot of children's science magazines when I was younger, which were all 'dumbed down' to a child's ability to understand. I don't have to settle for as watered down explanations, any more. I can understand articles targeted towards adults, and in certain fields, even the primary literature. And then there's the agency, of having control over your own life. Sure, it comes with more responsibility. But it also comes with more sense of pride in your accomplishments, not to mention the freedom to do what you want to do. You can also add in maturity and perspective, and the peace of mind that brings. You don't get so caught up in peer pressure or social cliques (the middle school years are especially bad for this). And then you get into things like you mentioned in the question – alcohol, the discretionary income that comes with a career, and the intimacy I share with my wife. Those just drive home the point of how much better adulthood is than childhood. There's still plenty to enjoy in childhood. Carefree summer afternoons. Free time to participate in various clubs and sports. The built-in social life of school and the activities that come with that. So I definitely enjoyed my own childhood without necessarily yearning for adulthood. But I still looked forward to becoming an adult, and now that I am one, I have no desire to go back to being a child.

Question: What do atheist think about the birth of Jesus Christ?
Answer: I think the most likely scenario is that Jesus was conceived and born in the normal manner to Mary and Joseph, without any particular intrigue or scandal. Then, as the legend around him grew after his execution, the stories around the virgin birth and the Nativity developed and got added to the legend. The earliest surviving Christian writings we have, Paul's letters, don't make any mention of a virgin birth. Further, the earliest two gospels, Mark and Matthew, don't make any mention of a virgin birth, either. In fact, reading between the lines of certain passages in Mark's Gospel seems to imply a perfectly ordinary birth (Bart Ehrman - Does Mark's Gospel Implicitly Deny the Virgin Birth? - The Bart Ehrman Blog). The idea of a virgin birth in Christianity doesn't appear to arise until the later gospels. So, the virgin birth probably wasn't trying to explain away an illegitimate birth, but just an expansion of the legend around Jesus being the Son of God (moving away from the more adoptionist view of Mark). The whole Nativity story likewise doesn't appear in the earliest Christian writings of Paul and Mark, and only shows up in Luke and Matthew. But the stories almost certainly aren't true. For one, there are too many contradictions between them (including events that would mark the year he was born). They simply can't both be true (though, of course, they could both be wrong). Both they also include rather dubious historical details – the Massacre of the Innocents in Matthew (there’s no mention of this atrocity in any other surviving historical records), and the weird census in Luke (people don’t have to travel to their ancestral home towns for a census – it kind of defeats the purpose). These stories probably developed in the decades after Jesus's ministry as the rest of the legend around him developed. They not only made his birth seem more impressive and befitting of a god than a normal, biological, human birth, but they also attempted to serve theological purposes. In Matthew's case, that was Jesus fulfilling prophecies from (what's now called) the Old Testament. In Luke's case, it was to show Jesus as the son of God from birth, in contrast to the adoptionist views of other early Christians (like Mark), who believed that Jesus was born as a normal man and only became the adopted son of God at his baptism. But in any case, there's little reason to believe in either the virgin conception or the Nativity. Portions of this answer were adapted, nearly verbatim, from previous answers. Question: If atheists see religion as an irrational belief, why don't they help their religious friends see reason and logic and give up religion?

Question: What is the longest recorded day on Earth? What factors can cause a day to be longer than usual?
Answer: Well Quora Prompt Generator, you've managed to post another question that has a more complex and intriguing answer than many people might realize. First is the question of what you mean by a day. We all know that it takes roughly 24 hours for the Earth to rotate around its axis, which is known as a sidereal day. But the Earth is also in orbit around the Sun. So, in the time it takes the Earth to complete one rotation around its axis, the Earth has traveled a bit further along its orbit, and isn't quite aimed back towards the Sun, anymore. It needs to rotate roughly 1° more (1 part out of 365 days), which takes about another 4 minutes. ABOVE SOURCE: Solar and Sidereal Days But the Earth's orbit is also slightly elliptical, meaning it moves through its orbit faster when its closer to the Sun, and slower when its further away, making solar days just a bit longer when the Earth is traveling the fastest (it has further to rotate to be aimed at the Sun again). And this is complicated even more by the tilt of the Earth not being perpendicular to the orbit. It turns out that 24 hours is the average length of a solar day, but the true length varies by around ±30 seconds. ABOVE: The vertical axis is in seconds, representing the difference from a 24 hour day. The red curve shows the effect of the elliptical orbit. The blue curve shows the effect from axial tilt. And the black curve shows the combined effect from both sources. SOURCE: How the length of a day changes over the year But that's not all. Since the Earth isn't a perfectly rigid body, the length of a sidereal day isn't constant, either. Between tectonic plates, the oceans, the atmosphere, melting glaciers, and the annual water cycle, mass shifts around the planet ever so slightly. And much like the famous example of a figure skater pulling in or extending their arms, mass shifts on the Earth likewise result in changes to the rotational speed. Granted, on the scale of the Earth, these mass shifts are pretty small with correspondingly small effects, but they can be measured, especially with the advent of super accurate atomic clocks. Here's one graph showing this variation going back to the 1960s. You can see that there's a yearly cycle on top of longer term variation on the order of a few milliseconds. ABOVE SOURCE: Day length fluctuations - Wikipedia Before atomic clocks, you couldn't quite get day to day measurements of this variation, but you could use certain astronomical events to get year to year measurements. Here's a graph that used that other data to reconstruct the length of a sidereal day back to the 1600s: ABOVE SOURCE: No, this winter solstice wasn't the longest ever. Scientists explain what we got wrong. There's also an even longer term trend due to the interaction between the Earth and Moon. Due to the Earth's rotation, the slight bulges that result from the tides aren't exactly aligned with the Moon, but are a bit ahead of it. This results in bit of a differential in the gravity, that creates a small torque slowing down the Earth's rotation. This is a very small effect, averaging about 2 ms per century, but over the span of billions of years, it adds up. Days probably would have been on the order of 10 hours back when the Earth first formed. ABOVE: Exaggerated diagram of the misalignment of tides SOURCE: The Days are Getting Longer. Anyway, when you put it all together, the longest days during the time period we can actually determine these things were in 1912. And by chance, in this period of history, the Earth happens to be closest to the Sun around the same time as the winter solstice, so the longest solar days of the year end up being right around the winter solstice. So the longest day we know of was most likely some time in December of 1912. Now, if you want to count day as daylight hours, all the same discussion above still applies. You just go with the summer solstice for whichever hemisphere you're interested in. Of course, by the time you get to the North and South Poles, the sun never sets in their respective summers, so you get the entire time from noon to noon as daylight hours for that ‘day’. Question: With Kamala now running, there’s so much more election misinformation due to the high stakes. I don’t know what to believe. From an unbiased and educated standpoint, who is realistically and legitimately leading in the polls, Kamala or Trump?
Answer: I and many others have found that about the most reliable source for these types of questions is 538, so named because of the 538 electors in the Electoral College: 538 doesn't perform any polling, themselves, but they do aggregate the results from many other polls, and then average them together while at the same time applying adjustments and corrections based on past performance of those polls. The end result tends to be fairly accurate. Even in the lead-up to the 2016 election, when all the polls showed Hillary Clinton with a commanding lead over Trump, 538 published the following article stressing that a Clinton victory wasn't at all a sure thing: As the headline states, normal polling error was all it would take for Trump to win. And unlike some of the more hyperbolic forecasts giving Clinton 99% odds of winning, their own prediction was that Clinton only had a 75% chance of winning, while Trump had a 25% chance. Or to put that in perspective, 1 in 4 odds aren't exactly horrible. You expect them to happen 1/4 of the time. While 538 has suspended their prediction of the presidential race for the time being (since Biden dropped out), I suspect they'll begin updating it again once the dust settles and reliable data starts rolling in. So keep an eye on this page: In any event, as of right now, it looks like it's going to be another close race. And because of the structure of the Electoral College, it's a very real possibility that Trump may win again while losing the popular vote. But there's still a lot of time between now and November for things to change. And of course, the only count that really matters is the one in November*. *Well, technically, the Electoral College doesn’t officially vote until December, but you know how the vote is going to end up after election night in November.

Question: I know y'all get tired of these questions, but I'm not trying to upset anyone. I legitimately want to know thoughts and feelings. Would witnessing the rapture and the coming of the antichrist change your minds about being an atheist?
Answer: Actually, that mindset was one of the big things that bothered me about Left Behind back when I read it. Here's how I put it when I reviewed the book on my personal website*: I think one of the most interesting aspects of the book is what it revealed about L&J's [LaHaye and Jenkins'] view of the world (and by extension, those people with similar outlooks). L&J portrayed non-believers as being skeptical of religion, or just not being very interested in religion at all. But remember, they're writing about a post-Rapture world. Everybody on Earth had already witnessed the miraculous defense of Israel during the Russian attack, and the sudden disappearance of billions in one instant. These aren't miracles on the scale of seeing the Virgin Mary in a potato chip. These are the types of events that would make James Randi and Michael Shermer sit up and take notice. Given the continued skepticism of religion exhibited by many characters in the book following these miracles, I can only imagine that that's the way L&J see the world, now. They must think that evidence for the divine is obvious, and us skeptics choose not to see it. I'm not sure if they understand how much some of us have looked for that evidence, or the sincerity of our non-belief. If you permit me to quote just a bit more, going beyond the letter of the original question: There's a similar theme with conspiracy theorists. In the world of Left Behind, there's a global cabal pulling all the strings behind the curtains. Buck Williams knows an informant who's told him of various meetings and decisions of this group. But despite the informant being right, even on extremely unlikely events (like predicting the global economy consolidating on three currencies - dollars, marks and yen), Buck still treats the guy as a bit loony because he's a conspiracy theorist. In the real world, conspiracy theorists are mocked not just because of their outlandish ideas, but because of their lack of evidence to back them up. If any conspiracy theorists could back up their ideas the way Buck's informant did in the book, people would start taking them seriously. Again, I wonder if this comes from L&J's own experience. They're entirely convinced that their own outlandish ideas are true, yet they've been mocked repeatedly for those ideas. Is that just how L&J think the world deals with (what they consider to be) true ideas? I guess what I'm getting at, is that in the minds of many religious folks, they just take it as a given that God is real, and assume that it must be obvious. This then biases their views on non-believers. They think we must be ignoring the obvious, rather than understanding that many of us have made sincere efforts to investigate their religion, and came to the justified conclusion that it's not true. But yes, if evidence as obvious as the Rapture were to happen, that would certainly be evidence that would make most non-Evangelical Christians reconsider their views. Now, whether we would worship a character like the God of the Bible is a different question. But believe in its existence? Yeah, probably. *Source of those quotes: More Thoughts on Left Behind After Finishing the Book

Question: What makes Google Maps superior to Apple Maps?
Answer: One reason – north up maps. Maybe I'm just old fashioned from the old days of using paper maps*. But I really, really, really prefer maps to always be oriented as north up when I'm driving. I know it might not be the most intuitive when you need to make split second decisions. But in the long run, it gives you a much better perspective and sense of orientation. Especially when you're in an area where you might be spending some time and not just driving through once, it really helps you learn the area. I have a sense of the actual cardinal direction I'm heading, not just 'straight ahead'. I can see where neighborhoods lie in relation to each other. I can build up a mental map that corresponds to the map I see on the screen. In contrast, the maps that are constantly rotating to align with your direction of travel just completely destroy that sense of awareness and perspective. When I spent a few months in El Paso a couple years ago, I learned my way around much quicker thanks to Google Maps always keeping the map with north up. Otherwise, despite an ignominious beginning**, Apple Maps has grown into a decent app. It even seems to do better than Google Maps at some things, like telling you which lane to be in, and giving you more than one next step at a time. But until Apple decides to put in an option for users to keep the map oriented as north up even in guidance mode, I'm simply not going to use it. *I remember back when I was a kid, on road trip vacations, or when we first moved from Pennsylvania to Maryland, and I'd sit in the back seat of the car following along on a map to see where we were. Maybe it was all those years of practice that helps me follow along on north up maps, when so many other folks I know seem to get confused by it. **If you look at the other answers to this question, the ones trashing Apple Maps tend to be several years old. It really is a decent app, now, minus that one, monumental shortcoming.

Question: Could Kamala Harris beat Donald Trump?
Answer: Yes. And Trump could beat Harris. Presidential elections in the past 30 years have all been relatively close. Roughly half the votes will go to either candidate, plus or minus a few percent that decides who will win (and a few more percent to third party candidates). And of course, that whole process gets filtered through the electoral college, so a candidate doesn't even need a majority of the popular vote to win the election. ABOVE SOURCE: United States presidential election - Wikipedia This year will be no different. Trump will get around half the vote. Harris will get around half the vote. Whoever performs best in the swing states will win the overall election. Sure, you've got plenty of people right now making 'guarantees' about who will win. And given that it's really a binary choice, a lot of those people will inevitably end up picking the eventual winner. But it doesn't mean they actually had any better insight than the rest of us. It means they just got lucky by calling the coin toss. I think we can safely predict, at least, that Robert Kennedy is not going to win. Side note: I don't mean to discount polling as worthless. I think it still is useful and valid as long as you understand it's limitations. It's just that polling can't tell you much when elections are decided by less than the polling margin of error. Another side note: This question is from 2016, but for obvious reasons, it's taken on a new found relevance.

Question: Hey atheist, you say that not believing in God is not a loss because you don't know what real loss is because you have never loved anyone more than yourself. Well, why?
Answer: I've told this story on Quora before, but I think it fits this question, so I'll tell it again. One of my first indications that I was truly on the path to abandoning Christianity occurred one Sunday morning in church. One of the readings that day was the story of Abraham and Isaac, and how God tested Abraham by commanding him to sacrifice Isaac as an offering. And I remember sitting there in the pew, thinking to myself that this story could have been so much better if Abraham had refused. It would have demonstrated the profound love of a father for his child, that he would be willing to go up against impossible odds against an all powerful God to try to defend his son. Instead, Abraham caved like a craven toady, and was ready and willing to brutally murder his son before God finally stepped in and told him it was all just a test, anyway (and then proceeded to provide a ram for the sacrifice, instead, because of course something needed to be killed to satisfy God's bloodlust). My point is that if religious folks want to start casting aspersions over prioritizing who we love, perhaps they should take a look inward, first. We atheists aren't the ones who think it's virtuous to be willing to sacrifice your own children in subservience to a divine dictator.

Question: Think of a small submarine 10 miles deep in the ocean, 1 gallon of water now drives a generator at 80k PSI, then energy is used to separate hydrogen from water and moved to the surface for use. Any holes in this thought experiment?
Answer: I don't see any 'holes', per se. It just doesn't seem practical for any real world purposes. If I understand the description in the question, you'll end up with something like this on your sub: You've got a tank big enough to allow 1 gallon of sea water to drive a turbine to generate power, and that power will be used for electrolysis to create hydrogen and oxygen. Pressure can be thought of as energy per volume: So, just rearranging a bit, energy is pressure times volume. You need some type of pressure differential to get any work out of that, which is why the contraption has that tank at atmospheric pressure in the diagram above. But since atmosphere pressure is so much lower than the water pressure that deep, we can just assume it's negligible. Anyway, assuming everything was 100% efficient (which it won't be), using the correct value of 16k psi for the pressure in the deepest part of the ocean, and that I’ve done all my math properly, that 1 gallon of water has a potential energy of 308k ft-lb or 0.156 hp-hr, or in terms more familiar to folks who aren't U.S. based engineers, 418 kJ or 116 Wh. In contrast, a AA battery has roughly 3.9 Wh. So your device, at most, has the potential to generate as much energy as 30 AA batteries. In actuality, after all of the efficiencies are accounted for, it will be even less than that. I think your sub is going to need more than 30 AA batteries worth of energy to complete its mission, so you're spending more energy to perform this mission than what you get out of it. So, while this device could theoretically generate hydrogen in principle, there are far more practical ways of generating power.

Question: How is it possible that if I have an addiction, the law allows my children to be stolen and kept away from me and then I have to pay child support?
Answer: Children aren’t property. You don’t own them. They are citizens in their own right, with an expectation of protection from the state. Parents have an obligation and a civic responsibility to raise children properly. If they can’t meet that responsibility, or (not necessarily in your case) perform actions like abuse in outright opposition to that responsibility, then it’s the state’s responsibility to step in and protect those young citizens. And of course, biological parents are still obligated to pay child support since it was their actions that brought these children into the world. Otherwise, I wish you well in your recovery, and that you may be reunited with your children, or at least be able to form a healthy relationship with them. Of course, once they’re old enough to have a say in the matter, their feelings about a relationship would need to be reciprocal.

Question: Should religious organizations be required to hire people who do not believe in their religion?
Answer: It depends on the circumstances. In general, no. If it's a purely religious organization focused on purely religious pursuits, then the First Amendment is clear, and if they want to hire only religious folks, they're free to do so. If, however, it's an organization that drifts into more secular pursuits, things can get trickier. The issue is that bigoted folks can try to use religion as an excuse to avoid the same laws that apply to everyone else. Are they sincerely religious, or are they just using religion as a cover? Does it matter? I know that things have changed in the largest Mormon denomination, but up until the 1970s, racism and segregation were baked right into official church doctrine. Would it really be fair to let, say, a homeless shelter or a food bank discriminate against black people because the people running it didn't want needy black folks mingling with needy white folks? Personally, I don't think so. I think that a homeless shelter or food bank are moving enough away from religion and into secular pursuits that they should have to follow the same laws as everybody else. I know. The above isn't a perfect example for this question since it addressed who the organization served, not who the organization hired, but I think it's still helpful. Basically, if the scope of your organization is purely religious, then you can discriminate against people outside your religion as much as you want. But if your organization starts moving beyond religious pursuits into the broader world, at some point you'll be expected to follow the same rules as everybody else, and not fall back on your religion as an excuse for bigotry.

Question: Will drinking beer while still on a calorie deficit affect my fat loss?
Answer: As the old saying goes – everything in moderation. If you don't drink in moderation, it can be a real whammy to weight loss. First you get all the calories from the beer itself. Beer can range anywhere from around 100 calories for an American light lager to over 300 calories for a Belgian triple. Drink a bunch of craft beers and IPAs for a night on the town with friends, and that could add up to a few thousand calories worth of beer alone. Then, you get the munchies that come along with that, combined with the lower inhibitions caused by the alcohol, and that 3 am trip to the drive thru (with your DD driving, of course) to pick up a double bacon cheeseburger with a large fries sounds like just the thing. Then you've got the hangover the next day, with yet more cravings for greasy fried foods, just adding to the calories. In short, aside from any of the other reasons to avoid overdoing it with beer, you definitely don't want to do so if you're trying to lose weight. But if you do stick to moderation, you should be fine. The key to losing weight is to consume less calories than you expend, and you don't need to stick to diet food to achieve that goal. I myself lost around 60 lbs by eating a normal balanced diet, just less of it. And yes, I still treated myself to occasional desserts and sweets, and usually a few beers over the weekend. Complete abstinence just leads to temptation.

Question: How did first eye evolve? Where did all the parts come from and how did those parts ”knew” to combine so as to form an eye?
Answer: Eyes are a great example of how evolution works by small, incremental changes that offer benefits at each stage*. And there are actually plenty of living animals that have preserved many of these stages, so it's not mere conjecture or just-so stories that these stages could have been useful. We see animals actually making use of these different types of eyes throughout nature. The most primitive 'eyes' I know of personally are those of hydras, tiny freshwater predators that normally attach themselves to something stationary and catch passing prey with their tentacles. They don't even have brains, but just a sort of nerve net. Their proto-eyes are little more than light sensitive individual neurons located throughout their bodies. But even these simple photoreceptors are enough to induce specific day-time and night-time behaviors, modulate the way they discharge their stinging cells, and guide them towards light sources when they do actually move. ABOVE: Anatomy of a hydra. Some of those 'sensory neurons' are photosensitive. Although not shown in this particular figure, such photosensitive neurons are more common in the tentacles in conjunction with the stinging cells. SOURCE: https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.12.14.422784v1.full Moving on, let's focus on just molluscs. Here are various eyes known from living molluscs: The first is simply a patch of light sensitive cells, and can be found in limpets. It can't distinguish direction, but having an entire organ dedicated to light detection is a bit more sophisticated and sensitive than the individual neurons of the hydra. Next comes the cup eye, such as is found in abalone. This eye still can't form an image (there's no way to focus the light), but it does provide more information about the direction the light is coming from, so it still offers an advantage over the limpet's eye patch. It shouldn't be hard to imagine how a cup eye could gradually develop a more pronounced recess to enable even better direction discrimination. But if you keep carrying on that process, you'll eventually end up with a recess so pronounced that you actually can start to form an image. And so, you end up with a pinhole eye like that found in a nautilus. And from the pinhole eye of the nautilus, it's not hard to imagine the benefit of fully enclosing that eye with a transparent membrane (to keep out debris and keep the pinhole itself from getting clogged), and then for that membrane to gradually take on the role of a lens to better focus the image, and allow the opening to be bigger to gather even more light, such as the primitive lens in a marine snail. And from there, it's just more gradual evolution and improvements until you end up with a full, complex camera type eye of an octopus or a squid. So, to address the wording of your question, the 'parts' came from gradual evolution over many generations, as mutations incrementally improved the functionality of what was originally just light sensitive neurons. And of course, the parts didn't 'know' anything about the process. That's the whole point of the theory of natural selection. The organisms that acquired those traits, purely by chance, just happened to have more success in reproduction than their relatives who didn't. But, since these mutations are random, and can only be inherited by descendants of the individuals in which they first appear, not every lineage is necessarily going to acquire these mutations. And if an animal occupies an ecological niche where vision isn't all that important, then not having these more advanced eyes isn't going to be much of a detriment, anyway. So, while some lineages did evolve more complex eyes, various other lineages have gone on maintaining more primitive versions of the organ. But this still goes to show that those more primitive versions are indeed useful. Note: Portions of this answer adapted from my previous answer: *That introduction was simplifying things a bit. Evolutionary changes don’t necessarily have to be beneficial at each stage. They can also be neutral or nearly neutral, as in the case of genetic drift. But the main point is that organisms must be fully functional and adapted to their environment in every generation. You don’t get mutations in anticipation of future benefit.

Name: Jeff Lewis
Question: What was your initial reaction to learning about evolution in school? Did you immediately believe it or did you have doubts about its validity?
Answer: It was a revelation. Prior to that, my exposure to evolution was pop-science articles or the way it was casually discussed in nature documentaries. And while those treat evolution as a given, and may even discuss evolutionary relationships, they hardly ever go into detail of the mechanisms or how evolution actually works. So, like many folks, I had a more Lamarckian view of evolution, of use and disuse and even intentionality on the parts of organisms. I remember one example in particular that left me dumbfounded, of a symbiotic relationship between certain plant and ant species, where the plants provided food and shelter for the ants in exchange for the ants protecting the plants. How could either one of them have intentionally initiated such a relationship? How could organisms with such little to no cognitive ability do anything intentional at all? ABOVE SOURCE: Ecological and Evolutionary Responses of Protective Ant-Plant Mutualisms to Environmental Changes (Chapter 11) - Ant-Plant Interactions When I was finally formally taught the mechanisms of mutation and natural selection, it all fell into place. You don't need any intention. Mutations are just mistakes on a mechanical level, so diversity is inevitable. And as soon as you have diversity, differential reproduction is also inevitable. Evolution didn't just make sense. There was simply no way it couldn't happen. Even my ant-plant example finally made sense. All you needed was some type of mutation on a plant to attract certain ants, and given ants' aggressive behaviors, that would protect the plants from other organisms that might try to eat them. And from there, additional mutations just refine the relationship further. So while I might have said that I already accepted evolution prior to my high school biology class, I didn't actually understand it. By learning how evolution actually works, that class made me much more certain in the truth of evolution. I still had a period of minor doubt a few years later when Intelligent Design was at its peak popularity, wondering if I was being a good Christian when so many other Christians insisted you had to accept some form of creationism. So I researched evolution even deeper than that high school biology class, and given that the evidence really is overwhelming, I only became more certain of evolution. (I might add, that while it's certainly possible to be a Christian and accept evolution, this incident was one of the stimuli to start me on the path to atheism.)

Name: Jeff Lewis
Question: I totally believe the evolution theory because it has tons of scientific evidence, but I don't get it how marine life evolved to have lungs, limbs, developed, and somehow intelligent brain to live on land?
Answer: I think part of the problem is people only think about a stereotypical, generic fish, and don't know about or don't think about the wide variety we see in living fish. You mentioned lungs and limbs, so let's take a look at those. And let's start with the limbs, since it makes for cooler videos. First, here's a frogfish. To be clear, frogfish aren't particularly closely related to the first tetrapods. They're adapted to a fully aquatic lifestyle without ever venturing onto land. But yet, they walk underwater, because it's a better way for them to get around, and especially to use their fins to sit on the ocean floor waiting to ambush prey. And here's a type of walking shark. Again, these are fully aquatic sharks. Their walking isn't some type of planning ahead for a life on the land, but a very useful means of locomotion to prowl around a reef. Next, let's move on to lungs. Air breathing is in fact quite common in many lineages of fish. Oxygen is much more consistent in the atmosphere than in the water, so many fish will surface to swallow gulps of air. Somewhere around 400 million years ago, the common ancestor of bony fish evolved a primitive lung as an outgrowth of the stomach as a way to improve oxygen absorption from these swallowed gulps. Over time, some lineages developed more advanced lungs, while others actually went in a different direction, and the lung evolved into a swim bladder. It just so happens that the lineage that evolved a swim bladder has gone on to become the most successful lineage of fish, so it somewhat biases our perception of what's normal. But a look at the bony fish family tree shows lungs to be rather widespread: ABOVE: The lineages in solid black still have lungs, while the lineages with the dashed outlines evolved swim bladders. SOURCE: How did fish evolve the ability to breathe on land? But even in the lineages that traded lungs for swim bladders, in certain environments, it's still beneficial for fish to be able to breathe air, and so various lineages have evolved new adaptations to allow this. Some fish, like bettas, are so dependent on atmospheric oxygen that they'll 'drown' if they can't get to the surface to take a breath. ABOVE SOURCE: Accessory Respiratory Organs of Fishes (With Diagram) | Chordata | Zoology So, just looking at living species of fish, walking and breathing air are relatively common. And from there, it's not a big step (get it?) to begin spending some time on land. Even that is common enough in living fish, from mudskippers to walking catfish to another species of walking shark that I didn't show here (Epaulette Shark Walks on Land). And once you have fish spending some time on land, well, it's not hard to see how they could become even more specialized to spend even more time on land. In other words, there's no need to ponder any special or unique conditions for why our ancestors would have evolved legs or lungs to make the transition from water to land, since we see plenty of analogs in fish alive right now. They’re simply useful features for some fish to have.

Name: Jeff Lewis
Question: If tiktaalik evolved into acanthostega, why are there no intermediary forms? Why are there no intermediary forms between any two creatures that one evolved from?
Answer: This reminds me of an old joke. A creationist complains to a scientist about a gap in the fossil record between an ancient animal and a modern one. The scientist gets lucky and finds a transitional form intermediate between the two. But the creationist just replies, 'Well now you've made the problem even worse. Instead of only one gap, now you have two.' Tiktaalik was only discovered in 2004. At the time, it was heralded as a near-perfect transitional form between fish like Panderichthyes and Eushthenopteron and early tetrapods like Acanthostega and Ichthyostega, and even acquired the nickname of being a 'fishibian'. It seems it didn't take long for creationists to now see two gaps instead of just one. But to actually answer the question, the reason is because fossils are quite rare. When most organisms die, their remains are completely consumed by scavengers and decomposers. It takes a very unique and unlikely set of circumstances to preserve their remains and go through the fossilization process. And then it takes another fortuitous set of circumstances for those fossils to be exposed through erosion, and then found before erosion carries on further and destroys them completely. The fossils we've found only represent a small subset of all the life that has ever existed on this planet. Just for perspective, consider the non-bird dinosaurs. We've only found something like 700 – 1000 non-bird dinosaurs species from their entire 165 million year history. In comparison, there are 6500 named mammal species just in the present, not counting unnamed living species, or the many, many species that have existed in the past and are now extinct. So we know that the actual number of dinosaur species over that entire 165 million year history must have been orders of magnitude higher than the mere 1000 species we've found so far. And it's the same for other groups of organisms. We know that the fossil record is largely incomplete, especially the fossils we've found so far. Some transitions are extremely well documented (like older apes to modern humans). Some remain pretty much entirely undiscovered (like non-flying animals to pterosaurs). But most fall somewhere in between (like fish to tetrapods). As researchers make more and more discoveries, they continue to fill in the gaps in our understanding. And for the time being, at least, this process shows no signs of slowing down. But even though we'll probably never know all of the details, everything we have found points squarely to natural evolutionary processes. Just as a side note, given how incomplete the fossil record is, it's very unlikely that we've found direct ancestor to descendant relationships in most cases. The transitional forms are more like cousins of the actual ancestors. In some cases, we know that certain fossils can't be ancestors because of the timeframes, but that instead they've preserved certain ancestral conditions.

Question: Has a company ever done something so annoying that you swore off ever buying any of their products ever again?
Answer: My dad taught me a good lesson years ago. It was about banks, but I think it’s still relevant here. He said that if you quit doing business with every bank that pisses you off, you’ll eventually run out of banks to do business with. Every employee has their bad days, mental lapses, or what have you, so you’re bound to catch somebody on one of their bad days from time to time. And managers and executives will make their own mistakes, and so every company will occasionally have a bone headed policy for at least a little while until they decide to fix it. Heck, with large companies, even leadership may completely turn over every decade or so. So no, I’ve never sworn off any company forever. One bad experience on its own is merely something to take note of. A pattern of bad experiences might make me avoid a company for a few years, but I’ll still check back eventually to see if they’ve changed their ways. Okay, maybe there’s one. The owner of a local pool supply place was such an asshole to me one time that I’ve avoided that company every since, going to the chain stores and big box stores, instead. But now that I admit that, I realize that maybe I should follow my own advice and consider that that might have just been a bad day for him, and give them another shot.

Question: Is it true that the shooter at Trump's rally was a registered Republican with conservative beliefs and a gun enthusiast? Why are conservatives blaming the left for this incident?
Answer: There's simply not much to go on to identify his political leanings at this point. Back in 2021, when he was 17, he made a $15 donation to a progressive organization, ActBlue. And yes, despite online rumors, it most likely really was him. When he was old enough to vote, he registered as a Republican. This could mean he legitimately was a Republican. But given that Pennsylvania has a closed primary, this could also mean he wanted to participate in the Republican primary rather than the Democratic primary. As a liberal living in Texas with an open primary, I've voted in the Republican primary before, since I figured it was my only realistic option of trying to influence the governor's race (the Republican I preferred still lost). He seemed to like guns, trying out for his school's shooting team and being a member of a local gun range. At the time of the shooting, he was wearing a t-shirt for a gun enthusiast YouTube channel. But while enthusiasm for guns does skew a bit towards conservative political leanings, it's not at all a sure thing. I like taking my own pistol to the range, for example, and I know plenty of other liberals and Democrats who own and shoot guns. (I'll add that I've seen a few gun enthusiasts trying to use a No True Scotsman argument, claiming that a true gun enthusiast wouldn't have missed this shot, would have used a different rifle, etc. But you don't have to be an expert marksman to merely like guns and like going shooting.) In interviews with former classmates, one student who took an American history course with him stated that he "definitely was conservative", and went on to add about a mock debate that, "The majority of the class were on the liberal side, but Tom, no matter what, always stood his ground on the conservative side." But there's any number of reasons to take this hearsay with a grain of salt (the classmate could have been talking big just to get attention; he might not have known the shooter as well as he claimed, the shooter might have just enjoyed arguing, etc.) I'd also point out that people's political motivations can be quite fluid around that age. Whatever he believed at 17 might not be the same as at 18 or 20. And finally, as I've seen many others point out, we don't even know if his motivation was political. The guy who tried to assassinate Reagan did it to try to get the attention of a movie star. At this point, anybody claiming to know definitively one way or the other which way the shooter leaned politically is not looking at the evidence objectively. And it's an even bigger stretch to try to definitively claim that politics were his main motivation. Investigators are doing their best to figure out his motives. So until then, or until more public evidence comes to light, let's try to keep our speculations grounded in what's actually known. Update 2024–07–22: While it’s still a bit early to say anything definitive about the shooter, the emerging picture seems to be that he was looking for notoriety by shooting somebody famous, not any particular political leanings. In addition to Trump, he’d been searching online for Biden and other prominent political figures. The proximity of the Trump rally to his hometown seems like it might have been the biggest motivator in him choosing Trump over any of the other people he’d been considering.

Question: How powerful is the almighty God?
Answer: It depends on if you mean in universe or in real life. In universe, it's further going to depend on exactly which story you're going with, since it's a bit inconsistent. There's this passage from Genesis 18:20–21, for example: Then the Lord said, “How great is the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah and how very grave their sin! I must go down and see whether they have done altogether according to the outcry that has come to me, and if not, I will know.” In other words, he only knew about those cities from essentially rumors and reports, and didn't actually know what was really going on in those cities until he went to visit in person. So, that kind of seems to argue against his being all knowing. There's also the rather infamous passage from Judges 1:19: The Lord was with Judah, and he took possession of the hill country but could not drive out the inhabitants of the plain, because they had chariots of iron. So iron chariots seem to have stymied the Lord's power. There's also this passage from 2 Kings 3:26–27: When the king of Moab saw that the battle was going against him, he took with him seven hundred swordsmen to break through opposite the king of Edom, but they could not. 27 Then he took his firstborn son who was to succeed him and offered him as a burnt offering on the wall. And great wrath came upon Israel, so they withdrew from him and returned to their own land. Although the current version Bible doesn't mention him by name, this appears to be the god, Chemosh, who granted his people favor due to that sacrifice, such that they were able to defeat the Israelites and their god, Yahweh Even in the New Testament, you have the whole story about the resurrection, and how even God himself had to go through with this elaborate ritual to forgive humanity of their sins. This seems to imply that there are even higher powers in the universe constraining what even God can do, or else he could have just forgiven humanity by divine edict. On the other hand, you have all of the Book of Job with God bragging about just how powerful God is in comparison to humanity. As I’ve written elsewhere, it’s sort of the ultimate might makes right argument, with God being the mightiest of all. So, in universe, I think it's fair to say that God is much, much more powerful than any person. But, at least per many of the stories, he's not exactly omnipotent. In real life, well, fictional characters don't have any powers.

Question: If atheists begin to believe in my god, what would they lose? They will not lose anything.
Answer: Your god must be the least demanding one out there, because a lot of the gods people believe in aren’t so laid back. For many Christians, there's the 10% tithe right off the bat. Sorry – I mean, how much we would 'donate'. Then there's the time investment. That's at least a couple hours every Sunday when I could be doing something else. Then there are lost opportunities. Southern Baptists would have me abstain from alcohol. Mormons would take that even further and have me abstain from even coffee and Diet Coke. If the ancient Greeks were right, where would I get my coins to cross the River Styx? If Hindus are right, then following some of the more hateful forms of Christianity might screw up my karma and yield me a pretty bad life in my next reincarnation. I know, not every religion has every one of these issues. But there are plenty of costs and negative impacts that can come from certain specific religions. And when you look at that in comparison to the likelihood of Bronze Age to Iron Age mythology actually being true, well, I'm not going to lose any sleep over ordering a bacon cheeseburger and a pint at a bar in the middle of a pride rally.

Question: If everyone around the world rides bicycles that generate electricity and store electricity, how much of humanity's electricity consumption can be offset?
Answer: The short answer is not much. The long answer is complicated, depending on exactly what you mean by bicycles and how much freedom you'll allow in interpreting the question. The first thing to note, that many people don't seem to realize, is that pedaling to power a generator gets harder and harder the more electrical power you have to provide. They just see the wires, and seem to think that it's no harder than pedaling a free-wheeling bike. But once you try to actually create current with those wires, they create magnetic fields. And those magnetic fields make it more difficult to turn the generator. The more power, the stronger the magnetic field, and the harder it is to pedal. It all goes back to the conservation of energy, and the fact that you can't get something for nothing. Moving on, if you mean stationary cycles, where instead of moving, you're just driving a generator, then you're not going to get much energy at all. Loring Chien already went through the math in his answer. Even taking it to the extreme of people riding such machines for 12 hours a day every day, you only get 10% of the world's electric consumption (the average person can only maintain around 50 - 100 W continuously). And of course, that extreme scenario is not at all practical. You can't do your real job when riding a stationary bike. So if you cut people’s time down to a somewhat more realistic 1 hr per day to leave them time to do other things, then you’re looking at less than 1% of the world’s electric consumption. But even that’s over-estimating the net results. If people are going to perform that much physical exercise daily, their calorie requirements are going to go up. That means more food needs to be grown, stored, and transported, and all of that takes energy. How much of that energy comes from electricity vs. petroleum based fuel is dependent on how quickly EVs displace IC engines, but it’s certainly going to be something (and non-negligible when you’re talking about changes to diet on the scale of the entire world’s population). If you meant adding a generator to regular bikes that generated electricity during the course of normal riding, the numbers come out even lower. Recalling that you can’t get something for nothing, a generator that’s driven through a direct mechanical connection is going to feel like riding the brakes, with the braking force being higher the more power you try to generate. Alternatively, a wind powered generator is going to increase your drag, again forcing you to have to pedal harder. Basically, since you need power to propel the bike, you have to settle for only a fraction of the power that the person can generate going to the generator. That’s why existing generators on bikes are only used for very lower power applications like lights. In short, you’ll generate well, well short of even the 1% from the previous scenario. What about the power savings if everybody rode bikes instead of driving in cars? Now, you’re looking at a double impact, because bikes are much smaller than cars and so don’t require as much power. i.e. The benefit is not just in using human power, but in not needing as much power to begin with. Of course, if you’re just looking at electricity, this is going to be a bigger effect as EVs become more common. What makes this complicated to analyze is that cycling can only replace some uses of automobiles, not all of them, so you have to take that into account. Here’s one study, Ditching the car for walking or biking just one day a week cuts carbon footprint,. If we take CO2 as a proxy for energy consumption, that study found “If just 10% of the population were to change travel behaviour, the emissions savings would be around 4% of lifecycle CO2 emissions from all car travel.” Based on a couple other sources (the Energy Information Administration and the Bureau of Tranpsportation Statistics), transportation in total makes up 37% of U.S. energy consumption, while light-duty short wheelbase vehicles (i.e. cars) makes up 40.3% of that, or around 15% of the total energy consumption. So a 4% savings on automobiles is around a half percent total energy savings. But if you upped that “10% of the population” to “100% of the population”, and it scaled linearly to a 40% savings on car travel, you’d end up with a 6% savings in total energy consumption. That’s not exactly huge, but it’s not negligible, either. To sum up, none of the scenarios result in huge energy savings. Loring Chien’s calculation of people riding all day, every day, still only results in 10% of the world’s electricity requirements. Reducing people’s time on the bikes to 1 hr a day drops that to less than 1%. Putting generators on existing bikes for transportation generates an even smaller percentage than that. The most realistic and achievable scenario is to get people to ride their bikes instead of driving their cars for trips where it’s feasible. Depending on how many people you can get to do this, you’re looking at around 0.5% total energy savings in a more feasible scenario, or 6% in an overly optimistic scenario. But a few percent here and a few percent there can eventually add up to significant savings.

Question: If someone was hypothetically able to view the light that left Earth 65 million years ago during the Cretaceous period, what would they see and witness?
Answer: I assume you picked 65 million years hoping to see dinosaurs. But in reality, you’re going to see something like this: ABOVE SOURCE: Jwst Feed (@jwstfeed.bsky.social) Yes, that’s an entire galaxy, not a single solar system, let alone a single planet like Earth. That is the galaxy known as NGC 3972, which is around 60–65 million light years away. This image was captured with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), which is one of the most powerful telescopes ever built. Here’s another photo of the same galaxy by another incredibly powerful telescope, Hubble: ABOVE SOURCE: NGC 3972 - Wikipedia The issue is that 65 million light years is a long way away. The other issue is that telescopes can only ‘magnify’ an image so much. Because of the wave nature of light, as opposed to being pure rays, there’s essentially a limit to how much you can focus the image depending on how big your mirror is. That in turn limits how much detail you can make out. It’s not an issue of cramming a higher resolution scanner into your telescope. That would just give you a higher resolution of an out of focus image. I’ve gone through the math before in other answers. But if you wanted to make out a triceratops to roughly the resolution shown below from 65 million light years away, you would need a telescope 260 light years in diameter. That’s not gonna happen. Even solar gravitational lens telescope proposals only increase the effective diameter to that of a star, which is still well short of 260 light years. (That’s Galileo in the bottom right for scale, by the way.) The other issue that people tend not to think about is exposure times. If you look up the image info for NGC 3972 at HubbleSite.org, it lists exposure dates from April - July, 2015. Now, I’m not sure if it was focused on that single galaxy for the entire time. But still, you’re looking at a long exposure time to generate such an image. So if you were hoping to see individual dinosaurs, they’re not going to sit still that long for a portrait. Basically, with any type of realistic telescope technology, the best your going to do is a nice picture of the Milky Way galaxy. Maybe you’ll be able to pick out the Sun, but trying to image Earth on it’s own, let alone in any detail to see individual animals, just ain’t gonna happen. Related answers:

Question: When a particle collides with an antiparticle, they are transformed into energy, Is it true that matter is annihilated and destroyed? Is this literally true? Matter is destroyed? Doesn't this completely contradict the law of conservation of matter?
Answer: Scientific laws aren't exactly ironclad dictates that apply across all conditions throughout the entire universe. They're short expressions or formulas that are useful as long as you understand their limitations. Take Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation, for example. It's extremely accurate at the scale of everyday interactions in our lives. It's still accurate enough to predict the orbits of most of the planets to within the precision of our ability to measure them. But it's not quite accurate enough to predict the orbit of Mercury, given Mercury's close position to the Sun. For that, you need Einstein's updated theory of gravity, General Relativity. But even though we know Newton's law of gravity isn't perfect, we continue to use it since it's still plenty useful and accurate for many applications. Another law that I used quite regularly in my own field of aeronautical engineering is the Ideal Gas Law. We know for an absolute fact that real gases don't behave exactly the same way as this law. But for the pressures I normally deal with for aeronautic applications, it's good enough: It's the same thing with the Law of Conservation of Mass. It also is extremely accurate at the scale of everyday interactions in our lives, enough that many of us engineers use it for things like designing airplanes or balancing equations for chemical reactions. But we also know that it's not accurate over all conditions. As Einstein famously pointed out, E=mC², based on the fact that mass and energy are fundamentally the same thing, and can be converted from one to the other. And while this applies to everything, the difference in most everyday situations is negligible (a warm can of soda will be ever so slightly more massive than when it was cold, but your kitchen scale isn't anywhere near sensitive enough to measure the difference). So, the issue is that you're trying to apply the Law of Conservation of Mass to a condition outside where it would be valid. Instead, you need to look at the broader law, Conservation of Mass-Energy. Keeping it to still simple terms, this basically boils down to: E 1 + m 1 C 2 = E 2 + m 2 C 2 If m2 < m1, it just means that E2 has to be increased to compensate. But the total value on each side of the equation has to be the same. Nothing is being lost or destroyed, just converted.

Question: If you believe the Bible is fiction, then why would anyone want to write such a work?
Answer: It's not fiction in the same sense as a novel, where one person sat down to write a story. Much of what ended up in the Bible were legends and stories that had been floating around in that culture for generations, spread largely by word of mouth and oral history. Sure, every once in a while some scribe might have written down a particular version of one of the legends, but these wouldn't have initially taken on the authority of 'scripture', and the legends would continue to develop within the larger society. As a more modern day example, consider Grimm's Fairy Tales. The Brothers Grimm didn't invent these stories themselves. They went around collecting stories from German folklore. You can see this in the books now referred to as the Pentateuch (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy). By using critical analysis to study these books, it's clear that they were the result of combining four prior traditions, now known as the Yahwist, Elohist, Priestly, and Deuteronomist sources, with a round of editing by a person or group known as the Redactor. As just one example from the Old Testament, the Noah's Ark story can trace its origins back to older Sumerian flood myths such as Gilgamesh and Atrahasis. And even the story within Genesis is an intertwining of the Priestly and Yahwist traditions, with conflicting details throughout the story, such as the number of animals to take aboard (one pair of each kind vs. seven pairs of the clean kinds), how long the flood lasted (40 days in the Yahwist source per Genesis 7:17 vs. 150 days in the Priestly source per Genesis 7:24), and twice repeating that Noah went into the ark (7:7-9 and again at 7:13-16). The New Testament development was a bit more rapid, but it was still the result of stories being passed along by word of mouth for decades before a few educated converts to Christianity decided to write them down. Some of those accounts eventually acquired enough of a reputation to be included in the official canon, but many more never acquired the status of 'scriptures', and are regarded as merely early Christian writing. Basically, it's the same as many other mythologies. Nobody necessarily sits down with the intent to create a story from scratch. It's stories that get passed on orally from generation to generation, that develop and morph over the years. Some scribes write down the stories from time to time, and the written versions that strike a chord become canonical.

Question: If you are an atheist, how do you explain conscience to yourself? As for YOU, where does it come from?
Answer: Our innate morality is an evolved instinct as a social animal. Depending on the conditions and the niche, social groups can offer animals synergistic benefits greater than the sum of the individuals. So, you see various levels of social cooperation in all types of packs, herds, tribes, troops, pods, etc., with ants and bees being some of the most extreme examples. Individuals living in such social environments need social instincts, not just to make the group successful, but, and this is the really important part in regards to evolution, so that they're accepted into the group so that they can take advantage of the group benefits for themselves. If you ever watched the show Meerkat Manor, you may recall that meerkats kicked out of the group had much, much worse chances of survival than meerkats living in the group, so there's a very strong selection pressure for meerkats to have instincts that keep them in the group with all the benefits that provides. But it’s not a hippie dippie love fest. There are also conflicting instincts to not be too selfless to the group, lest an individual sacrifice their own reproductive success. Conversely, all members of the group have an interest in identifying and punishing freeloaders and cheats, since they would drag down the success of the group as a whole. Along those same lines, individuals will have an interest in not doing things that would mark themselves as cheats, themselves, to avoid punishment. So, social animals evolve a whole range of complex and sometimes conflicting impulses to maximize their success in such settings. Even actions that go against their own short term self interest may be important in maintaining their long term acceptance within the group. Of course, most of us aren't so Machiavellian and calculating in our own behavior and internal thought processes, but, anthropomorphizing what is in fact a mindless process, natural selection was when it instilled those instincts in us. And so that brings us to where we are today. Perhaps it's easiest to understand the impulses towards selfishness and nepotism for the more direct benefits they would seem to bring us and our offspring. But empathy and conscience are just as important for social animals, since they're critical to our acceptance into social groups and the benefits we get from living in those groups. Note: This answer was adapted from a previous answer: I'll also note, that in the interests of brevity, I didn't even get into topics like kin selection, which add another layer of reasons to cooperate and have feelings of empathy.

Question: Why can't English rugby be as popular as American football in the USA?
Answer: Well, they started off from the same roots, but then developed along independent paths in their respective countries. So it's no wonder that the version that developed in the USA is more popular in the USA. Both rugby and gridiron football, along with the various other types of football, grew out of a family of British games known as mob football, with different 'house rules' among every group in every town and village that played it. Since it was British colonists who were the first Europeans to come to what would become the U.S. and Canada, they brought along their British sports, including mob football. Round about the mid 1800s, social conditions were finally ripe to begin formalizing these diverse rules with different governing bodies. At the time, the Rugby School's rules were very similar to the rules at several American and Canadian colleges like Harvard, McGill, and Yale (in contrast to the association football rules of Cambridge and the Sheffield Football Club). The New World teams went on to develop new innovations that moved the sport further away from its cousin, rugby, including the line of scrimmage, a system of downs, and then in 1906 the forward pass (Walter Camp was especially influential in many of these innovations). ABOVE: An 1895 football game between Auburn and Georgia looking a lot more like rugby than modern day gridiron football SOURCE: College football - Wikipedia ABOVE: Another pre-forward pass college football game – the University of Minnesota vs. the University of Michigan in 1902 SOURCE: College football - Wikipedia So basically, the two sports started off largely the same, but then went down separate paths in each country. So of course the rules that developed in the USA are more popular here. If most Americans had wanted to play a game more similar to rugby, they wouldn't have changed the rules in the first place.

Question: Is the Fahrenheit temperature scale calibrated so that 0 or 100 are meaningful (to something other than water)?
Answer: In a paper that Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit submitted to the Royal Society, he explained for himself the three points originally used to calibrate his thermometers (though in principle, only two points should have been required). If you can read Latin, the full paper is available here: Otherwise, you can find an English translation of a relevant portion here: Here is how he defined each point: The first is found in the uncalibrated part or the beginning of the scale, and is determined by a mixture of ice, water and ammonium chloride or even sea salt. If the thermometer is placed in this mixture, its liquid descends as far as the degree that is marked with a zero. The second point is obtained if water and ice are mixed without the aforementioned salts. When the thermometer is placed in this mixture, its liquid reaches the 32nd degree. I call this ‘freezing point’. The third point is situated at the 96th degree. Alcohol expands up to this point when it is held in the mouth or under the armpit of a living man in good health until it has completely acquired his body heat. So, zero was the lowest temperature easily achievable in a lab, with just water, ice, and salt. The upper point of human body temperature was set at 96°, which for people already used to traditional measurements is a nice, even eight dozen. From there, it seems that Anders Celsius's work had a major influence to use the freezing and boiling points of water (at standard pressure) as the main calibration points. So using the already defined 32° for the freezing point of pure water, Fahrenheit's scale was tweaked just a bit to make the boiling point 212°, which meant a nice round 180° between them (or a half circle's worth of degrees). By the way, that tweak undid his 0° calibration point. In the modern day Fahrenheit scale, that brine solution sits at 4°F. So, it was a bit of a meandering development, but there was some rationale for the original calibration points. At least Fahrenheit set cold temperatures as the lower values, unlike Mr. Celsius who originally set his scale with boiling at 0° and freezing at 100°.

Question: How exactly did ancient humans defend themselves against large carnivores such as the short-faced bear?
Answer: Don't think of humans as some special case that needs a special explanation. We're just animals, and our ancestors dealt with predators the same general way lots of other animals do: Sure, our ancestors had spears and projectiles that helped them punch above their weight class. And our social groups were especially tight knit compared to most other mammals. But that doesn't really change the fundamentals. Practically all animals have to deal with larger predators, and they still manage to carry on their species. That's just the nature of, well, nature.

Question: If a Starship without any payload can barely reach up to orbital speeds while expending almost ALL of the fuel within it, then could it be that SpaceX underestimated how easy/difficulty would be conceiving a fully reusable craft?
Answer: Look, I've got my reservations about SpaceX's approach to safety with their 'Let's just blow stuff up till it quits blowing up approach'*, and I think that they can sometimes be a bit overhyped by Musk fanbois.** But let's keep things in perspective. They're a company with tons of talent from professional aerospace engineers. Even if they underestimated the difficulty of this approach back in the very beginning, by the time you're building and testing full scale prototypes, you've already gone through feasibility studies, trade studies, preliminary design, detail design, and tons and tons of analysis. The vehicle is performing more or less as predicted, and has the potential to be a truly awesome rocket once all the bugs are worked out. Look to Frank Norris's answer or Steve Baker's answer for more details, but the bottom line is that this vehicle will likely achieve its goal of delivering 100 – 150 tons of payload to orbit in the reusable configuration. That is quite an achievement. *My reservations with their 'Go-fast-fail-fast' approach is in the mindset, that if something hasn't gone wrong yet, then it must be good. That's way too reminiscent of the mindset that led to the Challenger disaster. Coming from an aviation background, myself, the standard level of safety for airliners is a probability of catastrophic failure of less than 1 per billion flight hours. You can't demonstrate that with a mere 100 flights with only around 10 minutes each getting to orbit and another 20 minutes for re-entry and landing. You either need prohibitive numbers of test flights, or you need to do lots and lots of traditional analysis. But if it takes half a dozen attempts to get even your first successful full flight, then your traditional analysis couldn't have been all that robust. On the other hand, other rocket manufacturers have plenty of failures, as well, so extreme risk in comparison to aviation just seems to be part of the game (though when Musk starts his dreaming about sending millions of people to Mars, that's when this safety approach becomes irresponsible). **In fairness, while Musk fanbois might overhype SpaceX, there are plenty of folks who go too far the other way, criticizing SpaceX too harshly merely because Musk himself seems to be a bit of a jackass. Whatever you think of Musk shouldn't detract from the real accomplishments of SpaceX. And remember, the company has many, many more engineers and technicians working there to achieve their successes.

Question: Why do people say they believe science over God when science keeps changing what it says it’s proved and God has not changed?
Answer: What do you mean that God hasn't changed? He's changed quite a bit over the millennia as the mythology developed. Since you're using capital-G for God, I assume you're referring to the God of the Bible, Yahweh (YHWH). While Yahweh's earliest origins are a bit obscure (and understandably so, since we're talking about something thousands of years ago), the leading idea seems to be the Midianite hypothesis, where Yahweh was originally a god worshipped by the peoples of Midian, the region to the south of Canaan. The early Israelites and Judahites, who were themselves basically just a subset of Canaanite culture at the time, absorbed this god into their pantheon while they still had a polytheistic pantheon. Of course, not all scholars agree with the Midianite hypothesis, and there are plenty of other origins ideas, including that Yahweh was more of a 'home grown' deity within Israel/Judah. On this topic of the earliest origins of Yahweh, the perhaps oldest known records of belief in this particular deity are a couple of inscriptions from Egypt – one from the period of Amenhotep III (14th century BCE), the other from Ramesses II (13th century BCE). In describing a certain group of people, both inscriptions use a phrase translated as something like "The Land of the Shasu yhw" or "Shasu of Yhw". Assuming that Yhw is the same god as YHWH, and that modern ideas of the Shasu being nomads of the region south of Canaan are correct, this seems to support the Midianite hypothesis for Yahweh's origins (though it should be noted, some people think the transfer went the other way around, with the Shasu adopting Yahweh from the Israelites). ABOVE: The inscription describing Shasu of Yhw SOURCE: Shasu - Wikipedia At any rate, no matter how Yahweh first entered the Israelite pantheon, his earliest appearances in Israelite religion were as just one god among many, and not even the most important. I've already discussed Deuteronomy 32:8–9 several times here on Quora, which clearly shows Yahweh as one of the sons of El, receiving Israel as his particular land to rule over, while other sons of El received different lands (more info: Jeff Lewis's answer to Can atheists prove there's no God, since they don't believe in His existence? in Divine Atheist). The earliest writings about Yahweh in the Bible also seem to present him as a storm god and god of war. The New Oxford Annotated Bible is an excellent resource, with very informative essays and copious footnotes from Biblical scholars. They mention this association with a storm god in several footnotes. For example, here was the footnote in reference to 2 Samuel 22:11–16: The LORD is depicted here as the storm God. Cherub (v. 11 ), a mythical, griffin‐like creature. God's voice (v. 14 ) is thunder (Job 40.9; Ps 29.3 ), and he throws lightning bolts at his enemies (v. 15 ). The psalmist envisions the world as flat; he is trapped in the underworld beneath the foundations of the world, which the LORD's roar uncovers (v. 16 ). Other footnotes made reference to "God's storm-cloud chariot" several places, including for Psalm 68:4 ("Who rides upon the clouds, God's storm‐cloud chariot (v. 33; Ps 65.11 )") and for Psalm 65:11 ("Your wagon tracks, God's rain‐cloud chariot."). Personally, reading the Bible on my own, I thought Psalm 77:16–20 was especially in line with those early conceptions of Yahweh as a storm god: When the waters saw you, O God, when the waters saw you, they were afraid; the very deep trembled. The clouds poured out water; the skies thundered; your arrows flashed on every side. The crash of your thunder was in the whirlwind; your lightnings lit up the world; the earth trembled and shook. Your way was through the sea, your path, through the mighty waters; yet your footprints were unseen. From those origins, Yahweh went through a transformation within the religion, gradually blending with El to become the primary and most important God of Israel, then through a stage where he was the only God that the Israelites were supposed to worship, though not yet the only god in existence, before the eventual transformation to full monotheism some time around the Babylonian exile. I have another answer where I discussed archaeological finds from during this transition which covers these next two examples in much more detail (Jeff Lewis's answer to Atheists, what are your top 5 reasons for not believing in God and/or Christianity? Please answer with something besides "No proof". in Atheism Now). First is the Mesha Stele, which recounts the same battle as told in 2 Kings 3, but from the point of view of King Mesha of Moab, and is actually older than the Biblical narrative. This stele shows how the Israelites were likely still worshipping more than one god ("the fire-hearth of Daudoh"), and that even their worship of Yahweh hadn't yet been centralized to the Temple of Jerusalem, contradicting the Biblical narrative. The second is the Kuntillet Ajrud inscriptions, showing that Yahweh had a wife or consort at the time, the goddess Asherat. And like the Mesha stele, these inscriptions also contradict the Biblical narrative of a centralized worship at the Temple of Jerusalem. And of course, the character of Yahweh continued to develop and change over the generations, including the rise of Rabbinic Judaism after the destruction of the Second Temple, Christianity and it's updates in their scriptures, Islam and their updates, continued revisions in various sects over the years such as the Protestant-Catholic schism, and even more modern updates like Mormons and Jehovah's Witnesses. So in contrast to your implication, Yahweh has changed very much over the generations, from a storm god within a polytheistic pantheon, to the multiple conflicting conceptions of God among modern day Jews, Christians, and Muslims, and all the varying sects within those major branches. God seems to bear all the hallmarks of a mythological character who develops along with the culture of those folks who believe in him. As to the other part of your question, trust in science hardly even deserves a detailed explanation. But just to completely answer your question, here's an excerpt from my self-published book on religion (God? Leaving Christianity | jefflewis.net): One reason to be confident in the scientific process is pragmatic – just look at the results. Science as the formalized discipline that we think of has only been around a few hundred years, getting started in the Renaissance, but not really coming into its own until after the Enlightenment. And look at how fast our technology has progressed in that short time compared to the previous millennia of human existence. We’ve invented telescopes, steam engines, automobiles, semiconductors, airplanes, computers, TVs, radio, lasers, vaccines, antibiotics, cures for some cancers. We’ve sent people to the moon. These accomplishments are all based on knowledge that we’ve learned through science. We wouldn’t have been able to accomplish all of that if we didn’t have an accurate understanding of reality. Granted, there are other fields of science that haven’t yielded practical applications, and possibly never will. The Big Bang may not ever give us any new technologies. But given the technologies we have developed from so many other fields, we know that the methods produce reliable results.
