Question: Is baldness a survival benefit, in the sense of Darwin's evolutionary theory of "The Survival of the Fittest"? How is baldness adventagous for survival?
Answer: Meh. Who knows? Stephen J. Gould and Richard C. Lewontin wrote a seminal article cautioning against ultra-adaptationist thinking all the way back in 1979: Here's a good excerpt from the paper: We fault the adaptationist programme for its failure to distinguish current utility from reasons for origin (male tyrannosaurs may have used their diminutive front legs to titillate female partners, but this will not explain why they got so small); for its unwillingness to consider alternatives to adaptive stories; for its reliance upon plausibility alone as a criterion for accepting speculative tales; and for its failure to consider adequately such competing themes as random fixation of alleles, production of non-adaptive structures by developmental correlation with selected features (allometry, pleiotropy, material compensation, mechanically forced correlation), the separability of adaptation and selection, multiple adaptive peaks, and current utility as an epiphenomenon of non-adaptive structures. The moral is, before you try to invent just-so stories about the evolutionary advantage of a trait, you have to demonstrate that it was positively selected for in the first place. It might very well just be the result of random drift, with no real effect on fitness. A different, more recent, article by Larry Moran, On the importance of random genetic drift in modern evolutionary theory, contained these examples: Take a favorite example of Richard Lewontin who points to the fact that the African rhinoceros has two horns while the Indian rino has only one? Is this an example of natural selection? Are two horns better than one in Africa or is the null hypothesis just as likely? What about the difference between red pine, with two needles per cluster, and white pine, with five? Are those adaptations or are they just due to neutral alleles that have become fixed in the two species? Is it possible that the genes that lead to baldness have some benefit? Sure. Maybe baldness itself is attractive to some women and so affected by sexual selection. Maybe the genes that lead to baldness have other effects that are beneficial. But this type of speculation is turning into the just-so stories that Gould and Lewontin warned against. Not every feature that we've evolved was necessarily down to natural selection. Random chance plays its role, as well. I did find one fairly reasonable article that described a study showing that bald-headed men are "consistently rated as more intelligent, influential, knowledgeable, well-educated, high social status, honest and helpful – traits collectively known as social maturity." So maybe there is something to that. But it's still pretty speculative at this point.

Question: Is it possible to believe in God if you are an atheist?
Answer: It's not really about possibilities. It's about definitions. If you don't believe in any gods, you are, by definition, an atheist. If you do believe in any gods or deities, you are, by definition, a theist or a deist, and not an atheist. It's certainly possible for somebody who was an atheist to have a change of heart and become a theist or deist. But at that point, by definition, they cease to be an atheist. So no, a person can't be both an atheist and a believer in some god, because it's simply a contradiction in terms. But there's nothing stopping individual atheists from becoming believers (or vice versa).

Question: Can atheists prove there's no God, since they don't believe in His existence?
Answer: It depends on what you mean by 'prove'. It's very hard to prove a negative. What you can do, however, is to lay out an alternative scenario that seems much more likely, which is probably about as close as you can get. Imagine if I said that Darth Vader is actually based on a real historical character who really did live a long time ago in a galaxy far, far away. How would you prove me wrong? You can't find evidence around Darth Vader's non-existence, per se. You could point to the utter lack of evidence for a real Darth Vader. But you can even go beyond that, and find evidence of how George Lucas developed the story, how he developed his drafts over time into the final scripts, how the movies were made and edited, etc., all of which point to a process whereby this character was created as fiction. So while someone could propose that Lucas came upon a story from an ancient, alien civilization about a real Sith Lord and adapted that story into a movie based on real events, the far more likely explanation is that Darth Vader is simply a fictional character invented for the movie. When it comes to capital-G God, we can make a very similar argument. First is the utter lack of credible evidence for this god. But beyond that, by looking at clues within the Bible and evidence from other sources, we can see how the books of the Bible developed, how the conception of Yahweh developed over time, and how Yahweh actually developed out of a polytheistic Canaanite tradition as just one of many gods. *There are a lot of hints of these polytheistic origins throughout the Bible, from all the times God refers to 'we' and 'our' in Genesis, to the way the First Commandment demands that "you shall have no other gods before me" rather than claim that Yahweh is the only god. But one of the most obvious is Deuteronomy 32:8–9: 8 When the Most High apportioned the nations, when he divided humankind, he fixed the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the gods; 9 the Lord's own portion was his people, Jacob his allotted share. There's another version from one of the Dead Sea Scrolls (i.e. not canonical) that's even more explicit: When Elyon divided the nations, when he separated the sons of Adam, he established the borders of the nations according to the number of the sons of the gods. Yahweh’s portion was his people, [Israel] his allotted inheritance. The ancient Israelites believed that El, or Elyon, was the primary god, and that each of his sons received their own region of the world to rule over. Yahweh, being one of El's sons, received Israel as his share, and so that is why he called Israel "his people." You can find plenty of other examples throughout the Bible and from other sources that reveal this development. Here's an answer where I already went through and compiled links to many of these examples, so rather than duplicate that list here, I'll just direct you to that link, if you're interested: Basically, much as with Darth Vader, all the evidence we do have points to a process whereby the character of Yahweh developed as mythology within an ancient culture. And it's not like this is some novel explanation just to try to discredit this particular god. It's the same process we see occur with basically all other gods, as well, from the Greek and Roman pantheon to the Aztec gods and more. If anything, the onus is on believers in Yahweh to provide evidence showing that this particular conception of a god is different from all the other obviously mythological gods (and without resorting to special pleading, I might add). In short, this type of cultural development really does seem to be the far, far more likely explanation for the capital-G God of the Bible. So even if we can't exactly find evidence to prove this particular god doesn't exist, the evidence we do have very strongly points to God being a mythical character. *This section on Deuteronomy 32:8–9 adapted from my self published book, linked here solely as a reference (not as spam):

Question: If Noah's Ark was real, would it have been large enough to hold all the animals and supplies needed for the journey?
Answer: Well, the story obviously isn't real. We know it developed from earlier Sumerian versions of the myth, and that even the Bible version is a blending of the Yahwist and Priestly versions of the story, with conflicting details right within the Biblical narrative. There's no archaeological evidence of such an event. And so, so many details are so ridiculously implausible that there's no way it could have happened as told in the Bible. So, right off the bat, playing a hypothetical game of 'what if', you're already having to make plenty of concessions or adjustments to try to bring the story into the realm of reality. So the question is, how fast and loose do you play with the details of the story to pretend that it’s real. If you want to include all animal species that couldn't have survived a worldwide flood, then it's just flat out impossible. Just consider how many different species there are of beetles, nematodes, ants, etc. And keep in mind that even plenty of aquatic organisms require specific conditions that wouldn't have existed in the flood waters, and so the ark would have required aquariums for those animals, as well. There's a very good article written all the way back in 1983, The Impossible Voyage of Noah's Ark, where somebody did take the time to try to figure out the actual implications of carrying every animal species. They determined the ark would have needed to hold a grand total of 3,858,920 animals. They also determined that the ark would have had 1,063,125 cubic feet of usable internal space (after accounting for structure), which would have left just 0.275 cubic feet of space for each individual animal. Sure, plenty of those animals were small, but they still need room to move around. And you still need their food on top of that. And provisions to access their enclosures for waste removal. Etc. In other words, this scenario is just flat out impossible. But creationists have a trick they like to use, pointing out that the Bible didn't use the word 'species', but 'kind', which they like to define as roughly equivalent to the genus level. In this view, for example, Noah wouldn't have had to take wolves, dogs, foxes, coyotes, and all the other canids. He could have just taken a breeding pair of the canine kind. And then after the flood, their descendants would go on to 'adapt' (because they can't use the word 'evolve') into all the different canids alive today. Of course, that would require a form of hyper-evolution much faster than anything that ever happens in reality. But it lets them come up with a semi-plausible hand-wavy explanation to save a literal reading of the myth (semi-plausible in the same way that getting bitten by a radioactive spider gives you spider powers). A good review of such an explanation using 'kinds' can be found here, Noah's Ark: A Feasibility Study (written back in 1996 – we're not talking cutting edge science required to debunk creationist nonsense). This article addressed what was essentially a feasibility study by John Woodmorappe based on these creative assumptions. Woodmorappe's estimate brought the number of animals down to a somewhat more manageable total of 'just' 15,754. This wouldn't actually be enough animals even to save every kind, but I already said we'd have to bend reality in some places to answer this hypothetical, so we'll just roll with it. So this scenario provides 67.5 cubic feet per animal. Consider that a small elephant requires 214 cubic feet of space for transport (not long term living), and that most animals will be much, much smaller, so this scenario does look like it's plausible to at least cram all the animals aboard. But even then, if you look to modern zoos, and the various requirements for actual long term living space, food storage, food preparation, waste removal, etc., there's still no way that you could keep that many animals alive in that type of space for that length of time (40 days per the Yahwist source, 150 days per the Priestly source). So to sum it all up, the answer is no. It's just flat out impossible if you're considering every single species of animal. And even if you play word games with 'kinds', while it might be physically possible to cram that many bodies aboard the ark, it wouldn't be under survivable conditions, or with anywhere near enough supplies to support the animals until the flood waters subsided. Question: If “burger” now includes fish and chicken sandwiches instead of only ground meat patties, what is the boundary between burgers and other sandwiches?
Answer: In American English, 'burger' on its own most certainly refers to a ground beef patty on a bun. You can stretch the definition a bit by adding a description of some other ingredient besides beef, such as a chicken burger or a veggie burger, but the implication is that it's still a ground food of some sort formed into a patty. For example, this is a chicken burger. Note the ground chicken formed into a patty: ABOVE SOURCE: Natasha's Chicken Burgers While this, since it contains a whole piece of chicken that's been breaded and fried, is a chicken sandwich: ABOVE SOURCE: The OG Chick-Fil-A Sandwich Where you can run into a bit of a gray area is a ground beef patty that's not on a bun. If you put the patty in between two slices of grilled bread with cheese, then it's a patty melt. And then it's just a question of semantics as to whether or not you think a patty melt is a type of burger or something separate. The article I copied that image from does refer to it as a specific type of burger, and I tend to agree since the defining feature of a hamburger (with it’s origins from a Hamburg steak) is the ground beef patty. ABOVE SOURCE: This Is Why Whataburger Patty Melts Are So Delicious - Mashed Yes, I know that in some other countries, practically anything on a bun is referred to as a burger. I was a bit surprised (and relieved) one time going to a get together with my German friends, when they said they were going to make chicken burgers, but they were actually making what I would call chicken sandwiches. So to answer your question, in American English, the boundary between a burger and other sandwiches is using a ground meat (or veggie) patty. No patty – no burger.

Question: Why are people losing the movie-going habit?
Answer: This is actually the future many of us dreamed of. Okay, maybe not the death of movie theaters, per se, but the conditions that are leading to the demise of theaters – big screen TVs and movies on demand from the comfort of your family room. I was a high school student in the early to mid '90s just as home computers were becoming more or less 'modern', with photo realistic images, realistic sound, video clips, online services and the Internet becoming mainstream, etc. There was talk of movies on demand eventually becoming a thing, but it seemed like distant future sci-fi. The first streaming video I remember, RealVideo from 1997, seemed like a revolution at the time (watching a video without having to download the entire file, first), but the results were impressive more for the novelty than the actual video quality. The difference between modern day Netflix and early Internet video is just astounding (I'm sure broadband Internet access is a huge contributor here). TVs and monitors have come just as far. Even in 2004, the average screen size was only 25.4", and even 'large' CRT TVs from the '90s were in the 27" - 32" range. And standard definition TV was still the standard – roughly equivalent to 640×480. A crappy stream quality on a 640x480 27" TV just isn't going to compare to watching a movie in the theaters. But with flat screen TVs, sizes and quality have exploded. The average screen size in 2019 was 47", but even 80" and bigger is now available without breaking the bank. And TVs these days come in Full HD (1920×1080), 4k (3840×2160), or even 8k (7680×4320). Those are in the ballpark of the actual projectors at movie theaters, so you're not really losing any detail watching a movie at home. So basically, we now have the ability to watch movies on demand from the comfort of our own homes, on TVs that are comparable in quality to theaters. Why are people losing the movie-going habit? Because we're living in the future. ABOVE SOURCE: reddit

Question: Is the platypus related to dinosaurs or birds in terms of evolution?
Answer: All life is related through common descent. So the only question is, how closely? And that's going to depend on your perspective. So sure, in comparison to a rose bush, mammals (including platypuses) and dinosaurs are pretty closely related. If you want to look at the similarities between mammals and dinosaurs, we're both eukaryotes, then animals, then vertebrates, and then tetrapods. So we're more closely related than any organism outside of those groups. But if you're wondering if platypuses are more closely related to dinosaurs than to us, then no. Platypuses are definitely mammals. They have fur, mammary glands, and a host of other features firmly placing them as mammals. However, the lineage that eventually gave rise to platypuses did split off from our lineage a long time ago, before our lineage had developed several other features that we now think of as typically mammalian, such as more developed teats and live birth. So although platypuses have evolved in their own way since the split, they've retained the ancestral condition on things like laying eggs and having a cloaca. Now, there is one other feature of platypuses that sometimes confuses people in that their snout bears a superficial resemblance to a beak, or to a duck's bill. But that really is only superficial. If you compare the skulls, you can see that the underlying structure is not at all similar. A duck's jaw is basically the same shape as the beak, with just a thin coating of keratin on top of the bone (keratin is the same substance as our fingernails). A platypus jaw is very different, and the bone is covered in soft tissue and skin to give it its characteristic shape. The snout is also covered in thousands of electroreceptors it uses to find prey underwater. And as one last note, while baby platypuses are born with teeth, those fall out by adulthood. What looks like possible molars on the skull below are actually bony plates, not teeth. ABOVE: Duck skull on left vs. platypus skull on right - there’s not really any mistaking the two SOURCES: Amazon and Skulls Unlimited, combined by me Anyway, if you want to know how closely related any two different organisms are, a great website is: You can type any two species that are within its database, and it will give an estimate (based on published research) on how long ago their last common ancestor lived. So, for platypuses and us humans, it gives an estimate of 180 million years ago. For platypuses and blue jays (to pick a dinosaur at random), it gives an estimate of 319 million years ago. (And just to be clear, since platypuses are mammals just like us, our last common ancestor with blue jays was also 319 million years ago.) And since I mentioned it up in the beginning, the last common ancestor between all of us animals and a rose bush was around 1.53 billion years ago. So, even though our last common ancestor with a platypus was a long time ago, the last common ancestor with dinosaurs was even longer ago than that, and that last common ancestor with a rose bush was much, much longer ago than even that. Question: Why is the left so adamant in their denial that COVID-19 came from the Wuhan virology lab? It's like a chocolate flood in Hershey, Pennsylvania. Might it be from the candy factory?
Answer: Let's start off with the likelihood of where the pandemic originated before getting into the politics. First, although I realize that appeals to authority aren't a strictly logical argument, expert opinion is still a very useful heuristic. These are folks who have in depth knowledge and expertise on a topic, and much more likely to have a well informed opinion than a random stranger on the Internet. And the natural animal origin (zoonotic origin if you want to get technical) is the clear consensus. That's not to say that a lab leak is impossible. It just seems much less likely at this point, especially among the folks who have devoted their careers to studying such things. ABOVE: Results of a survey of 168 virologists, infectious disease epidemiologists, and other scientists SOURCE: The Origin and Implications of the COVID-19 Pandemic: An Expert Survey | Global Catastrophic Risk Institute (click through to the PDF report) I also came across a very informative debate about the issue. If you have a half hour or so, I'd really recommend reading the whole thing: I think the two pieces of evidence that I found the most convincing had to do with the original cases. They were centered around the wet market in Wuhan, not the Wuhan Institute of Virology: ABOVE SOURCE: Practically-A-Book Review: Rootclaim $100,000 Lab Leak Debate And even more specifically, the cases within the market were centered around a racoon dog vendor, an animal which is a known carrier of COVID-19: ABOVE SOURCE: Practically-A-Book Review: Rootclaim $100,000 Lab Leak Debate In fact, two years before the pandemic, a scientist who was visiting that very same market took a picture of the conditions of the racoon dogs, because he was told even back then that "This is the kind of place that has the ingredients for cross-species transmission of dangerous pathogens." ABOVE: Conditions of racoon dogs and birds in the wet market back in 2014 SOURCE: NPR IMAGE CREDIT: Eddie Holmes As that debate I linked to put it: People say it would be a surprising coincidence if a zoonotic coronavirus pandemic just so happened to start in a city with a big coronavirus research lab, and this is true. But it would be an even more surprising coincidence if a lab-leak coronavirus pandemic just so happened to first get detected at a raccoon-dog stall in a wet market! The other piece of evidence concerning the first cases has to do with the two separate early lineages of COVID-19, Lineage A and Lineage B. Lineage B is the one centered specifically in the wet market. But even Lineage A was first found in a neighborhood nearby the market. Quoting that debate once more: Again, it would be a bizarre coincidence if a lab leak pandemic was first detected at a wet market. But it would be an even more bizarre coincidence if a lab leak pandemic separated into two strains, and both were first detected at a wet market! Another strong piece of evidence is that COVID-19 seems most likely to have evolved from a related coronavirus, BANAL-52. But BANAL-52 wasn't discovered until after the pandemic, once interest in the origins of COVID-19 had spiked and people were trying very hard to determine where it came from. It's hard to study a virus in a lab that you haven't discovered yet. Of course, there's plenty more detail to it than that. Like I already said, I'd highly recommend reading that debate I already linked to. Here's another good, somewhat shorter article from a few years ago, and a podcast that I've heard is good (but I prefer reading to listening to podcasts, so I haven't listened to it myself): [ETA - Here’s another good link I just ran across:] None of this is to say that the natural origin is 100% likely, or that the lab leak has a 0% probability. But it certainly does seem like the natural origin is the more likely explanation. Okay, so what about the political aspect of it? I'd like to say that it's because 'my' side of the aisle is always rational and evidence based, and so they're just following the science. And there's certainly a troubling strain of anti-intellectualism and anti-science infecting the Republican party right now, as I explained in a previous answer (Some worry that the United States is in an unusually anti-intellectual period right now. Is this really the case? Haven't societies always been composed mostly of people who are rather unthinking and just want "bread and circuses"?). But as I also noted in that answer: I'm a bit cynical about the Democratic support of science. While I'd love for it to be authentic, I suspect it's mostly virtue signaling in opposition to the Republican distrust of science. But at least lip service in support of science is still better than organized opposition. In other words, I suspect many folks on the left are so adamant in their support of the natural origin of COVID-19 not because they understand the science, but because so many people on the right seem to support the lab leak hypothesis, and so this issue, like so many others, has become divided along party lines, and a way to advertise your allegiance to your own tribe. But just to return briefly to the main point of this answer – the evidence really does point to a natural origin of COVID-19 as being the most likely explanation. Maybe not 100% certain, but more certain than a lab leak.

Question: Will electric kettles ever catch on in America?
Answer: I think we’re all guilty of the occasional spontaneous purchase of at least a few kitchen gadgets. And I have to admit, we’ve got one of these electric kettles taking up cabinet space in our kitchen. My wife bought it during an extended stay at a hotel when she was working a contract, thinking the kettle would be useful in the confines of a hotel room when she otherwise only had a microwave and hot plate in her kitchenette. The times I stayed with her, we hardly ever used it. I mean, what’s the point? Nearly anything you cook needs to simmer for a while, not just take a one time hit of boiling water. And for the few times a year you do need hot water on its own (i.e. cup o’ noodle or hot chocolate), we’ve already got microwaves and stovetops. It’s not worth digging the electric kettle out of storage. And I’m not going to leave the kettle out all the time when it gets used so rarely in the first place. Plus, we have a Keurig coffe maker which already dispenses 4–12 oz of hot water on demand. It might not be quite boiling hot, but it’s good enough for hot chocolate. So although we own an electric kettle, I’m not at all surprised that they’re not more popular here in the U.S. They’re just one more kitchen gadget taking up shelf space, for a task that’s already accomplished by at least three other tools in the kitchen.

Question: Question for atheists- how do you feel about Christians talking about their faith with you if they are nice about it (ie not screaming that you are going to Hell)? Do Christians in this manner bother you? I hope my question makes sense.
Answer: I love it. I really, really like civil debates/arguments with friends. I mean, what's the fun in just agreeing about everything all the time? Especially when it comes to controversial subjects, these types of discussions are where we truly test our own positions. Do we really have a firm foundation for our beliefs? Have we really thought things through? I mean, it would be easy to only hang out in Internet echo chambers and just pat yourself on the back amongst folks who already agree with you, but that's where you run the risk of holding beliefs for superficial reasons. It's only when you test out your arguments among people who are going to challenge you that you can be sure that those beliefs are well founded. I also realize that atheists are still a fairly small minority in this country (USA), and that there's still a fair amount of stigma towards atheists. So by having these conversations, I can help to educate the person I'm talking to about atheism, and help de-stigmatize atheists. I can think of plenty of folks who were shocked to learn I was an atheist, because the stereotype of atheists in their mind was based on straw men and falsehoods. And just maybe, I'll plant some seeds of doubt about Christianity, helping them to see the light and embrace reality rather than ancient superstitions. I don't mean to imply that this is all one way street with me talking down to the Christians. It does me good to remind myself that not all Christians are like the con-men, hucksters, liars, and bigots that get so much publicity like Kent Hovind, Joel Osteen, Jimmy Swaggart, Benny Hinn, Ray Comfort, Fred Phelps, Robert Jeffress*, etc., etc. No, most Christians I meet in real life are just regular folks trying their best to live good lives, but it's hard to escape childhood indoctrination and cultural pressure. And I often learn things myself from these conversations. Perhaps not as much when it comes to religion (since I've studied it more than most of the religious folks I know), but certainly with many other controversial topics I'll argue with my friends about. And of course, everything in moderation. While religion is an occasional topic of conversation amongst me and my friends, it's not the only topic of conversation. There's a whole lot more to life that we spend more time on. As a real life example, just a few months ago, I had a couple Mormons show up in my driveway. They told me a little bit about their beliefs. I told them a little bit about the documentary hypothesis to explain the origins of parts of the Bible, and how Yahweh had developed from previous traditions within Canaanite polytheism. I'm not sure I convinced them of anything, but at least they knew I wasn't some stereotype who called myself an atheist merely because I was angry at God. It was all nice and friendly, and we were smiles and handshakes as they left. So yeah. I love conversations like these when they do happen. They're how we challenge ourselves and each other to be sure that our beliefs are well founded and robust, and they help to remind us that people who disagree with us on certain topics are still just regular folks. *I almost feel a bit guilty about Jeffress, since he used to head up a Baptist church here in Wichita Falls, where I live. Even though I never supported him while he was here, I still feel a tiny bit of guilt by association, that somehow we unleashed him on the rest of the world.

Question: Do pilots tip the nose down when flying a plane to account for the earth’s curvature?
Answer: Yes, but unconsciously, since it's such a subtle adjustment that you don't even notice compared to all the other routine control corrections. Think about driving a car on a straightaway. You can't just take your hands off the wheel and let the car go. Due to imperfections in the roadway, wind, small bumps, or whatever, your car would eventually start to drift. So, you have to keep your hands on the wheel and make constant tiny corrections, even when driving straight. It's the same in an airplane. Between winds, turbulence, temperature changes, your aircraft getting lighter as fuel burns off, etc., you're constantly making minor control corrections to hold your heading and altitude. The amount you have to pitch nose down to follow the curvature of the Earth just gets lost in all those other corrections. But we don't just have to hand-wave it away. We have math. We can run the numbers. I've already done that in a previous answer* for a 747 flying at 580 mph (850 ft/s) at an altitude of 30k ft (i.e. 20,932,464 ft away from the center of the Earth), so I'm just going to copy and paste that math here: s = r θ s t = r θ t V = r ω 850 f t / s = ( 20 , 932 , 464 f t ) ω ω = 0.00004061 r a d / s ω = 0.002327 d e g / s So yeah, you're looking a pitch rate of 0.002327 deg/s to account for the curvature of the Earth. To put that in perspective, the hour hand on a clock rotates at 0.008333 deg/s, or around 3.6x faster than the 747 is changing pitch. That's basically an imperceptible pitch rate, and just comes out in the wash of all the other constant minor corrections. BTW, pilots themselves (or at least, this particular pilot) don't think about the curvature of the Earth per se. We pay attention to our altitude and pitch (among other things). If we tried to fly a true straight path, our altitude and pitch would increase as our path took us away from the surface of the Earth. ABOVE: What it would look like if we didn't correct for the curvature of the Earth. SOURCE: Borrowed from Airplanes Will Never Fly Into Space, then adapted for this answer So, just by trying to hold a constant altitude and keeping a more or less level pitch relative to the Earth directly below us, we pretty much automatically accommodate for the Earth's curvature. And in the planes I fly which only cruise at around 100 mph, or around 1/6th the speed of a 747, it means our pitch rate is correspondingly 1/6th lower than the 0.002327 deg/s of the 747, which is a really tiny number. In short, yes, we do have to account for the curvature of the Earth. But it’s such a tiny adjustment that we don’t even notice compared to everything else we’re doing. * You can find that previous answer I copied the math from here: And here are a few more related answers/articles:

Question: What version of Bible is good to have as an hard copy? While I have “Christian faith” and attend church on and off. I do not believe that one church is better than the other. it would be good to have a read.
Answer: I've already answered something similar, so I'm going to mostly copy that answer here with only minor editing*. There's one Bible in particular that I've recommend several times – the New Oxford Annotated Bible**. It has very good essays as introductory material to each individual book, as well as each larger collection of books (e.g. The Pentateuch, the Historical Books, etc.). The essays were written by serious Biblical scholars, some religious themselves, some not, and hence do their best to present well backed up scholarly consensus not biased by either religious or anti-religious motivations. They explain things such as the origins and authorship of each book from a scholarly perspective (e.g. the Documentary Hypothesis, as opposed to the traditional authorships), themes, styles, etc. Throughout each book, it has extensive footnotes to explain in more detail these subjects, translation issues, historical background, etc. At the end of the entire book, it has another couple hundred pages of supporting materials, including more essays, a glossary, concordance information, an index, and maps. To give an idea, here's an example spread from Isaiah. Note how much information is provided in the footnotes below the Biblical text: ABOVE SOURCE: New Oxford Annotated Bible NRSV 5th Edition Beyond that, the translation used is the New Revised Standard Version (NRSV), which is one that seems to be very well respected among the Biblical scholars I've read, such as Bart Ehrman, the late Hector Avalos, and the late Bruce Metzger. In contrast to another well known translation, the New International Version, the translators of the NRSV really do seem to have tried their best to present the message that the original writers meant, rather than letting their modern day religious views bias their efforts. The NRSV is also based on more source materials and with better scholarship than an older translation like the King James Version. Here's a bit more info on the topic of translations, if you're interested: Now, given that the essays and footnotes are written by Biblical scholars, you won't get a broader discussion of something like a comparison of Genesis to a scientific understanding of the history of our universe. But you will get explanations from critical analysis with a bit of archaeological discussion to explain how we know that those stories are myths and not literal history. (And just to be clear, yes, many religious folks accept the moral lessons of the Bible without believing that the stories are literally true.) Of course, reading the entire thing is a project. It's over 2000 pages long, with a small font size to boot. But with all the background information and commentary, it gives a much better understanding than you'd be likely to get by reading a non-annotated version of the Bible on your own. And since the essays and footnotes are written by Biblical scholars, you know you're getting mainstream scholarly consensus, not polemics. * Here’s that prior answer: ** I've also heard that the Harper Collins Study Bible is also very good (and there are likely more), but the New Oxford Annotated Bible is the one that seemed most recommended back when I was looking for a study Bible, so it's the one I went with.

Question: Can a jet break windows if it breaks the sound barrier far away from the building but then it flies by it?
Answer: I think I see the misconception in the way you worded the question. A sonic boom isn't a one time event that occurs just at the instant an airplane surpasses the speed of sound. It's a shockwave that trails behind the aircraft the entire time it's flying faster than the speed of sound. When pressure waves move out away from an object, the wavefront is a sphere expanding at the speed of sound. That's basically what the speed of sound is, since sound is itself pressure waves in air. As long as you're below the speed of sound, those pressure waves can expand faster than the aircraft is moving. But once you hit the speed of sound, those pressure waves can't expand out faster than the aircraft is moving, so they pile up on the front side, creating a 'wall' of high pressure air known as a shock wave . As the aircraft flies even faster than the speed of sound, this shockwave trails behind the aircraft in the shape of a cone. This conic shockwave travels along with the aircraft. When it passes you by, that sudden increase in pressure is the sonic boom. So, it doesn't matter how long ago the aircraft first exceeded the speed of sound. It matters how fast it's going when it's flying over you. If it's supersonic, it will still be creating that shockwave, and you'll still experience the sonic boom as the shockwave passes you by. In reality, with all the different parts of an aircraft sticking out into the air, you'll have multiple shockwaves coming off of the aircraft. But with those shockwaves being so relatively close together, and the aircraft flying so fast, you'll experience them all combined as one event.

Question: Some people say Jesus didn’t resurrect but was resuscitated by Joseph of Arimathea, after which he lived secretly in other parts of the world till the age of eighty. If true, why didn’t the apostles know about this and allegedly died as martyrs?
Answer: I've seen a few of these ideas with a mix of skepticism and credulity, where they're skeptical of the divinity of Jesus and the supernatural aspects of the stories, but they still treat the overall accounting of events as a fairly reliable narrative. Other similar ideas I've heard include Jesus only being in a coma, or disciples secretly stealing the body. But why? If we already think that the gospels are unreliable accounts, then why accept anything in them at face value that needs any more explanation than simply saying it was made up? Now, I don't necessarily mean that all of the stories were intentional lies (though I'm not ruling it out, either). But rather, the gospels weren't written down until decades after the supposed events had taken place, by people who never met Jesus in person and were relying on oral history that had plenty of time to morph and become exaggerated in the retellings. Any stories in the gospels are just as likely (if not more so) to be urban legends or mythologizing than anything based in fact. So, assuming that there was a real Jesus at the core of this legend, and that he was indeed executed by the Roman authorities, how do we explain what happened to his body? More than likely, it was left up on the cross for a while as an example. And whenever it was taken down, it was probably thrown into a mass grave with other executed criminals and political dissidents. Whatever the inspiration for the belief in the resurrection (and I cover some possible scenarios here - Jeff Lewis's answer to What does a Quoran atheist, with a Christian upbringing, think actually happened following Jesus Christ's crucifixion?), there's little reason to trust most of the details in the gospels, and thus little reason to try to think up more rational explanations. There may well never even have been a Joseph of Arimathea in the first place. As far as apostles and/or disciples dying as martyrs, those stories are partly in the same category. The stories in the New Testament of Christian martyrs are themselves of dubious accuracy, so we really don't know just how widespread martyrdom was. And as far as it did happen, well, people believing in urban legends and conspiracy theories is hardly surprising. You can find plenty of modern day examples in just a few minutes on Facebook – even folks so committed to their beliefs that they staged an attempted coup on the U.S. Capitol, and one man who even martyred himself when he lit himself on fire in protest of a criminal trial against former president Donald Trump. People within echo chambers and cults can build themselves up to committing extreme actions that those of us on the outside find shocking and irrational. In short, there's no reason to spend undue effort trying to rationalize all the different details in the gospel stories, when perhaps the most likely explanation of most stories is urban legends and mythologizing that grew over the decades the stories spread as oral history. But just like in the modern day, there were at least some people who did very much believe in those urban legends, probably enough to lose their lives over those beliefs.

Question: Why did it take until the 1900s before flying was invented, when the kite was invented in the 5th century?
Answer: Engines. Although it might seem primitive by today's standards, here's the engine that powered the Wright Brothers' first plane, designed and built by their mechanic, Charlie Taylor. ABOVE SOURCE: 1903 Wright Engine That engine weighed 180 lbs and put out 12 horsepower. Again, that might not seem like much compared to the hugely powerful engines we have today, but horsepower really is roughly equivalent to what a horse can manage continuously (though they can go much higher for short bursts of a few seconds), so that 180 lb engine is basically doing the work of 12 horses. That's a lot. Steam engines probably could have gotten there. In fact, some of the earliest experiments with unmanned flying machines did use steam engines. And more modern steam engines have had decent power to weight ratios. ABOVE: The steam powered, unmanned Aerodrome No. 5 in flight in 1896. SOURCE: This Odd Early Flying Machine Made History but Didn't Have the Right Stuff Spruce and fabric are old technologies, so people could have built the frames and wings of aircraft for millennia. But prior to steam engines and internal combustion engines, people simply didn't have a power source with enough power at a light enough weight to enable flying machines.

Question: Do atheists actually believe they are monkeys? Do they have an urge to climb trees? Is it sad to only believe in one’s self?
Answer: Let's take these one at a time: Do atheists actually believe they are monkeys? Meh. It's a semantics issue. I'm definitely an ape. And I'm definitely a primate, and definitely a mammal. And on and on for all the various larger taxonomic groups we're included in. But whether or not you think we're monkeys comes down to whether you think monkeys are a monophyletic, paraphyletic, or polyphyletic group. You can debate it, but it doesn't change the reality of the animals we evolved from. (FWIW, I have come around to thinking monkeys should be monophyletic, and that us apes are just a slightly specialized branch of monkeys.) ABOVE: Aegyptopithecus, which was a close cousin to our ancestors, and thus would have been very similar. SOURCE: Aegyptopithecus (note: the above image itself is valid, but Reptile Evolution is a bit of a dubious site - David Peters started off as a decent paleoartist, but kind of went off the deep end a couple decades back) Do they have an urge to climb trees? Yes. Don't you? I climbed trees all the time as a kid, and now that I'm an adult, it's only decorum (and aging joints) that keeps me from climbing them more often. But I still do climb trees from time to time. And when I got some scaffolding to do some work around the house, I told my wife it was like having a grown up jungle gym, and that it gave me an excuse to climb on it for 'work' instead of just playing around. Is it sad to only believe in one’s self? What does that have to do with atheism? I have eyes. I can see an entire world full of other people, animals, plants, etc. There's very much just here on Earth to believe in besides myself. And that's before you start looking at pictures of space, and the untold number of entire galaxies besides our own.

Question: What is the reasoning behind atheists thinking it's illogical to believe in god? Should people be allowed to have their own beliefs without being challenged by others?
Answer: Let's take your latter two questions first: Should people be allowed to have their own beliefs... Yes without being challenged by others? Absolutely not. This is the type of delicate little snowflake mentality that so many people complain about. All beliefs should be robust enough that they can withstand inspection. If they're not, then maybe they weren't such good beliefs in the first place. Now, I'm not saying life needs to be one continuous debate during all waking hours. There's a time and place for everything, and there's a difference between debate and badgering (or to make a verb of a different animal, sea lioning). But yes, you should at least occasionally have discussions with people who disagree with you about challenging topics – politics, religion, morality, pineapple on pizza, etc. If you never challenge yourself, you'll never grow. And if you limit yourself to echo chambers of only like minded people, you'll never truly understand the wider world and why different people do things differently from you. I can think of plenty of examples from my own life where I'm grateful to the people who challenged me and helped me to see things differently. As far as your first question, well, that could be an entire book. But the short of it is, all the evidence we do have for God and Christianity is best explained as a mythology that developed out of previous mythologies. Heck, we even have evidence of Yahweh's origins in the Canaanite pantheon as a storm god – NOT the one and only God and creator of the universe. Other religions and their holy books are largely similar in that they've developed over generations as mythology. And the other big, glaring problem that they all have is a complete lack of credible evidence. Oh sure, Hindus, Buddhists, Christians, and Muslims all get warm fuzzy feelings when they pray, and some even manage to convince themselves that unlikely events and coincidences are evidence of their particular god(s) (but obviously, not the other gods). But this evidence hardly ever seems credible to outsiders who don't already share their beliefs. So there you go. We think it's not reasonable to believe in gods in general because there's no good evidence, and the capital G God in particular because the evidence we do have shows that he's a product of human myth making. And while we all certainly have a right to hold any beliefs we want, we should also be open to being challenged about those beliefs. That's the only way we grow as individuals.

Question: If you see an iPhone in the dessert, you'd say someone created it. Why can't the same be said for humans?
Answer: I've gotta admit – although I've come across Paley's watchmaker analogy plenty of times, thinking about it just now in terms of an iPhone really drove home just how silly of an argument it is. We know exactly how iPhones are made. We can go visit the factories where they're built, or the engineering offices where they're designed. There's a direct trail of evidence to understanding that they're human artifacts. ABOVE SOURCE: Inside Apple's iPhone Factory We also know how people get 'made' (sorry, but I can't include a picture of that one on a family site). There are no factories or engineers involved (well, outside of engineers having kids the old fashioned way). If I come across a human in a desert, I would suspect that they were conceived, born, and raised in the natural way, not that they were some sort of artificial creation. If you want to argue that people are some sort of engineered beings, show the evidence of the factories and designers the same way we can for an iPhone. What's more, beyond the way that individual people are conceived, we have plenty of evidence for evolution for the origin of our species as a whole. We know the mechanisms and patterns. We understand many of the genetic processes. We've found fossils showing the evolution of humans from prior ape species (and plenty of other evolutionary histories besides just us people, but I'm sticking to the topic of the question). ABOVE SOURCE: Julian Norris's answer to What is the most complete visual human evolution chart available? So if you're going to try to argue that humans are somehow engineered or designed, not only do you need to find evidence of the factories and the designers, you have to also account for all the evidence we have that currently seems to point exclusively to evolution. Were all those older hominids previous models? Did the designer(s) release upgrades every few millennia? Assuming the designer(s) designed other organisms besides just us people, why did they seem to self-impose limitations of a nested hierarchy, never taking good design improvements (like feathers or mammary glands) and using them in a different group? It would be like when GM first introduced airbags in the Oldsmobile Toronado, and that all subsequent installations of airbags would be limited to other Oldsmobiles, and never carried over to other products in GM's portfolio, and never adopted by other designers at other automakers. Basically, iPhones and biological beings are completely different things. It just seems silly to try to compare the design and manufacture of iPhones to people.

Question: For Atheists, who is Jesus to you, given historical evidence of his existence?
Answer: Which Jesus are we talking about? The Jesus of the Gospels, or the historical Jesus without all the myth and legend tacked on? By way of example, consider Saint Nicholas vs. Santa Claus. Santa Claus may be based on a real, historical Saint Nicholas, but the legend has diverged so far from reality in all that time, that the characters contain very little in common. What's more, we don't actually know all that much about the real Saint Nicholas, so it's tough to say too much about him. That's the same way it is for the historical Jesus vs. the Gospel Jesus. The historical Jesus probably existed, but there's just very little in the way of reliable evidence on what he might have been like. Paul's authentic letters are some of the earliest mentions we have of Jesus, but they don't contain much in the way of biographical details. The Gospels are much more detailed, but also come from decades later, and were almost certainly second hand accounts spread by word of mouth before educated Christians finally committed them to paper. Considering how quickly urban legends can pop up in the modern day, and how often we see misattributed quotes (Mark Twain didn't say nearly so much as the Internet memes claim he did), a decades long gap is a lot of time for the legends around Jesus to grow and morph. So it's really tough to say much of anything about the historical Jesus – whether he was an honest preacher whose image got embellished over the years, a conman who intentionally mislead people with lies and sleight of hand tricks to build a reputation as a miracle worker, a bit of a crazy religious zealot who might have believed a lot of what he said, or just about anything else you can imagine. We've got plenty of modern day religious figures as examples for any of those scenarios. As far as the more legendary Jesus of the Gospels, as I've said before, my opinion is a bit mixed. Everyone is plenty familiar with the good things he said (feed the poor, love your neighbor, don't judge others, etc.), so there's no need for me to repeat all that here. But he also had plenty of more troubling teachings. Since I've already written about this before (Jeff Lewis's answer to Being an atheist, I know you do not believe in God, but do you see Jesus (the character) as being a good role model? Why?), I'm going to quote that here: But let's not forget who the historical Jesus was – a religious extremist and a cult leader. He supposedly told his followers things like, "Whoever is not with me is against me," and "Whoever comes to me and does not hate father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, yes, and even life itself, cannot be my disciple." If a Jim Jones, David Koresh, or L. Ron Hubbard were to say such things we'd call them out as gigantic red flags. Just because Christianity went on to become a major religion doesn't mean it was okay when (if) Jesus said those things in the first place. Although Christians were quick to rationalize/accommodate Jesus's failed prophecies, he himself seemed to believe that the coming age of the Son of Man was imminent, "Truly I tell you, there are some standing here who will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom." That, and his belief that God would take care of people with enough faith, led to several teachings that are rather irresponsible if you actually have to plan for the future. "Therefore do not worry, saying, ‘What will we eat?’ or ‘What will we drink?’ or ‘What will we wear?’ For it is the Gentiles who strive for all these things; and indeed your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things." Or his admonition to the rich young man, "If you wish to be perfect, go, sell your possessions, and give the money to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me." At times, Jesus also had a bit of a black & white way of looking at the world that lacked subtlety or nuance. One that's bothered me for a while is the way he equated temptation to actually acting on it. Consider his teaching on lust, "But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lust has already committed adultery with her in his heart." Seriously, ask any married person if they'd be as upset at their spouse for a momentary feeling of lust, or actually committing adultery. This type of teaching just sets people up for failure. Instead of framing it as a positive that someone was able to overcome their temptations, it berates people for having normal, natural emotions in the first place. [Going even further, you could frame that as adultery being no worse than lust, so if you've already lusted after somebody, you're not doing anything worse by actually carrying trough with action.] Then there's the whole episode with the money changers in the temple, which very well may have been the incident that led to his crucifixion. Now, it's one thing to have strong principles and to stand up for them. But it's another thing altogether to go onto somebody else's property to cause a major disturbance, vandalize the premises, and assault the people there. I mean, I can think of one church in particular here in my own town that I don't like, but I'm not going to show up there on a Sunday morning, smash up their altar, and start chasing people out of the pews. That's not how mature, sensible people handle disagreements. Finally, this last one may be a little unfair to the historical Jesus, since it comes from one of the stories that arose after his death, but I've always hated the doubting Thomas story. "Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe." No, no, no. It is not a virtue to believe things without evidence. It's this type of gullibility and naivety that leads people to give all their money to Nigerian princesses. Critical thinking and skepticism (not to be confused with cynicism) are skillsets that should be nurtured and celebrated, not discouraged. So, it's tough to say anything about the historical Jesus, because we just don't have much reliable evidence to know what he was really like. The Jesus of the Gospels was a mixed bag, with some good teachings, but plenty of troubling ones. Related:

Question: Why are there still altruists evolutionarily?
Answer: I hate to say it, but the other answers to this question, even from folks who normally write good stuff, are wrong, misleading, or fudging the definition of altruism. True altruism goes beyond mere cooperation or being helpful. It means being helpful without any benefit to yourself, or from an evolutionary perspective, at least a benefit to your own genes. And natural selection is never going to favor such behaviors of pure altruism. To the extent that altruism does happen and has an evolutionary origin, it's because evolution is a mindless process without perfect aim, and some behaviors are missing their target. To begin with, there's the concept of kin selection. What's really important to evolution is increasing the copies of your genes. When parents help their direct offspring, nobody refers to that as 'altruism', since the offspring share half of the genes from each parent, so it's obvious that the parents are protecting their own genetic legacy. But you share genes with more relatives than just your own children. As the famed biologist JBS Haldane supposedly once quipped, "I would gladly give up my life for two brothers or eight cousins." Promoting your own genes by helping relatives is not altruism, at least in an evolutionary sense. Cooperation beyond relatives can also be favored by natural selection, but that's because cooperation brings benefits to all parties involved, so it's not really altruism, either. This can even cross species boundaries, such as the textbook example of cleaning stations in coral reefs, where cleaner fish and shrimp will pick the dead skin and parasites off of larger fish, even fish that could easily eat them if they tried. The cleaners get a meal, while the cleanees get improved hygiene. Everyone benefits from this cooperation (well, everyone but the parasites). One of the other answers to this question used the example of helping an injured member of your tribe to recover, so that they can once again become productive and contribute to your tribe in the future. Well, that's the ulterior motive right there – their future contributions. Going even further, in complex social groups like we humans form, individuals benefit immensely from being a part of the tribe, but everybody also has a vested interest in keeping out freeloaders and cheats. So public displays of charity help to increase your social capital, showing that you are a valuable, contributing member of the tribe, which will provide you with indirect benefits down the road. So even public displays of charity aren't altruistic in these conditions. (I’m not saying people are so conniving in their motivations, but why evolution would have instilled such instincts in us.) The tribalism that's so common in human societies helps to show that these behaviors really are for the benefit of the individual, and not altruism. From a selfish perspective, it makes sense to help out those in your own tribe, since they're more likely to be family in the first place (kin selection), or folks who will be able to help you out in the future (long term cooperation). People are much, much less charitable to non-relatives, or to those outside their own tribe (the other). But like I said way up in the beginning, evolution doesn't have perfect aim. It's not a conscious creator who implements designs the same way an intelligent designer might. Evolution often results in good enough, not perfection. So a general instinct to help those in your own tribe will be helpful, but could spill over into helping strangers. Parental instincts to help your own children and those of your near relatives can spill over into helping babies in general. And of course, in the more intelligent animals like us apes, dolphins & whales, some birds, and a few others, our extremely complex personalities provide even more opportunities for individuals to consciously choose actions that may not be in their evolutionary best interests. It doesn't mean natural selection favors those choices, but rather that natural selection does favor the larger set of complex behaviors, because their benefits outweigh the occasional 'poor' choice (poor in an evolutionary sense, not necessarily in a moral one). Finding examples of true altruism that weren't just the occasional misfiring of otherwise evolutionarily beneficial behaviors would actually be a major blow to our current understanding of evolution. Outside the somewhat controversial theories of group selection, there's no mechanism to explain why an organism would help out another organism if it didn't gain at least some benefit for itself or its genes. But cooperation, tit-for-tat, kin selection, and complex behaviors in intelligent animals do all go to show that the alternative isn’t a cut-throat, dog eat dog world. There are still plenty of reasons evolution will favor cooperation, since cooperation can bring benefits to everybody.

Question: What is the evolutionary reason for biological ageing?
Answer: It's often helpful to think of evolution in terms of reproduction. As my one friends put it, "Forget survival of the fittest – the only reason survival is important in evolution is because you cannot reproduce when you're dead."* And while all things being equal, staying alive forever would certainly enable you to make more babies, all things aren't equal. Even if we didn't die of old age, something would end up killing us eventually – accidents, infections, predators, etc. Depending on the specific organism and its niche, there's some age by which it's overwhelmingly likely to be dead, anyway. On top of that, consider that maintaining a body doesn't come for free. It takes calories to repair injuries, maintain an immune system, suppress cancer, etc. And calories that are going towards that maintenance aren't going towards reproduction (mating, raising babies, defending territories, etc.). So, evolution finds a balance – put enough calories into maintenance to live long enough to reproduce, but just enough to maintain your body until the odds are likely that you'd be dead from something else, anyway. Since there's so little chance of any organisms within a certain species surviving past that age, it doesn't matter what happens to their bodies after that. You can see how this plays out by comparing the lifespans of different species. Something like a whale, which has very few natural predators, does have a very high likelihood of surviving year to year, so they have evolved to put significant energy into maintaining their bodies – over a century, in some cases. Same thing for large land tortoises on the Galapagos Islands. They do benefit by surviving for many breeding seasons, since it gives them that many more opportunities to reproduce. But something like a mouse, which is being hunted by everything from rattlesnakes to housecats to owls, isn't likely to last long in this world. Their best bet is to have as many offspring as quickly as they can, before something kills them, and not waste much energy on maintaining their bodies. Consequently, even if raised in captivity, mice won't live much past 1 to 3 years. Unlike some popular misconceptions might imply, it has nothing to do with gene turnover to promote evolution, or older generations making way for the next generation to avoid competing over resources (because honestly, from an evolutionary perspective, outside your own personal offspring, who gives a damn about the neighbor's kids – they're not carrying your genes**). It's because death is inevitable, so evolution finds the right balance of maintaining your body for long enough, and then putting everything else it can into reproduction. * That quote is from Scott Solomon, in his book, Future Humans: Inside the Science of Our Continuing Evolution: Solomon, Scott: 9780300208719: Amazon.com: Books ** Of course, that's oversimplifying things a bit. Kin selection does mean that it's beneficial to help relatives besides just your direct offspring. And various strategies of cooperation can be mutually beneficial even among non-related organisms. Still, it's never in an organism's evolutionary interests to sacrifice its own reproductive success for the sake of a non-relative.

Question: Are beneficial mutations rare?
Answer: Yes. Beneficial mutations are rare. While I've never been able to find actual numbers specifying just how rare beneficial mutations are in comparison to deleterious or neutral mutations (admittedly, I'm not an expert on this), I have found plenty of general statements from technical and/or reputable sources about beneficial mutations being rare, along with one calculation I found that implied they were basically negligible in comparison to neutral or deleterious mutations. I actually spent a decent amount of time researching this for one particular debate in the comments section of another of my answers*, so I'll share a bit of what I found then, along with another paper I just found recently. Like I said, most of what I found was broad or general statements in those sources, especially in the background sections or in general discussion. So here are the links to those sources along with excerpts of what the authors stated. In each case, the bolding was done by me, to highlight the most relevant statements. The Effects of Deleterious Mutations on Evolution at Linked Sites Brian Charlesworth MUTATIONS that increase the fitness of their carriers are, of course, the basis of adaptive evolution. For this reason, the literature on evolutionary genetics is full of studies that document “positive” selection on genetic variants in natural populations—with the advent of data on the resequencing of numerous whole genomes from the same species, we can expect a tidal wave of such examples. But, as was pointed out long ago by geneticists such as Timofeeff-Ressovsky (1940) and Muller (1949, 1950), most mutations that affect the phenotype must be deleterious, because biological machinery has been subject to billions of years of selection to improve its performance. Because the nucleotide sites at which deleterious mutations can arise are numerous and distributed throughout the genome, the constant mutational production of deleterious variants and their elimination by “purifying” selection have major effects on the mean fitness of a population, its level of inbreeding depression, and its genetic variability with respect to fitness components. The population genetics of beneficial mutations H. Allen Orr The history of population genetics, especially theoretical population genetics, presents a paradox. Although population genetics arose from the fusion of Darwin's theory of adaptation by natural selection with Mendel's theory of inheritance, the field has been concerned historically far more with deleterious and, later, with neutral mutations than with beneficial ones. The paradox has, of course, a simple solution: population geneticists were looking under the lamp post. In particular, mutations having negative or negligible effects on fitness are more common and thus easily studied, while those having positive effects on fitness are far rarer and thus studied only with difficulty. Genetic Mutation Laurence Loewe A single mutation can have a large effect, but in many cases, evolutionary change is based on the accumulation of many mutations with small effects. Mutational effects can be beneficial, harmful, or neutral, depending on their context or location. Most non-neutral mutations are deleterious. In general, the more base pairs that are affected by a mutation, the larger the effect of the mutation, and the larger the mutation's probability of being deleterious. Neutral Theory: The Null Hypothesis of Molecular Evolution Laurent Duret It must be stressed that the neutral theory of molecular evolution is not an anti-Darwinian theory. Both the selectionist and neutral theories recognize that natural selection is responsible for the adaptation of organisms to their environment. Both also recognize that most new mutations in functionally important regions are deleterious and that purifying selection quickly removes these deleterious mutations from populations. Thus, these mutations do not contribute—or contribute very little—to sequence divergence between species and to polymorphisms within species. Rather, the dispute between selectionists and neutralists relates only to the relative proportion of neutral and advantageous mutations that contribute to sequence divergence and polymorphism. Revisiting the genetic load argument with Dan Graur Laurence A. Moran The most difficult part of these calculations is estimating the percentage of mutations that are beneficial, neutral, and deleterious. Population geneticists have rightly assumed that the number of beneficial (selected) mutations is insignificant so they concentrate on the number of deleterious mutations. The estimates range from about 4% of the total mutations to about 40% of the total based on the analysis of mutations in coding regions. I even found one paper that calculated the fraction of deleterious mutations as 1 – fo, where fo is the fraction of neutral mutations. In other words, beneficial mutations were so rare that they were considered negligible and didn't even enter into the calculation. So, I know that doesn't do a great job quantifying it, other than to say that beneficial mutations are much more rare than neutral or deleterious mutations. * The answer with that debate in the comments section was Jeff Lewis's answer to How does an evolution denier explain the different covid-19 variants that have emerged?

Question: How could a human evolve from a cluster of cells to a fish-like creature then a monkey and then a human? How is that possible?
Answer: The short answer is small, incremental changes every step of the way. And each one of those steps still had to be a fully developed and functional organism in its own right. Some folks seem to have a misconception that evolution would have to create features in anticipation of some future benefit, but that's pretty obviously problematic. Natural selection can only act on organisms as they exist in their own time. Evolving into a 'cluster of cells', for example, began first as communities of single celled organisms living together for mutual benefit. Over generations, those communities became more organized, allowing some members of the community to take on specialized roles to increase the productivity of the whole. Eventually, these clusters crossed the murky threshold from communities of individuals to a multicellular organism. And you can keep going from there as multicellular organisms slowly developed new organs and structures generation by generation, eventually resulting in the variety of life around today, including us humans. The long answer is beyond the scope of a Quora answer, so I'm going to recommend a book, instead: From the Beginning - The Story of Human Evolution, by David Peters*. Published back in 1991, it's a little bit dated at this point, and is missing some newer discoveries to fill in some of the gaps, but it's still a great overview of our entire evolutionary history from the first cells to us. You can download the entire book as a PDF for free from the following page: Although I think the book addresses this well enough, as a caveat, don't misinterpret evolutionary histories like this to imply anything special or 'predestined' about human evolution. You could trace the evolutionary history of any organism alive today through its own ancestry all the way back to the first life. For obviously self-centered human reasons, this book is looking at the particular path that led to us people, but every single organism alive and extinct has its own corresponding path. I have written somewhat related answers to smaller portions of your larger question, so here are a couple of those if you're interested: Anyway, I hope that's enough explanation to get you started. But if you really want more detail, go download that book. It's free, and it's got a lot more information that I could put into a Quora answer. * I will caution you a bit on David Peters. As a paleoartist and popular science writer, his books from the '80s and '90s were great. But after that, he seems to have become a bit eccentric in his own personal paleontological efforts, leading to some rather tenuous claims that don't have much of any support from the rest of the scientific community. Question: How long did it take for humans to evolve from monkeys? Why are there no living monkeys that have evolved into humans?
Answer: Although I usually avoid answering the A.I. Quora Prompt Generator (QPG) questions, there are already several other answers to this one that all took a different approach than I would have, so let me add my 2¢. Trying to pin specific numbers to this answer comes down to what you want to call a monkey, and whether you think monkeys should be monophyletic, paraphyletic, or polyphyletic. It doesn't change the actual evolutionary history of humans, just the semantics of what's a monkey and what isn't. Here's a diagram to help understand those terms: ABOVE SOURCE: Monophyletic, Polyphyletic, & Paraphyletc Taxa Here are the written definitions from that page: ...a monophyletic taxon is defined as one that includes the most recent common ancestor of a group of organisms, and all of its descendents [as in (a)]. ...a paraphyletic taxon [is] one that includes the most recent common ancestor, but not all of its descendents [as in (c)]. A polyphyletic taxon is defined as one that does not include the common ancestor of all members of the taxon [as in (b)]. Now, here's a broad evolutionary history of primates: ABOVE SOURCE: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960982212008068 So, the semantic question comes down to, what on that diagram is a monkey? If it's only the New World monkeys and Old World monkeys but not the 'Early simians', then monkeys are a polyphyletic group. That would mean we humans evolved from simians, but not monkeys, so the QPG's question can't be answered. If you think those early simians are themselves monkeys, but want to split apes off into something separate, then monkeys would be a paraphyletic group. Our lineage, the apes, would have split off from the monkeys around 36 million years ago, which would make the answer to the QPG's question 36 million years. (Though to be clear, you could say the same thing about all the other modern apes, as well. For example, that it's taken chimpanzees 36 million years to evolve from monkeys.) But if you think monkeys should be a monophyletic group, then everything descended from those early simians should be counted as monkeys. And then the question is back to being unanswerable, since we humans would still be monkeys, ourselves. My most recent monkey ancestors would be my mom and dad. I personally descended from monkeys in the late 1970s. That last point does address the QPG's last question. The living monkeys that evolved into humans are us. And the reason why no other monkeys or apes are evolving to be more like us now is because of the Competitive exclusion principle. We humans already occupy the niche of being hyper social technological primates. So other primates need to specialize in other niches that don't compete with ours. Anyway, while the question did come from the QPG, I have seen real people sincerely ask similar questions, so I think this was worth answering. And although the answer comes down partially to semantics, the evolutionary history of people in that diagram up above is still accurate no matter which creatures you think are monkeys or not.
