Question: Why do people have a problem with Christianity so much? Or is it because they think it might/could be the true religion?
Answer: As an atheist, I don't think any religions are true. But living in the U.S., our country is so saturated with Christianity that Christianity is the religion that affects me by far the most. Here, for example, are the results from a fairly recent poll on the religious makeup in the U.S.: ABOVE SOURCE: The Largest Survey Ever Conducted of American Religious and Denominational Identity: 14 Major Findings from a Landmark Study Note that all the blue and green slices are Christians. Purple and grey are unaffiliated or people who didn't respond. Only those small orange slices are non-Christian religions (and arguably, Jehovah's Witnesses should have been included with the Christians instead). None of those other religions make up a large enough percentage of the population to have much influence. Anecdotally, I've never had a Buddhist come knocking on my door to preach their scriptures. I've never found Muslim tracts hidden in books at the bookstore. I haven't seen Hindus shouting with a megaphone on a street corner when I was just trying to get into the Stars game. But I've experienced all of those, and more, from Christians. And that's not even getting into the political influence of those Christians. Notice how nearly a quarter of those folks in the above graph were Unaffiliated, and it's actually closer to 30% in more recent surveys (How U.S. religious composition has changed in recent decades). But do you know what the Congress and Senate look like? ABOVE SOURCE: Faith on the Hill In the House, nobody specifically identified as unaffiliated, atheist, or agnostic. Though a whopping 1 person did identify as Humanist, and 3.7% responded with "Don't know/Refused to answer". In the Senate, there was 1 senator who identified as unaffiliated, and a further 4 who went with the "Don't know/Refused to answer". So in a nation where around 30% of the population is religiously unaffiliated, and only around 2/3 are Christians, 88% of House members are Christian, while 85% of Senators are. Now, I know that plenty of Christians are perfectly capable of separating their religious beliefs from secular concerns, and do respect the First Amendment's separation of church and state, and that it's not all Christians trying to enforce religiously based laws. But still, for those of us who aren't Christians, it would be nice if our government representatives were a little more representative. Basically, we have 'so much' of a problem with Christianity, because that's the religion that actually causes us problems. I don't think any of the other religions are right*, either, but they simply don't have much influence in the U.S. *Okay, technically, not all religions spend much effort on the supernatural, and are more about philosophies, e.g. Unitarian Universalists. So they're not necessarily wrong in the same way as religions which make objective claims about reality.

Question: Do people with little animal door flaps ever get unwelcome intruders in their homes?
Answer: More than once. A Midnight Visitor The first time was close to my daughter's 15th birthday. And I know that specifically because we had a full house of relatives who were in town for her quinceañera. Our doggie/cat door was from the house to the garage. We then left the small back door of the garage open to the back yard, so that the cats and weenie dog could get in and out that way. We'd occasionally had issues with racoons in the past when I kept the dog food out in the garage, but after I started securing the lid better, they started leaving us alone. But that evening, we'd left the big garage door open, and a family of racoons got into the garage. We thought we'd chased them all out, so we completely shut all the outside garage doors, thinking that would keep the entire family out. Sometime around two in the morning, the weenie dog started barking and barking, waking up everybody in the house. I came downstairs, and there he was, with a baby racoon cornered in the family room and a gathering crowd of family members. I guess one of the racoon family had been left behind and found its way through the doggie door. My uncle told me it was just a baby so why don't I just go and grab it. I shot back why doesn't he go grab it. In the end, we called animal control, and they came and got it. A Nosy Neighbor We went for years without any more unexpected visitors to the house. In the meantime, our previous cats and dogs had all died, and we'd become roommates with a new cat, who started off feral using our garage, and who I was able to eventually coax into the house and teach him how to use the cat door. My wife named him Chester. He was a long haired tabby cat. There was another long haired tabby cat running around the neighborhood who looked very similar. At first, I named this other cat Not Chester. But I eventually learned that he was an actual pet who belonged to our neighbor two houses down, who we then began calling Sir William Wallace the Gentleman. Well, being a house cat himself, he understood the concept of cat doors, and I began catching him, or evidence of him, in the house on a pretty regular basis. It was especially irritating to find the butter I left out on the counter with a whole bunch of cat sized bites taken out. The last straw was when I was in our upstairs office working from home, and he had the audacity to come all the way upstairs to the room I was in. After that, I investigated higher tech options, and bought an electronic cat flap that you could program to only unlock for your specific cat's RFID chip (which meant Chester also got a trip to the vet to get chipped). Problem solved, mostly. A Thief in the Night One problem with this cat flap is that the way it locked under normal operation, it only blocked the flap from opening inward. For going out, the flap could still swing open. This worked fine for most animals, but racoons aren't most animals. We had a container full of pecans in the dining room, close to the garage door, and I came down one morning to find pecan shells all over the dining room floor. I didn't think too much about it, and just cleaned them up. But when it happened again, I knew there was a problem. It seems that the racoon had figured out how to get just enough of a grip on the flap to pull it open from the outside. Somewhat fortuitously, that was just around the time I was getting ready to head to El Paso for a month, taking Chester with me. So I set the cat flap to the completely locked mode (which wouldn't open in either direction), and put a trash can right in front of it on the inside of the house. I think the racoon figured out that his free meal ticket was over, so that seemed to put an end to it. Still a Nosy Neighbor Now that we've had the electronic flap for a couple years, it doesn't swing quite as freely as it did when new. So sometimes when Chester comes in, it won't swing back all the way shut to where it gets locked. And so, just a month or two ago, I was downstairs with Chester on my lap, when I heard something eating his cat food. I looked, and there was Sir William Wallace stealing Chester's food. So I chased him out again. So yeah, we've had our share of uninvited guests thanks to the doggie/cat door. The electronic one seems to have solved most of the problems, but it hasn't stopped them completely.

Question: If statistics are correct that one in ten men are gay, then which one of the twelve disciples of Christ was gay? One of them had to be a closet case.
Answer: That’s not how probabilities work. Taking your statistic at face value, the probability that at least one of the 12 disciples was gay would be calculated as: 1 − ( 1 − p ) n 1 − ( 1 – 1 10 ) 12 71.8 % And sure, 71.8% is decently high odds, but it’s not guaranteed that “One of them had to be a closet case.” Take in other potential objections, such as whether or not that stat truly is accurate, or whether folks 2000 years ago even had the same conceptions of gay vs. straight as we do today, and it’s problematic to try to draw any conclusions around this.

Question: If you don’t reach escape velocity, but with as much fuel as you need, would you be able to leave Earth?
Answer: There are a several things to understand here. First is what escape velocity actually means. It's the velocity you would have to be moving, that without any more thrust (i.e. just coasting from then on out) that you would be on a path to eventually 'escape' Earth's gravity (or whatever other body you're talking about escaping, such as the Sun, the Moon, or other planets). Next, escape velocity is dependent on your distance from the Earth (or whatever other body), since the influence of Earth's gravity decreases the further away you get. At the surface, escape velocity is 25k mph (40k km/h). But as you get further away from Earth, the escape velocity drops pretty rapidly at first, and then slowly begins approaching zero. But another big consideration is something known as the sphere of influence (or the related Hill sphere). While it's technically true that gravity from the Earth extends to an infinite distance, there are so many other bodies in our own solar system and broader universe, that at a relatively 'minor' distance (in astronomical terms, at least), the Earth's gravity becomes negligible compared to other bodies. Within our solar system, for example, the Earth's sphere of influence (per Wikipedia) is 577k miles (929k km), which is roughly 2.4x further away than the Moon orbits the Earth. Once you get further than that from the Earth, the Sun's gravity will overwhelm the Earth's, and an object's motion will be governed almost entirely by the Sun's gravity (assuming it's not within some other planet or moon's sphere of influence). So, if you were thinking of escape velocity as 25k mph, realize that that's only close to the surface of the Earth. If you had some means to continuously provide thrust and continuously move away from Earth, eventually you would get far enough away that whatever speed you were moving would be greater than the Earth's escape velocity at that distance – it will just be a lot lower than that 25k mph at the surface. Or, if you were to travel far enough that you went past the Earth's sphere of influence, then the Earth's gravity would be negligible compared to the Sun's, and your path would instead be dominated by the Sun's gravity. (And of course, if you could somehow keep moving away from the Sun, you would eventually get far enough away that the Sun's gravity would be negligible compared to the overall galaxy.) The kicker, though, is how you would actually accomplish that continuous thrust, and just exactly what you mean by "with as much fuel as you need". Rockets already are designed to get the most bang for the buck out of the fuel they can carry. They accelerate so quickly because it is the best way to do it. Consider the extreme – imagine if you had a rocket that generated just enough thrust to hover*. You'd sit there burning fuel, but not climbing. You'd eventually run out of fuel without going anywhere, no matter how much fuel you carried. If you barely increased your thrust, you'd climb slowly, but you'd still run out of fuel before you made it very far. And it's not simply a matter of carrying more fuel. That extra fuel is going to make you heavier, which means you'll need even more thrust, burning more fuel, in a vicious cycle of diminishing returns. You really need to read up on the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation if you want to understand this mathematically, but the best use of your fuel is to accelerate as quickly as possible. As long as we're stuck using rockets, slow, leisurely climbs just aren't a realistic possibility to get into space. *Of course, this thought experiment is still simplifying things, since your rocket will get lighter as it burns off fuel. But I suppose you could be using rocket engines that could be throttled, so that you can constantly adjust the thrust to that required for hover.

Question: What evidence supports the theory of natural selection and evolution as the origin of life on Earth, according to Charles Darwin?
Answer: Well Quora Prompt Generator, this is actually a good question. While some of the strongest modern day evidence we have for evolution lies in DNA and the fossil record, DNA wasn't available at all to Darwin, and the fossil record wasn't anywhere near so well known, so Darwin had to rely on other forms of evidence to understand evolution and natural selection. You can get a quick overview just by looking at the titles of the chapters in his landmark book, On the Origin of Species: 1. VARIATION UNDER DOMESTICATION. 2. VARIATION UNDER NATURE. 3. STRUGGLE FOR EXISTENCE. 4. NATURAL SELECTION. 5. LAWS OF VARIATION. 6. DIFFICULTIES ON THEORY. 7. INSTINCT. 8. HYBRIDISM. 9. ON THE IMPERFECTION OF THE GEOLOGICAL RECORD. 10. ON THE GEOLOGICAL SUCCESSION OF ORGANIC BEINGS. 11. GEOGRAPHICAL DISTRIBUTION. 12. GEOGRAPHICAL DISTRIBUTION—continued. 13. MUTUAL AFFINITIES OF ORGANIC BEINGS: MORPHOLOGY: 14. RECAPITULATION AND CONCLUSION. In the first two chapters about variation, Darwin was looking at existing animals. One of his insights was the arbitrary distinction between 'varieties' and 'species', and that these distinctions weren't actually very clear cut. If species had been created separately and distinctly, you would expect identification to be straightforward. But if species were gradually morphing generation by generation, then you would run into these types of difficulties that Darwin identified. Rather than the differences in individual organisms being slight variations around a common archetype, there wasn't really any metaphysical archetype at all, nothing constraining what was 'normal' within a population or stopping the population from shifting over time. I'll also note that Darwin spent a lot of these chapters looking at pigeons, since those were a popular animal among breeders at the time, with lots of examples of different varieties and changes through breeding. The Struggle for Existence was more laying the groundwork to introduce natural selection. It seems rather obvious, now, but when you look at just how many offspring most organisms have, it's way, way more than what the environment can support (e.g. sea turtles lay hundreds of eggs each nesting season – if they all survived, the world would be quickly overrun by sea turtles). So, that necessarily means that the vast majority of organisms are killed without ever reproducing themselves, setting up an implicit competition. The fourth chapter is obviously where Darwin explicitly explained Natural Selection. Whether you want to count that as evidence or not, it was where he proposed a plausible framework for evolution. And the way science actually works in practice, you need that combination of evidence and explanatory framework to make a truly successful theory. The chapter on Laws of Variation looked once again to many types of living organisms, and the types of variation within populations – birds (and more pigeons, again), beetles, blind cave animals, various plants, etc., and especially the patterns of variation, and how those patterns were better explain by common descent than by special creation. Chapter 6 was about Difficulties on Theory. Darwin did highlight the lack of known transitional forms in the fossil record at the time. This is also the chapter that includes the statement loved by creationists, that the evolution of the eye "seems, I freely confess, absurd in the highest possible degree." However, for each of the potential difficulties he raised, he went on to offer responses and potential mitigating reasons, and still kept his conjecture based on evidence from living organisms (e.g. even though he got it a bit mixed up, highlighting the similarity of swim bladders to lungs as a potential evolutionary pathway; though in truth, lungs actually came first and evolved into swim bladders). And in the case of the fossil record, he's certainly been vindicated, as more extensive study in the century and a half since he published that book has found innumerable transitional fossils. In fact, one of the best examples, Archaeopteryx, was discovered in 1861, just 2 years after he published The Origin in 1859. Darwin himself noted that the chapter on Instinct could have been included in the previous chapter, but he decided to give it a fuller treatment. And again, his approach was to show plausible scenarios for adaptations that might at first blush seem too far fetched. He even introduced the idea of kin selection, "that selection may be applied to the family, as well as to the individual, and may thus gain the desired end." The next chapter was about Hybridism, and taking a close look at fertility and infertility when hybridizing organisms from different species and varieties. This was an in-depth analysis to support his previous point of the distinction between species and varieties not being clear cut, which is what you'd expect from common descent. The next two chapters dealt with the geological record. The first of these two was a more detailed treatment of the issues raised in Chapter 6 about the incompleteness of the geological record, while explaining what was known at the time. As far as evidence, this was obviously pretty heavy on geological strata and formations. The next chapter built on that, synthesizing the facts previously laid out and introducing a few more fossils to explain how the evidence that did exist was entirely consistent with and indicative of common descent. Moreover, and perhaps based on his time on the Beagle, he described how fossils in different regions were more consistent with each other and the still living life in those regions, rather than other regions. If creatures had all been created rather than evolved, why would you see this pattern of regional similarity? The next two chapters were some of the lines of evidence that impressed me the most – Geographical Distribution. This built upon the idea touched on in the last chapter, of the similarity of organisms in certain regions compared to different regions, even when two regions may have broadly similar habitats. To give one striking example of two similar habitats that were even extremely close to one another yet geographically isolated, "No two marine faunas are more distinct, with hardly a fish, shell, or crab in common, than those of the eastern and western shores of South and Central America; yet these great faunas are separated only by the narrow, but impassable, isthmus of Panama." Some of my favorite bits of evidence from this chapter come from experiments Darwin did himself to try to better understand the ways in which seeds could be dispersed to spread the range of particular species. In one experiment, he immersed several types of seeds in salt water, periodically pulling some out and planting them, to see how long the seeds could survive such conditions (up to months in a few cases). In another, and getting his hands a bit dirtier, "In the course of two months, I picked up in my garden 12 kinds of seeds, out of the excrement of small birds, and these seemed perfect, and some of them, which I tried, germinated." In those chapters on geographical distribution, I was especially struck by his observations and data of the life on oceanic islands. Islands (or at least some of them) are self-contained, isolated habitats. From the framework of special creation and the immutability of species, the types of life on them could be anything the creator desired, and you might suspect a sort of specialized island ecosystem that was the same from island to island no matter where on Earth. But the reality is that life on islands is most similar to life on the nearest mainland, without actually being the same species. Moreover, the kinds of life on islands isn't just a representative subset of mainland life, but is biased by certain other considerations. For example, Darwin specifically noted that no mammals were ever found to be indigenous to islands more than 300 miles away from a continent, while they were indigenous on islands closer to continents. Darwin's key insight in all this was that these patterns are explained by life arriving at islands from the mainland, and then evolving to adapt to their new island life once there. The bias is explained by the types of animals that can survive the journeys. That puts birds and flying insects as very likely island inhabitants (for example, getting caught by the winds of a storm), while cold blooded animals with low food needs could survive long 'rafting events' on vegetation mats or floating debris, while mammals with their high food needs could only survive short journeys. The chapter on Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings looked at the well known similarities in the anatomy of various organisms, and how those similarities naturally form into nested hierarchies. He went into details such as homologous organs, vestigial features, embryology, etc. I haven't quoted much from Darwin throughout this answer, so here's a bit of a longer excerpt where he gets a bit more excited than normal (he used an exclamation mark): How inexplicable are these facts on the ordinary view of creation! Why should the brain be enclosed in a box composed of such numerous and such extraordinarily shaped pieces of bone? As Owen has remarked, the benefit derived from the yielding of the separate pieces in the act of parturition of mammals, will by no means explain the same construction in the skulls of birds. Why should similar bones have been created in the formation of the wing and leg of a bat, used as they are for such totally different purposes? Why should one crustacean, which has an extremely complex mouth formed of many parts, consequently always have fewer legs; or conversely, those with many legs have simpler mouths? Why should the sepals, petals, stamens, and pistils in any individual flower, though fitted for such widely different purposes, be all constructed on the same pattern? Of course, the explanation as put forth by Darwin is common ancestry, and modifying the anatomy of ancestors, rather than a creator creating organisms from scratch without constraint. The last chapter was just a summary (recapitulation) of the book as a whole, so not much for me to add in this answer as it pertains to evidence. So, that's a summary of the evidence for evolution and natural selection as according to Charles Darwin. The way we so often think of evolution as a study of the past, when I first read On the Origin of Species, I really was struck by how much Darwin relied on evidence from the present day and living organisms, and how he was able to infer common descent from the patterns in existing life. And even that was enough to convince most naturalists of his day of the truth of evolution. I think Darwin himself would be amazed to see just how many fossils people have found since then, and how many details later scientists were able to fill in.

Question: Is Terrence Howard right that 1 + 0 = 1 and 1 x 1 = 2?
Answer: I came across a recent video about this, posted just a week ago, and which has around 1.2 million views so far: What's a bit amazing is how many people in the comments seem to agree with him. I'm not sure how many are just trolling, but just in case there are folks who really are confused by this video and Howard's weird 'math', let's take a closer look. I'll start off this answer with super basic math, but then try to get into some discussion that's hopefully a bit more interesting. For those interested, Howard's book, which goes into even more detail, is available online for free: So let's start off with those basics, and why it really is true that 1×1=1, and not Howard's odd claim that 1×1=2. I apologize if all this seems rather basic, but one of the easiest ways to visualize multiplication is with grids of squares. Here are a few that I drew up in Excel. If you have a grid that's 3 squares by 2 squares, that can be written as 3×2, which is obviously 6 squares. If your grid is only 1×3, then you have 3 squares. And if your grid is 1×1, then it's just 1 square. This is all simple math and pretty obvious. Contrary to the way Howard seems to want math to work, a 1×1 grid does not produce 2 squares. Howard also seems to have a problem with multiplying by zero. He never actually proposes what he wants 1×0 to be, but this one's also pretty obvious from looking at grids. It doesn't matter how many hypothetical columns you have in your grid if it doesn't have any rows. 1×0=0 just like 10×0=0. Okay. Let's move on to something a bit more interesting – units. When you multiply real life things, you have to pay attention to the units. For example, even the video mentioned something about areas. Say you had a rectangle 1 ft × 1 ft. When you multiply those, you're not just multiplying the numbers 1 × 1. You're mutliplying (1 ft)×(1 ft). Or, to reorganize it just a bit, since you can multiply in any order, that's the same thing as (1×1)×(ft × ft), which gives an answer of 1 ft². And of course that makes sense. A 1 ft × 1 ft floor tile is one square foot, aka 1 ft². To get 2 ft², you would need two floor tiles, 1 ft × 2 ft. The video used an example of multiplying a penny by a penny. But this is something that doesn't make much intuitive or physical sense. What is it even supposed to represent? If you remember to pay attention to the units, it would be 1 ¢ × 1 ¢, or 1¢². But what is ¢² supposed to be? The value of money isn't measured in ¢², but just ¢, or more often $. (Or to use the video's exact nomenclature, 1 penny × 1 penny = 1 penny², but the unit of penny² doesn't correlate to counting pennies.) Let's look at an example of multiplying with money that makes more sense (lol). Say you had a bunch of boxes with 1 penny in each box. If you wanted to figure out how much money you had, you'd use a formula something like: (1 ¢/box)×(N box) Lets do a little bit of 'unit analysis' on that, going through a few steps of basic algebra: (1 × N)×((¢/box) × box) (1 × N)×(¢ × box / box) (1 × N)×(¢ × 1) N ¢ So the math works out to an answer that is just ¢, which is what we're interested in for the value of the money. If the units didn't work out that way, it would mean you had a formula that was calculating something else. So, to get back to Howard's claims, let's consider that we had one box: (1 ¢/box)×(1 box) = 1¢ So, the math works out to 1 ¢, which matches exactly what you'd already know without going through the math. One box with one penny inside is still just one penny, not two pennies. And just to be clear that this is multiplication, if you had a scenario with 2 pennies per box, and 3 boxes, you would have: (2 ¢/box)×(3 box) = 6¢ Or, looking at Howard's weird objections to multiplying by zero, if you had zero boxes, the math would be: (1 ¢/box)×(0 box) = 0 ¢ And of course, the math still works out. By not paying attention to units, Howard became even more confused when trying to multiply with pennies. A penny has a value of 1 ¢. But in different units, it has a value of $ 0.01. Those are the same value, because it takes 100 ¢ to equal $1. So even though it doesn’t make sense to multiply a penny times a penny, when you do legitimate math with money (like my box example above), pay attention to whether you're using $ or ¢ and don't get them mixed up. There's a tad bit more interesting discussion around his weird ideas around √2. First, he seemed a bit amazed that √2 + √2 = (√2)^3. But it's just a quirk of doing these calculations with 2, since adding a number to itself is the same thing as multiplying by 2. To do a tad more algebra, and understanding that √2 is simply another way to write 2^½: √2 + √2 2√2 2^(3/2) (√2)^3 Of course, that won't happen with any other number (besides zero), because when you add them together, you're not multiplying them by themselves. In other words, while √2 + √2 = 2√2, when looking at a different number √4 + √4 = 2√4, and not 4√4. However, if you add √4 together 4 times, √4 + √4 + √4 + √4 = 4√4 = 4^(3/2) = (√4)^3. So really, there’s a general pattern where you just have to add the numbers together the same number of times as the number itself. If you’ll indulge just a bit more algebra: x√x = x^(3/2) = (√x)^3 Going beyond just the video and looking at his book, Howard also lacked a full understanding of irrational numbers or how calculators work. He went off on one line of thought where he criticized the √2, because when you calculate it on a calculator, you get 1.414213562373095. If you multiply that number by itself on the calculator, the calculator will give an answer of 2. But when you multiply that number by itself by hand, you get 1.999999999999999861967979879025, which isn't actually 2 (I’m assuming his math is right – I didn’t double check him). This boils down to two things – first, irrational numbers can't be represented exactly by any type of fraction, including decimal notation. The string of digits after the decimal point is infinite (somebody calculated 10 trillion digits of √2 in 2022, which is still nothing compared to infinity). Second, calculators and computers don't have infinite memory, so they have to make do with approximating these numbers with a limited number of digits. But these approximations also apply to the answers of the math. So, when the calculator multiplies 1.414213562373095 by itself, the result of the algorithm is 2.000000000000000, because that's as accurate as the calculator can do it. So this is really just a limitation of calculators being tools to make pragmatic calculations that are accurate enough. There are very, very few cases where you would need a calculator to be accurate to more decimal places than that. For the types of scientists and engineers who do need that extra accuracy, they use special programs/computers to do so, but they still can’t calculate numbers to infinite decimal places. (FWIW, for my own day job designing airplanes, regular calculators and computer programs are more than accurate enough.) Most of the rest of the video (when it wasn't rambling about how profound all this was without actually explaining anything about it) was baseless nonsense, some of it from his failure to understand basic math, and some from wild conjecture without understanding anything about the fields he was talking about. If I wanted to respond to the rest of the video point by point, this answer would be huge (and it's already long enough), because just about every single claim is wrong. I mean, you can string words together into sentences that make grammatical sense, but that doesn't give them any credibility. I mean, he tried to say that sound will travel through space by 'inventing' something he called "the most wonderful vibrating preatomic geometry". But we've been to space, both actual astronauts and robotic satellite, probes, and rovers. We know for a fact that sound doesn't travel through space, despite Howard's fanciful imagination. Perhaps one of his points that might resonate with some people is that we humans can only see a small sliver of the electromagnetic spectrum with our own eyes, which is true. For what it's worth, that's also true of all other animals on Earth, because of the nature of how electromagnetic waves interact with matter based on the wavelength (see Bill Otto's answer to Is it possible for human eyes to work as an X-ray? for a more detailed explanation). But you know what we humans do have? Machines and instruments to detect things we can't see with our own eyes. That's how we know about the existence of the broader electromagnetic spectrum in the first place. I'm not saying humanity will ever know everything there is to know about the universe, but it's a bit ironic that Howard is using our ability to use science to detect things beyond our senses as a criticism of science. How would he have known how little of the electromagnetic spectrum we could see if it wasn't for science figuring that out? The video also closed with a bit of discussion of a fiat money system vs. the gold standard. Of course, the only reason the gold standard was valuable was because everybody agreed gold was valuable, not because of any intrinsic value of that particular metal. So a fiat money system is merely taking money one level of abstraction further, where everyone agrees to the value of the thing we call a dollar (or whatever currency another government uses). But there are plenty of other explanations of fiat money systems, so I'm not going to delve into that here. Anyway, that's as much as I'm going to write about Howard's ideas in this video and his book. I know that the basics of why his math is wrong are, well, basic. But hopefully the information I wrote about units and √2 was a bit more interesting.

Question: How is it possible for a specie to pass on evolved genes when it has no power to send genetic messages to its descendants billions of years down the line? I don’t expect anyone to know the answer to this one?
Answer: You've correctly hit on a major misconception that many people seem to have about evolution – that certain mutations or traits should somehow appear in anticipation of some future adaptation. But as you pointed out, that can't happen. Just take a look at the natural world around us today. Every organism is adapted to its current environment and niche. All organisms throughout history have been the same way. The only mutations that were favored by natural selection were beneficial to those organisms in their own time and place. Where some creationists go off the rails is failing to see how certain adaptations could have been the result of countless intermediate stages. Perhaps the quintessential example is eye evolution. The common creationist argument is something along the lines of eyeballs being exquisitely interconnected systems that wouldn't function without all of their current components in place. As I've seen it put too many times, 'What use is half an eye?' But less complex eyes than our own really are useful and functional. We see them in living animals, from something like a hydra which has only photo-sensitive neurons, to starfish with pigment spots, to snails with pigment cups that can detect direction of light without making an image, to nautiluses with pinhole eyes without a lens, to complex 'camera' eyes like us humans or squids. ABOVE: Evolutionary pathway for camera eyes SOURCE: Visualizing the Evolution of Vision and the Eye ABOVE: And since not all eyes are like ours – Evolutionary pathway for compound eyes SOURCE: Visualizing the Evolution of Vision and the Eye Evolution didn't need to preserve adaptations towards a full camera eye in anticipation of that complex configuration. Every step along the way was a useful adaptation, improving the vision in each of those organisms. I've seen this question asked about plenty of other adaptations as well, from arms and legs, to the lungs of us land animals (many people don't seem to know how many existing fish breathe air), and more. I don't want to make this answer too long, but if you're curious about some of those other traits, here are a few more answers you might want to read: Anyway, I hope this answer helps. You're correct in that natural selection can't favor mutations in anticipation of some far off future benefit. Mutations have to be beneficial to an organism in its immediate surroundings. But over many generations, building incrementally on the benefits of generations past, this has still lead to remarkable adaptations.

Question: Why do creationists think the Earth is less than 4,000 years old?
Answer: Because they take the Bible seriously. (Though as a slight correction, you got a bit mixed up on 4000 years old vs. the date of 4000 BC, which was actually around 6000 years ago: 4000 years BC + 2024 years AD). You can get a lot of the way there yourself looking at just two chapters of the Bible. Really, go take a look at these for yourself: These list genealogies from Adam all the way to Abraham, stating the ages when fathers had their sons. If you accept these genealogies, the Biblical account of creation, that Adam was the first person, and that Abraham was a real person who interacted with Egyptian pharaohs, then you've already got a good ballpark guess. I did a quick estimate myself. The only real ambiguity in those chapters comes in two places – the age of Noah when he had Shem, and the age of Terah when he had Abraham. But you're not looking at discrepancies that would be consistent with the Earth being 4.5 billion years old. After Noah was five hundred years old, Noah became the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth. When Terah had lived seventy years, he became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran. So, for my estimate, I just used 500 and 70 for those two ages. I figure people who care about this issue more than me can dig deeper into getting better estimates. Here's what I came up with: So basically, 2000 years from the date of creation to the time of Egyptian pharaohs. If we go with the Middle Kingdom of Egypt, which was very roughly around 2000 BC, that puts the Biblical date of creation around 4000 BC. You can go further, looking at other books of the Bible, especially when all the various kings of Israel and Judah reigned and for how long, but that's a lot more digging to find all those individual verses. Of course, other folks have put in the effort. One of the most meticulous and rigorous, and for this reason also one of the most famous, was Archbishop James Ussher. Contrary to what a lot of people seem to imply, he wasn't the only scholar to do this, nor was he some eccentric outlier in thinking you could accept these Biblical sources as more or less reliable. His estimate just happened to be particularly well respected, so it's the one most remembered today. And going through all that detailed math, he came up with an estimate of 4004 BC. Of course, I hope it hardly needs to be said that modern science has shown this 'history' to be more than a bit off. But if you take the Bible seriously and at more or less face value, as plenty of people did for generations, you end up with an implied date for the creation of the world some time around 4000 BC. Full disclosure: It actually depends on which copy of the Bible you're using. Two of the major 'versions' are the Septuagint and the Masoretic Text, and they list different ages of the fathers throughout Genesis 5 and Genesis 11, resulting in around a 2000 year discrepancy. Still, they do have full genealogies from Adam to Abraham, so unless one of those guys lived to be 4 billion years old, they're still not in line with the actual age of the Earth.

Question: Does anyone think of how to combine the Bible and science?
Answer: Back a couple decades ago when I went through a crisis of faith, I had that youthful combination of naivety and arrogance to think that I could be the one to do this myself. Up until then, I had accepted both science and religion, and reconciled the discrepancies with hand-wavy explanations about trying to explain science to primitive people with no real understanding of geologic time scales or the scale of the universe. You've no doubt heard similar arguments plenty of times, such as the days in Genesis actually representing ages rather than literal 24 hour periods. However, once you start taking a closer look at Bible stories, these rationalizations don't really hold up – at least, not if you're looking for some way to keep the biblical narrative lined up with reality. I mean, according to Genesis, God didn't create the Sun until the fourth day, after the Earth, oceans, and even plants. You can't reconcile that with reality just by saying the days were supposed to represent very long ages. You can try getting even more creative with your interpretations and the symbolism, but by that point, you're really just trying to shoehorn the Bible to match reality, not interpreting it in any type of way that would be obvious without already knowing the science. I've seen others argue that you shouldn't even try to reconcile Genesis with reality, that it's not even a simplified narrative of reality, but just pure allegory (e.g. What is the Relationship Between the Creation Accounts in Genesis 1 and 2? - BioLogos). One issue with this is that it's not obvious from the Bible itself that this is the case, as evidenced by the centuries and centuries that people did take the stories seriously, and did believe that the Earth was only a few thousand years old. It was only once we learned the truth through science that people were forced to reinterprate the Bible out of necessity. And even if you want to say that the more mythical stories like Genesis are allegory, what about other parts like the conquest of the Promised Land? Those read much more like supposed history, but they're also largely inconsistent with real history. See for example, this excellent answer from Frans du Plessis: And once you do get past this preconception that the Bible has to be consistent with reality, you can recognize the actual beliefs of the culture that developed it. For example, the older books like Genesis really do seem to present a flat Earth cosmology. And once you recognize and accept that, you don't have to put yourself through cognitive dissonance trying to force the Bible to say things that the writers never intended. ABOVE CREDIT: Ben Stanhope, (Mis)interpreting Genesis: How the Creation Museum Misunderstands the Ancient Near Eastern Context of the Bible (Scarab Press: Louisville Kentucky, 2018), 88. SOURCE: Old Testament Cosmology Basically, even as somebody who started out from the position of wanting to reconcile the Bible with science, once I began looking into it in detail, I realized that the Bible really is just a collection of very human writings from an ancient society with no particularly special insights or inspiration from the divine. There's no more reason to expect scientific accuracy from the Bible than from any other ancient mythology.

Question: Why is there so much debate over the math question 12÷2(2+4) =?
Answer: A few other answers have said it's because the expression is ambiguous. But that's not really it. The expression isn't ambiguous at all. As an engineer myself, there's only one way to interpret that expression correctly. No. The issue is that lots of folks' exposure to math doesn't go much if at all beyond the high school level, and simplistic understandings of order of operations like PEMDAS or BODMAS. They don't know any further conventions that affect order of operations. The thing that makes this expression completely unambiguous is that there's no symbol in between the 2 and the parenthesis. That makes it clear that 2(2+4) is a single unit that can't be broken up. So the only appropriate way to interpret this expression is: 12 2 ( 2 + 4 ) What might have made this expression a bit ambiguous would have been to add a multiplication symbol: 12÷2×(2+4) Then it could be conceivable to interpret it a bit differently, perhaps instead as: 12 2 ( 2 + 4 ) However, even then, many engineers might interpret it the first way, keeping 2×(2+4) as a single unit as the denominator of the fraction. The reason is that when you're writing math 'inline' as opposed to formatting it the way math should really be written, division symbols are often treated as the fraction bar, with everything to the left assumed to be the numerator, and everything to the right assumed to be the denominator, and not cluttering things up with parentheses. As just one example, here are the definitions of some coefficients from one of my own engineering books, which I can assure you follow the convention that I just described (“my own” is in I own it, not that I wrote it). Really, if you wanted it to be 12/2, you'd probably put the parentheses around that to make it clear that 12/2 was a fraction, and instead write something like: (12/2)(2+4) But just to summarize, the expression as written in the original question isn't ambiguous. The issue is that lots of folks with only limited exposure to math don't know all the conventions affecting order of operations. And if there ever are any questions about ambiguity in an expression you’re writing, don’t be afraid to use parentheses.

Answer: Quite simply, the servers hosting social media are private property, owned (or at least leased/rented) by the social media companies. Just like you have control over your own property, and can tell me what types of signs or billboards I'm allowed to post on your yard, social media companies have control over their property, and can tell people what they're allowed to post on their servers. I'm perfectly free to post whatever signs or billboards I want on my own yard (within zoning restrictions at least). Likewise, if you want to spend the money for your own website, you're free to post whatever you want there. But what you're asking for is to ignore the private property rights of the companies that own the servers hosting social media, and to give you special concessions to infringe upon those companies' property rights. Question: Do atheists believe that cucumbers could evolve into kangaroos if given enough time?
Answer: Well, I'm not going to say it's flat out impossible, but it does seem very, very unlikely. This is a great example of how historical contingency constrains evolution, since that's not at all the way us animals evolved in the first place. Here's an evolutionary tree of eukaryotes, which is the group that includes both us and plants. Land plants, which includes cucumbers, are in the top left, while us animals (metazoans) are in the bottom left: ABOVE SOURCE: https://bsapubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.3732/ajb.1300314 This figure also shows multicellularity vs. unicellularity vs. colonial species. Based on the pattern, it appears that multicellularity evolved independently in several lineages. Or in other words, our common ancestor with plants was still unicellular, and that we and plants each took a different path to arrive at multicellularity. The lineage that led to plants had already developed photosynthesis before evolving multicellularity, so all of their development towards multicellularity was geared around that lifestyle. Likewise, our single celled ancestors were already consuming other organisms, so all of our development towards multicellularity was geared around that lifestyle. And at this point in the present, our different lineages are specialized for our respective lifestyles. What's more, they're not particularly compatible lifestyles. While sunlight is very plentiful, it's not particularly energy dense compared to eating other organisms. So, plants get by on a lot less energy than us animals, which is part of the reason they tend to be generally immobile (though you do get occasional fast responses like Venus fly traps). By contrast, when we eat a plant, we're basically getting all that energy the plant has stored up over time in just a few bites, before going on to the next plant and the next plant, so we can spend much more energy on things like moving around (not that animals have to move around, as evidenced by sponges). For something like a cucumber to evolve into something like a kangaroo is a drastic, drastic change in how those organisms make a living. Sure, if I get creative enough, I can think of kinda sorta plausible scenarios where it could happen, but truth be told, they don't actually seem genuinely plausible. What's more, as long as existing animals are around, you've got to worry about the competitive exclusion principle. What incipient animal-like plant would be able to outcompete existing actual animals? So yeah, given enough time, I'm not sure you could completely rule out something like this, but it does seem rather unlikely.

Question: Evolutionists have been debating the chicken and chicken egg question for a long time. Can evolution explain which came first?
Answer: No, because evolution helps us to understand that it's not the type of thing you can pinpoint. It would be like trying to define the precise second when dusk becomes night, or the precise date that a child becomes an adult. It just doesn't work that way. These are gradual processes that elude precise demarcations. Evolution is a gradual accumulation of genetic changes within an entire population. In sexually reproducing animals, there's no single individual that's a different species from their parents, or indeed, the entire population of which they're a part. Plus, there's plenty of genetic variability within a population, which will be recombined in all types of different ways as the animals mate. So you can't even pick an individual organism as the first chicken, after which all of its descendants will subsequently be chickens, as that individual and its descendants will still have to mate with other members of the population, continuing to mix up those genes. Question: Isn't it crazy that 1 man managed to convince billions of people that they evolved from an animal?
Answer: Actually, yes it is. That's why Darwin is held in such high esteem as the genius he was, and why he was granted the honor of being buried in Westminster Abbey. Other naturalists had proposed ideas of transubstantiation before Charles Darwin, including his grandfather Erasmus Darwin. However, none of those predecessors had managed to convince the larger scientific establishment to take evolution particularly seriously. And Edward Blyth had hit on ideas of natural selection before Darwin published the Origin, though Blyth's comments on the matter went largely unnoticed. Somewhat famously (at least among us nerds), William Wallace also discovered natural selection independently, and even submitted a joint presentation of papers with Darwin to the Linnaean Society of London in 1858. But this submission also didn't have much impact. What did have tremendous impact was when Darwin finally published his book, On the Origin of Species, in 1859. The arguments and evidence he compiled in that book were enormously compelling. Practically overnight, evolution and universal common descent went from a somewhat disreputable position among fringe academics to accepted mainstream science. It was a monumental work on par with the likes of Newton and Einstein. Much of science progresses by incremental contributions from many different researchers. The subsequent history of evolutionary science after Darwin does follow this more general pattern. Looking through the Wikipedia article on the Modern synthesis, you find plenty of contributors like Ernst Mayr, G. Ledyard Stebbins, Theodosius Dobzhansky, E. B. Ford, Bernhard Rensch, Ivan Schmalhausen, George Gaylord Simpson, R. A. Fisher, William Bateson, Julian Huxley, J.B.S. Haldane, and more. But none of those folks, as intelligent as they were, had the same paradigm shifting impact as Charles Darwin. To put it another way, human knowledge had finally progressed to the point where discovering evolution was practically inevitable. It would have happened eventually. But without Darwin, it would have been a more prolonged process that would have taken a bit longer, and the folks who contributed would probably still be mentioned in the history books, but they wouldn't be household names (just look to Alfred Wegener and continental drift). Darwin was a true genius, with a monumental impact on biology. So yes, it is always a bit crazy when you come across such singular geniuses.

Question: On what basis did evolutionists decide humans have a close common ancestry with apes, was it by looks? If so what about the kangaroo and the sloth? If by DNA, what about the banana? If it was by intelligence, what about the octopus?
Answer: Carl Linnaeus is known as the father of modern taxonomy. He developed the now traditional system that you probably learned in high school biology – Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species. This system is a nested hierarchy that we now recognize as being due to evolutionary relatedness, but Linaeus himself was a creationist (he died before Darwin was even born), and was merely trying to recognize the pattern of God's creation. And he based his system largely on physical similarity. Of course, he went deeper than superficial resemblances, and looked at the entire anatomy of organisms. That is how, for example, he recognized that dolphins and whales were mammals and not fish. And Linnaeus recognized the obvious anatomical similarities between humans and other apes, putting humans, chimpanzees, and orangutans all in the same genus, Homo (gorillas weren't yet known to European naturalists, or he almost surely would have included them, as well). I mean, the similarities between humans and other apes is sometimes so striking it's almost eerie: ABOVE SOURCE: Bonobo photos by Frans de Waal Kangaroos and sloths aren't nearly so anatomically similar to humans as the other apes. I mean, yes they're both mammals, so they're more related to humans than, say, a magpie or an oak tree, but not at that same level of similarity as the other apes. I mean, kangaroos are marsupials, for heaven's sake, with many, may differences to us placental mammals. Linnaeus recognized this over 200 years ago. DNA wasn't recognized as our hereditary molecule until the 1940s, and it's only been in more recent decades that scientists have been able to sequence DNA and otherwise study it in much more detail. Much like the anatomical comparisons that Linnaeus pioneered, you can also compare the similarity of the DNA of different organisms, and construct nested hierarchies of similarity. And when scientists did this, the resulting 'trees' matched up nearly spot on with the trees developed from traditional classification. In other words, while we knew from anatomical comparisons that humans were more closely related to apes than to sloths, DNA studies found exactly the same thing. So you have two different lines of evidence to do these comparisons, yet they produce essentially the same results. You mentioned bananas. Bananas are only distantly related to us people, and the genetics confirms this. While our DNA is roughly 98% the same with chimpanzees (it depends on how exactly you're doing the comparison), it's only around 50% the same with bananas. But bananas are multicellular eukaryotes, so even they are more closely related to us than some other life forms. Bacteria, for example, are even more distant relatives, with even less DNA in common with us. Your last question is about intelligence. The thing about lots of evolutionary traits is that they can develop separately through convergent evolution. When this happens, although the traits might have superficial resemblance, there will be lots of differences in the details. And octopuses and other cephalopods have brains that are very different from us mammals. They developed their intelligence through a completely different evolutionary path than us. So yes, anatomical similarities and genetic similarities are both used to determine the relatedness of organisms. But intelligence is a trait that can evolve independently, so it’s not as useful on its own.

Question: Why do they still teach evolution in schools if it's just a theory? I heard they were gonna stop a long time ago because there's no evidence for it. What happened to that?
Answer: Going in reverse of the order you asked the questions: I heard they were gonna stop a long time ago because there's no evidence for it. What happened to that? Even when I first got caught up in the evolution-creationism 'debate' over 20 years ago, this had already been dubbed The Longest Running Falsehood in Creationism, in the appropriately titled article: The author of that article, G.R. Morton, went through written materials all the way back to 1825 showing religious folks claiming that old Earth geology and then later evolutionary biology were about to be abandoned by scientists, because all the 'new' evidence confirmed the Biblical stories. Well, 1825 is nearly 200 years ago by this point, and geologists still think the Earth is far more ancient than a few thousand years, and biologists still see evolution as the fundamental theory of biology. I suspect that you simply heard one of the more recent creationists making a similar dishonest claim. And I'd bet you a steak dinner that they'll still be making the same claim another 20 years from now (I'd go even longer than 20 years, but then I'd never be able to collect on the bet). Why do they still teach evolution in schools if it's just a theory? I see you've already received 28 prior answers to this question, but just to reiterate... Scientific theories and scientific laws are completely different things. Theories are broad frameworks, while laws are concepts that can be expressed in a single formula or short statement. To go with a non-controversial example, think about Newton's 3 Laws of Motion: ABOVE SOURCE: Newton's Laws of Motion Note how simple and short each individual law is. But these laws are a small part of the broader theory of Classical Mechanics. Classical Mechanics is so broad that there are entire textbooks devoted to the theory. ABOVE SOURCE: Amazon, but I'm not going to link to it to be on the safe side regarding spam Evolution is the same way. The high level theory is known as the Modern Synthesis, or perhaps the Extended or Integrated Synthesis, depending on who you're talking to. This high level theory is itself composed of many other theories, laws, and principles, such as Gause’s Law, Bergmann's rule, or Dollo's law of irreversibility. Just like Newton's Laws, these laws within evolutionary theory are short, pithy statements or formulas to explain a concept, and not on the same broad explanatory level as an entire theory. ABOVE SOURCE: reddit So there you have it. Creationists have been claiming the imminent demise of science for nigh on two centuries, now, and I don't expect them to stop any time soon. They're the boy who cried wolf, but who then got their kids, grandkids, and great-grandkids to carry on crying wolf long after everyone else quit paying attention to them. And as far as evolution being a theory – of course it is. Theories are exactly the broad frameworks that get covered in science classes.

Question: Can urine actually be recycled into drinking water, like in sci-fi stories?
Answer: Absolutely. In a sense, nature already does this. There's only so much water on Earth*, so it constantly gets recycled. Human pee. Fish pee. Squirrel pee. Etc. Every drop of water we drink contains water that used to be urine. On a more direct level, yes. Around a decade ago when the town I live in, Wichita Falls, was in the midst of a pretty severe drought, our reservoirs were drying up. So the city built a direct potable reuse (DPR) facility, more affectionately known as toilet-to-tap. It was, from what I can gather, the first city to do so on this type of scale, with more than half of our tap water coming directly from recycled waste water. Of course, that waste water wasn't only urine, but urine was certainly a part of it. Once rain returned a year later, the DPR system was shut down. But it had a perfect safety record during its operation. In the next couple years, Wichita Falls developed and built an indirect potable reuse (IPR), where the treated waste water is dumped into one of our reservoirs, rather than directly back into the water supply. Then, water from the reservoirs is processed with more traditional water treatment facilities. And according to that article up above, this is supposed to be more efficient overall than DPR. But for around a year, we residents of Wichita Falls were drinking water that was recycled from waste water and put directly back into our tap water supply. *Actually, the water cycle is a bit more complex than that, since biological processes often split water into hydrogen and oxygen, and then recombine those again in other processes. So individual water molecules haven’t necessarily been around forever, but the constituent hydrogen and oxygen mostly have.

Question: How has technology changed our lives?
Answer: Technology essentially made our species possible. It's so ingrained into human existence that we barely even think about the most basic forms of technology, but we wouldn't be here without it. One of the most basic technologies, controlled use of fire, goes back at least around 1 million years. That predates Homo sapiens. It was probably Homo erectus that first developed that technology. Purposely shaped stone tools go back even further – 3.3 million years. That's before our ancestors had even evolved into the Homo genus. Those tools were probably made by something like Australopithecus afarensis or Kenyanthropus platyops. ABOVE SOURCE: Oldest stone tools pre-date earliest humans If you look at humans compared to a lot of other animals, while we're not as physically pathetic as some hyperbolic documentaries try to make us out to be, we're still on the slow, weak side when un-armed. But those ancient technologies that our ancestors developed allowed them to hunt, defend themselves, cook food, etc. That in turn allowed our ancestors to develop large, calorie hungry brains, while compensating with smaller muscles that didn't need as much nutrition as some of our bulkier cousins (I'm looking at you, gorillas, with your 5 to 10k calorie per day food requirements – The Influence of Seasonal Frugivory on Nutrient and Energy Intake in Wild Western Gorillas). Without that level of already existing technology in our pre-human ancestors, our own evolution just wouldn't have happened. And while we might consider those ancient technologies to be primitive, that's only from our spoiled perspective with our amazing modern technologies. You can see some uses of technology and tools in other animals, but our pre-human ancestors were already developing technologies beyond what other animals were doing. And by the time actual humans developed, there was a whole plethora of technologies – basket weaving, ropes, clothing, spears, etc. And once agriculture developed around 10k years ago and people could begin accumulating more possessions than just what they could carry, technology really took off. So how has technology changed our lives? By making our very existence possible.

Question: If you are an atheist, do you like Sam Harris? What about Richard Dawkins?
Answer: Out of those two, I only ever paid much attention to Richard Dawkins, so I'll limit my comments to him. He's... okay. Back around 20 years ago when I first started on my path to atheism, Dawkins was one of the leading voices for atheism and science (not the same thing, but so-called 'New Atheism' did/does rely heavily on science). He seemed to be a pretty sensible guy. He was involved in some good public campaigns for atheism (e.g. the Atheist Bus Campaign), and some more questionable ones (e.g. the Brights movement). But by and large, he was a reasonable voice for godlessness. If he was a 'militant' atheist, then there wasn't that much actual militancy within atheism. I finally purchased and read The God Delusion after I was already an atheist (I was too ashamed to be seen buying it at my local bookstore when I was still struggling with religion). It was a decent book that introduced me to things I'd never thought of before, though I haven't gone back to read it recently to see how well it holds up. The next book of his that I read was The Greatest Show on Earth, devoted to explaining the evidence for evolution. But I felt like he spent too much of that book harping on creationism, rather than focusing on the far more interesting topic of evolution itself. I read two other books on evidence for evolution around that same time, Jerry Coyne's Why Evolution Is True, and Donald Prothero's Evolution: What the Fossils Say and Why it Matters, and I recommend both of those books head and shoulders above Dawkins' Greatest Show on Earth. They both found a much better balance of dealing with creationism without it becoming distracting. After that, I read The Magic of Reality. This one was marketed to readers of all ages as a sort of broad science lesson on several topics, from 'Who was the first person' to rainbows to earthquakes. But once again, he harped so much on religion that it felt a bit like The God Delusion for Kids. His axe to grind against religion caused him to miss an opportunity to focus on the science. After that, I'm not sure if I drifted away from following him as closely, or if he himself drifted out of the public eye, but I didn't pay as much attention to him in the following years. I did notice from time to time that he seemed to stick his foot in his mouth on Twitter (I'm honestly not sure if he's even still active on 'X'). But given his age and the way plenty of old people don't keep up with shifting societal norms, while that might be a tad disappointing, it's not shocking (I cringed plenty of times listening to my own older relatives complaining about the changing times). Anyway, I found Dawkins to be a useful voice for atheism and science a couple decades ago when I first became an atheist and when I got involved in the Skeptical movement. After that, I found that he allowed his obsession with religion to mar what could otherwise have been better books. And then after that, I just kind of drifted away from following him, so I can't say too much about his present day activities.

Question: So why are pilots who have been flying for years all saying they know the earth is flat?

So, between my job and personal life, I know lots of pilots, aerospace engineers, and even a few air traffic controllers. And I don't personally know any of them who believe in a flat earth. It's the type of thing we joke about from time to time, but not something that anybody takes seriously. I don't know of any polls or studies to put numbers to this, but if you want some perspectives beyond my own, you can check out pages like this reddit thread: Or read this article from AOPA about a pilot's experience flying around the world: In short, there are so many pilots that I'm sure you can find a handful who think the Earth is flat. ABOVE: This cleaner is advertising a virtual 'genocide' on a microscopic level SOURCE: Uline So how do we value some lives more than others? What makes it wrong to kill an organism? As a short, simple thought experiment, just imagine if we ever did discover intelligent alien life. I'm nearly certain we would extend some types of rights or values to this life. But keep in mind that such aliens would be completely, well, alien. They wouldn't be human beings. They wouldn't be closely related to human beings. They wouldn't have genetics similar to human beings. Heck, their biochemistry might not even use DNA as the genetic molecule. So any arguments of value based on any of those things are, at best, incomplete, and at worst, not really the basis in the first place. It seems that the way we value life is some combination of intelligence and sentience, along with less objective emotional reasons. Dolphins, for example, seem to be very intelligent creatures, with rich emotional lives and social connections. So, many of us feel that killing a dolphin for no good reason is wrong. The bacteria on my kitchen counter, on the other hand, seem very unlikely to have any sentience. So, we don't bat an eye when we wipe down our counters with powerful disinfectants that kill millions of bacteria in one fell swoop. And then there are tradeoffs based on how those other lives affect us. For my own part, for example, I generally don't kill any bugs I find in my house, not even the stinging or biting ones like wasps or spiders. I'll either just let them be, or catch them in a glass and release them outside. But when I found termites getting into the framing around my garage door? You can bet I sprayed it all down myself, then called in an exterminator to treat the entire perimeter of my house. As soon as those termites crossed the line into damaging my property, I wasn't nearly so tolerant. As far as fetuses, and assuming you mean human fetuses as opposed to other mammals (which isn't really at all certain in a discussion on all life, so forgive me if I went too far in my assumption), it still depends on what you mean by 'value'? People can value inanimate objects, after all, so it's certainly possible for people to value a fetus simply because. And many would-be parents will certainly value a fetus for the potential it offers, to eventually develop into an actual person. But if you're asking if we as a society need to extend the same types of rights and protections to a fetus as to an actual person, I would return to my prior points, particularly sentience. This is the same type of consideration we use for end of life decisions, saying that it is okay to cease life support when it's clear that a person is brain dead. And it seems a fitting consideration for start of life decisions, and when a fetus transitions from a mere conglomeration of unconscious cells to an actual person capable of experience. So when does this transition happen? Here's an article that addresses this question: To quote the article: Consciousness requires a sophisticated network of highly interconnected components, nerve cells. Its physical substrate, the thalamo-cortical complex that provides consciousness with its highly elaborate content, begins to be in place between the 24th and 28th week of gestation. Roughly two months later synchrony of the electroencephalographic (EEG) rhythm across both cortical hemispheres signals the onset of global neuronal integration. Thus, many of the circuit elements necessary for consciousness are in place by the third trimester. So while the 'hardware' for experience is in place around the start of the third trimester, if you're looking to synchrony of the EEG rhythm to indicate consciousness, that doesn't occur until a couple months after that, well into the third trimester. So it would seem that throughout most of its development, even though a human fetus is alive in the sense of biological activity and metabolism, it lacks the sentience that would grant it larger considerations of human rights. Anyway, this answer of mine barely scratches the surface. There are other measures of value besides the value of the individual life form, such as biodiversity and the health of ecosystems. There are plenty of other philosophical considerations and moral frameworks, such as social contract theory, utilitarianism, virtue ethics, etc. And of course, my answer is only my own – I can't pretend to speak for all atheists. But hopefully this gives some small sense of the considerations that go into this issue.

Question: How do atheists respond to the saying "everything happens for a reason" after experiencing something negative? Is there a counter argument from an atheist perspective?
Answer: Why do we need a counter argument? You're the one with the saying with troubling implications for reality – that we're all at the mercy of some cosmic puppeteer putting us through the ringer for unfathomable reasons beyond our control. I mean, the common expression is to 'accept your fate', not 'embrace' it or 'rejoice in' it. There's a sense of resignation, of submitting to the biggest bully on the block. So I guess the simplest atheist 'counter argument' is that no, the universe isn't quite that bad. Bad things beyond our control may still happen, but at least it's not some entity toying with us on purpose. However, if you want some more common expressions, there are plenty. One of my favorites that I use quite often is, 'It is what it is.' If you want to sound a bit fancier using a foreign language, you could say 'Que será, será.' Or if you want to go a little more low brow, you can go with the old standby, 'Shit happens.' All of these have a similar intent behind them, that we live in a universe where many things will happen beyond our control. It does no good to dwell on why or what if*, because that still won't change it. Our best course of action is to accept those things, and then do the only thing we can do, control how we react and what actions we ourselves take going forward. *Of course, I don't mean to ignore causes altogether if understanding those causes can help inform your actions in the future. I mean 'why' and 'what if' in a more metaphysical sense. For example, understanding the causes of an airplane accident can drive regulations, retrofits, or training to avoid future accidents. But there's nothing we can do to change accidents that have already happened.

Question: What is the best way to lose weight fast?
Answer: ‘Fast’ is the problematic term here. Back a few years ago when I decided to get serious about losing weight, I did a lot of research, and pretty much every reputable organization recommends a rate of weight loss of just 1 to 2 lbs per week. You’ll find plenty of fad diets and gimmicks advertising much quicker weight loss than that, but they’re either unhealthy, lying about results, or if not outright lying, presenting a misleading picture that’s not representative of sustained long term fat loss. The truth is, between water weight, food in your guts, and maybe some other physiological processes I don't understand, your weight on the scale can vary quite a bit, even more if you weigh yourself in different clothing outfits. Even over the course of a single day, your bodyweight can vary by several pounds. When you first start a diet or an exercise routine, you'll probably see your weight on the scale drop by several pounds that first week. That's not several pounds of fat loss; that's merely those more temporary effects. If you go back to your normal routine, your weight on the scale will pretty much immediately jump back up to your prior weight, since there was only a small amount of actual fat loss in that one week. And if you do continue the diet, your weight won't similarly drop several pounds the next week. You've already 'used up' the short term effects. So any additional drop on the scale will have to come from actual fat loss, which is a lot slower. This is where a lot of the fad diets and gimmicks are misleading in their advertising – playing up how much your weight on the scale will go down in a week, even though there won't be much actual fat loss in that week, and even though that won't be a sustainable, long term rate. There are lots of different strategies for weight loss. Different ones work better for different people. I can point you to what I did myself (and note – I’ve maintained that weight even since I wrote that back in 2019): But the honest answer is that whatever strategy you use, it won't be fast. Losing the weight in itself is going to be a long term commitment. And if you want to maintain your new weight, then it's going to be a lifetime commitment. It's certainly possible. But it does take effort.

Question: If you work for a place like McDonald’s, do you eat there a lot at first and then get to where you never want to eat there after you've been there awhile?
Answer: I had two older brothers who worked at KFC for a few years, so we got lots of left over fried chicken from them. Then when I got old enough, I got a job at KFC, too, and worked there a few years myself (at a different location, since we'd moved by then). At least at the KFC I was at, you got a free meal per shift. I took it every time. And I got plenty of leftovers to bring home myself. Fried chicken is so damn good that I never got tired of it. And KFC, at least when we all worked there*, made good fried chicken. It all got marinated in store, then got more seasoning in the breading right before it went into the fryer (the trademark 11 secret herbs and spices). Well, to be completely honest, I did maybe get a little tired of cold leftovers. I mean, we tried not to be wasteful**, and plenty of leftovers got recycled in store for things like pot pies and the barbecue sandwiches, but there were still enough leftovers that employees could take home that I probably could have eaten KFC every meal for free if I'd wanted to, and that's just a bit too much. But still, fresh fried chicken at the store? Delicious. ABOVE: That still looks good. And I'd almost forgotten about the fresh made coleslaw (you had to be at least 18 years old to operate the shredder). I was on the wrestling team in high school, so I paid particularly close attention to my weight. And along with the official free meal, I snuck in snacks here and there. (And I don't feel overly guilty about it because I worked plenty of Friday night rushes as the only cook when there should have been two of us – I wasn't eating an extra cook's wages worth of snacks.) Anyway, I usually weighed at least 2 – 3 lbs more on days after working my shift. Unfortunately, there's no KFC located particularly conveniently to where I live now, so I haven't eaten there in years. But there is a Golden Chick right down the street. And that's my go to option for a weekend when I feel like splurging on fast food. So no, I never got tired of eating fried chicken. *I've heard plenty of folks complain that the quality of KFC has gone downhill. I don't know if that's really true, or just the general 'things used to be better in the good old days' complaining. Maybe next time I'm traveling I'll try to find a KFC to give it a try. **Well, there was one cook who would just fry up a ton of chicken so that he could close down the kitchen early to get out of there, but the managers let him go because he was wasting so much chicken that way and costing them too much money. But most of us actually did care about trying to serve good food to the customers, and so instead of cooking a big batch that would be old and dried out by closing, we did try to tailor our cooking to the needs.
