Question: What is the belief of atheists regarding the explanation of everything through science? Is there a possibility of something beyond explanation according to atheists?
Answer: Science is by far the best tool we humans have for understanding objective issues. If we can't understand an objective issue through science, we basically can't understand it at all. I think a lot of people have a misconception of science being stuffy or overly formal, and not understanding just how flexible it can be. Generally speaking, science is a method of gathering evidence, trying to come up with explanations for that evidence, and then trying to think of further ways to evaluate those explanations to be sure that they really are accurate. Throw in a bunch of lessons learned on how to avoid common pitfalls and cognitive biases, and you've got 'science'. And while the stereotype of science is white lab coats and beakers, all the various fields of science are far, far broader than that. Subjects like anthropology, history, religious studies, and linguistics all fall under the social sciences. ABOVE: Some examples of the social sciences, since most people are already more familiar with the physical sciences SOURCE: Branches of Sciences - Physical, Earth & Life Sciences | Leverage Edu Even many pseudosciences try to incorporate the trappings of legitimate science. When you look at ghost hunters, for example, they are trying to compile evidence around these issues, with things like electronic voice phenomenon, EMF meters, photography, eyewitness accounts, dowsing rods, Ouija boards, etc. What separates a pseudoscience like ghost hunting from legitimate science isn't the lip service to evidence based reasoning, but in the rigor of testing these explanations and properly accounting for those pitfalls and cognitive biases that can trip us up. But, if ghost hunting ever will become reliable and credible, it will be by addressing those shortcomings, more rigorously following the standards of legitimate science, and presenting evidence and explanations that are truly convincing. So many so-called 'other ways of knowing' may sometimes have value in subjective issues, moral lessons, teaching, or even entertainment, but they're no replacement for science when it comes to evaluating objective issues. Without evidence based reasoning, such methods are worthless at this task. And the more they do incorporate evidence based reasoning, the more they come into the fold of science, anyway. Of course, that's not to say that science can actually explain every objective issue. For example, as of right now, we don't know what caused the Big Bang, and may not ever know. But importantly, no other human endeavor besides science can address the question any better. For example, you may feel your religion provides an explanation, but your neighbor who practices a different religion might feel that their religion provides a different explanation, while yet another neighbor with yet another religion believes an altogether different explanation. How do you determine which religious explanation is right without resorting to evidence? Whoever claims to feel it the strongest? So like I said, science is the best tool we have for addressing objective issues. And when such questions are beyond scientific explanation, as they sometimes are, they're beyond any human explanation, at least for now. Yeah, yeah. I know. There are more things in Heaven and Earth, Horatio… But of course, that line was invented by a 16th/17th century playwright, trying to use ghosts as a plot device. It’s easy to diss on skeptics when you’re writing a fictional universe where you can simply make fantasy happen.

Question: How do you feel about reviving characters from the dead in books? Not in a zombie way.
Answer: I feel that it reduces the stakes and the tension in stories, especially if it's an ongoing series or serial, or happens early in a standalone story. Part of what makes death so profound and tragic is its finality. You no longer exist, and you will never again exist in the future. But when a story shows characters being revived from death, the stakes are dramatically reduced. Death is no longer necessarily final. You know that the writers can always pull some trick to bring any character back, so whenever somebody dies, you're never quite sure if they're really dead dead, or merely mostly dead. It's similar with a related theme of showing characters living in an afterlife, especially depending on how the afterlife is portrayed. In real life, even among folks who profess a belief in an afterlife, there's no way to be absolutely sure until you die yourself, and so there's always some level of doubt, and the possibility that us materialists might be right, after all. But in stories where an immortal afterlife is portrayed and becomes a certainty in that universe, then once again, death loses its sting. The character's not really gone. They've essentially moved, and the other characters just have to wait a while before they get to visit them again. That's not to say you can't still have good stories featuring 'resurrections' and afterlives. I already hinted at one with my 'mostly dead' comment. The Princess Bride was a great movie*. But you have to admit, that reviving Westley really set the tone for the remainder of the movie. It removed any doubt that the heroes would all somehow still be alive at the end. Coco was another great movie, this time showing folks existing in the afterlife. But, it was shown early on that this afterlife wasn't necessarily eternal, and you might still 'die' a second death – establishing real stakes. Also, when Abuelita died at the end, it wasn't really all that sad of a moment, because you knew she'd 'survive' in the Land of the Dead for a few more generations, at least. And as one final example, Star Trek Lower Decks has killed and then resurrected a few characters. But the whole point of doing it in this series was as parody, poking fun of the way the more serious Star Trek series have been so cavalier about resurrecting dead characters. So sure, you can still have good stories featuring resurrections or afterlives, but they have to be handled appropriately. At the very least, such stories reduce the stakes and tension around ordinary deaths, so the story writers need to find other ways to compensate, or just recognize that it's not a story dealing with such high stakes. *Yeah, I know most of my examples were movies instead of books, but it’s still general storytelling.

Question: If a ball is spinning and generating artificial gravity, would the force be on the outer surface or inner surface?
Answer: A ball is not really a great shape for this. When engineers talk about spinning a spaceship or space station to create artificial gravity, what it really is is centrifugal force. I'm not going to get into a big discussion on centripetal vs. centrifugal force. Just realize that in a rotating reference frame, centrifugal force is a 'useful fiction' to help engineers calculate forces while keeping their coordinate system aligned with the rotating object, and that centripetal force points towards the axis of rotation. ABOVE: Centripetal force is the 'real' force in a non-rotating reference frame. Centrifugal force is the useful fiction from the rock's point of view. SOURCE: Centrifugal Force- Definition, Principle, Examples (vs Centripetal force) For this reason, when engineers propose rotating space ships or space stations to create 'artificial gravity', they tend to follow a few standard forms that make the best use of centrifugal force. The simplest is putting your main crew compartment and some type of counterweight on opposite ends of a tether, and having them spin around their common center of gravity, with the tether holding them together. ABOVE SOURCE: Should we give up on artificial gravity? A common one in sci-fi stories for a bigger ship/station is to make it into a ring, so that you can take advantage of the entire ring for artificial gravity. Here's the classic example from 2001: A Space Odyssey: SOURCE: Sci-fi Gifs And here's kind of what it would be like inside such a station: SOURCE: Quora For the really fanciful sci-fi stories, they might use something know as an O'Neill cylinder. This is a truly gigantic version, where you have a huge cylinder spinning, which can create entire enclosed habitats: ABOVE: I know the labels are in Russian (I can't read them, either), but it's about the best diagram I could find SOURCE: Humanoid History (@HumanoidHistory) on X That said, there are some very significant engineering challenges to doing any of these configurations, such that none of them may be practical, especially in the near term. For any upcoming missions to Mars, for example, the astronauts are probably just going to have to deal with a zero-g journey. So, with all that explanation, I hope the answer to your question is obvious. The artificial gravity will be on the inside surface of your spinning ball, due to the centrifugal force 'pushing' you away from the axis of rotation. If you were on the outside surface, you would be flung away from the ship/station. But you should also see why a ball wouldn't be a great shape for this. Only the 'equator' would have the centrifugal force perpendicular to its surface. Everywhere else would be on a slope, like a hill. The points right at the axis of rotation would be completely vertical from an astronaut's perspective.

Question: According to Newton's 2nd law, F=ma, but when we push the wall, why does it not accelerate?
Answer: Well, the more typical way we saw that equation in my engineering classes* was: ΣF = ma Don't let the Σ scare you. It just means the summation, or that you add all the forces together. You typically do this with what are known as free body diagrams, where you depict all the various forces on an object. Here, for example, is a simple beam: SOURCE: How to Draw Free Body Diagrams with examples | DegreeTutors.com Two forces are being applied to the beam at different locations, one force of 45 kN (10,116 lbs), the other force of 30 kN (6744 lbs). But you know the beam is being supported at each end, so you know those supports are going to push back. I won't go through the math here, but it's a pretty basic statics problem to figure out what they are: SOURCE: How to Draw Free Body Diagrams with examples | DegreeTutors.com So, returning to ΣF = ma, let's just double check what all the forces add up to, keeping in mind the directions the forces are being applied: ΣF = 48 kN + (-45 kN) + (-30 kN) + 27 kN ΣF = 0 So, if ΣF = 0, then it also follows that a = 0. No acceleration. Newtons' Law still holds. And of course, for your particular question, when you push on a wall, it’s almost always attached to something, so there will be a reaction force pushing back, keeping the forces balanced. Once again, ΣF = 0, so no acceleration *Once you get out of school, people get a bit lazier about always including the Σ, since all engineers know that it’s implied.

Question: Are there benefits in reading the Bible even if you know from external study that it's not true in its claims?

Question: How does knob and tube wiring differ from modern wiring systems?
Answer: All AC house wiring has at least a hot line and a neutral line. The hot line carries high voltage and the power to run your appliances. The neutral line will be at essentially zero voltage relative to ground, and provides the return path to close the circuit. In knob and tube wiring, the hot line and the neutral line are carried in physically separated wires. These wires are ideally covered in insulation, and then further isolated from the framing of your house with the namesake non-conducting ceramic knobs and tubes. Though I say 'ideally' covered in insulation, because with the age of many knob and tube installations, the insulation may have degraded. ABOVE: The basics of knob and tube wiring SOURCE: Knob and Tube Wiring To branch out from the main runs in knob and tube wiring, the wires need to be spliced. The insulation will have been stripped away from a section of the wire, and then the spliced wire will be wrapped around it and soldered to make a good connection, before being covered up again with insulating tape. Here's what a good splice looks like from the outside: SOURCE: Knob & Tube Electrical Wiring FAQs And here's a diagram of what it typically looks like underneath the tape: SOURCE: electrical splices guide for residential electrical wiring and circuits Modern wiring typically uses a type of wire commonly referred to by the trade name of Romex (or more generically as non-metallic sheathed cable). The typical configuration is to have the hot line, a neutral line, and a ground line all within the same cable, with the hot line and neutral line being encased in their own insulation. The ground line won't carry any current under normal circumstances, but it provides an alternative path to ground as an additional safety feature. It usually ends up being connected to things like metal chassis/cases of appliances, so that if there was a short circuit to the case, the ground wire would carry that electricity rather than somebody touching the appliance. It's also possible to get Romex with even more conductors in a single cable, such as for appliances running at 240 V that need to the two hot wires at different phases, or for things like 2-way light switches, where the wires act as 'travelers', and may or may not be hot depending on the position of the switches. And there’s also metallic clad armored cable for when you need more protection than the PVC sheathing from Romex. SOURCE: Types of Wires & Cables ABOVE: Example of a traveler wire SOURCE: What Is a Traveler Wire and Why Is It Important? Modern wiring also does all connections in junction boxes, rather that at unmarked splices. In a few cases, this might be a pure junction box that does nothing but connect wires. But more often than not, the junction box is at an electrical outlet or switch, which lets you daisy chain outlets on a single circuit. ABOVE: Feed through vs. pigtail connections SOURCE: https://www.jlconline.com/how-to/electrical/q-a-to-pigtail-or-not-to-pigtail_o ABOVE: Typical wiring for multiple outlets SOURCE: https://www.reddit.com/r/ElectricianU/comments/m40m6a/wiring_outlets_in_seriesparallel/ Anyway, those are the basics. The general principles of electricity are obviously still the same. But there are a lot of differences in the details of how each system gets implemented, all based on lessons learned over the years to make modern wiring easier and safer.

Question: Why do scientist always discount the creation theory, as opposed to the evolutionary theory?
Answer: Well, they didn't always discount creationism. Back in the early 1800s, creationism really was the dominant paradigm in biology. It's pinnacle was perhaps William Paley's famous book from 1802, Natural Theology, which included his famous Watchmaker analogy. Darwin himself summarized the debate in the introduction to the 6th edition of On the Origin of Species (emphasis mine): I will here give a brief sketch of the progress of opinion on the Origin of Species. Until recently the great majority of naturalists believed that species were immutable productions, and had been separately created. This view has been ably maintained by many authors. Some few naturalists, on the other hand, have believed that species undergo modification, and that the existing forms of life are the descendants by true generation of pre existing forms. In his autobiography, Darwin wrote a brief passage about how even he had been convinced by Paley's creationist arguments prior to discovering natural selection (emphasis mine, again): The old argument of design in nature, as given by Paley, which formerly seemed to me so conclusive, fails, now that the law of natural selection has been discovered. We can no longer argue that, for instance, the beautiful hinge of a bivalve shell must have been made by an intelligent being, like the hinge of a door by man. There seems to be no more design in the variability of organic beings and in the action of natural selection, than in the course which the wind blows. Everything in nature is the result of fixed laws. If you want to see how much of The Origin was devoted to countering creationism, just open up a copy on your computer and do a search for 'creat', which will highlight all the incidences of creation, creationism, creator, etc. I did it myself and counted something like 128 mentions of creationism or related terms (make sure you avoid 'false positives' like creature). That's a whole lot of discussion of creationism. This answer is already hinting at why creationism is no longer taken seriously – it was replaced by a better theory that's a much better match to the evidence. And in the 150 years since Darwin published The Origin, that evidence has only gotten stronger. It’s very similar to why chemists no longer debate oxidation vs. phlogiston theory. Or to put it another way, this is a debate that was settled over a century ago, so scientists have moved on to more interesting questions.

Question: How many hours do you need to exercise to lose weight?
Answer: Exercise is very important for overall fitness and health, but not so much for losing weight. And even the benefits it does have for weight loss are a case of diminishing returns. In other words, if you exercise an hour a week, that is better for weight loss than sitting around doing nothing. But exercising for two hours a week isn't going to double the weight loss benefit. Your body has a certain basal metabolic rate that it needs simply for surviving. Even if you do nothing but sit at a desk all day, you know you still need to eat. And this basal metabolic rate is actually the biggest energy expenditure for most of us, accounting for something like 60–80% of our calories. ABOVE: Components of total energy expenditure for an average young adult woman and man. SOURCE: Why you shouldn't exercise to lose weight, explained with 60+ studies But as we start doing more physical activity, our body compensates. In order to save energy to help keep our food requirements down (because historically, starving was a much bigger danger than obesity), our body reduces the energy put into the basal metabolic rate. ABOVE: The body adapts to increased physical activity by reducing energy spent on other physiological activities. SOURCE: Why you shouldn't exercise to lose weight, explained with 60+ studies As you can see in the figure above, going from a sedentary lifestyle to a moderate amount of exercise does substantially increase your total energy expenditure. But as you keep pushing the physical activity higher and higher, the compensation from our body causes the total energy expenditure to somewhat level off. Sure, if you're an elite athlete doing tons of training, you'll need more calories than most of us. But most of us aren't elite athletes. And the calorie counters on your Fitbit or treadmill aren't all that accurate to begin with, and don't take into account any drop off in your basal metabolic rate. So just because your Fitbit says you burned a certain amount of additional calories by tacking on another exercise, don't think that that justifies you consuming that many more calories. The Fitbit is likely wrong. So, exercise for your health and fitness. It really is the right thing to do. But when it comes to losing weight, pay attention to what you're eating, and eat less.

Question: Can airplanes sometimes not store fuel in their tanks due to weight limitations? If this is the case, what are the alternatives for storing fuel in an airplane or other vehicle?
Answer: Airplanes are much more weight sensitive than the cars that most people are used to. Cars have fuel tanks that will typically let you drive somewhere around 5 hours before needing to refuel. And you don't need to worry all that much about how much you load up your car. It can be just you driving by yourself, or loading up the whole family with luggage. Your gas mileage might go down a bit, but unless you're looking at really heavy cargo, you don't have to worry about overloading the car. Planes, on the other, don't have that luxury. You get a combined 'useful load', which is how much you can load up an airplane before it becomes too heavy to fly. It's up to the operator to decide how much of that useful load to devote to passengers and other payload, and how much to devote to fuel. Take the Cessna 172 as an example, one of the most iconic general aviation airplanes. It has 4 seats, a useful load of 878 lbs, and gas tanks that can hold 318 lbs of fuel. If you're running the math in your head, you can see that if you filled up the tanks with fuel, you'd only have 560 lbs of payload left, which may be fine if you're flying by yourself, but doesn't leave a lot of weight for 4 passengers and luggage, especially if they're adults. ABOVE: A screenshot from Cessna’s website, with appropriate text for a discussion about fuel burn SOURCE: Cessna Skyhawk Piston | Textron Aviation But, that 318 lbs of fuel is enough to let you fly for over 5 hours. Do you really need to fly that long if you're just taking some friends up for a sight-seeing flight around town, or for the clichéd $100 hamburger at the next airport over? Probably not. So, you might only load up half the fuel, which still lets you fly over 2 ½ hours, but leaves you 719 lbs for passengers and other payload, which is getting much more reasonable for 4 people (not necessarily 4 large adults, but at least a mix of larger and more petit folks). It's all about giving the operator options. You could make the full fuel payload seem higher by giving them a smaller gas tank, but then they wouldn't have the freedom to fly longer flights. Or you could just give it two seats, but then they wouldn't have the freedom to carry more passengers. So, you give them the ability to decide how they want to use the plane. For the big boys in airliners, it's a lot of the same considerations. Is it a short haul flight between close cities? Only load as much fuel as you need and then cram it full of passengers. Is it a long range flight? Well, you might have to go lighter on the cargo. So to answer the question directly, yes, sometimes airplanes don't fill up the wing tanks in order to be able to carry more payload. But other times it's the opposite, filling up the tanks and carrying less payload. It's all up to the specific mission.

Question: What scientific fact, study, or research do you base your claim of God’s non-existence? Not one of you non-believers has provided a more suitable answer greater than lack of proof or evidence. Believer's faith is in the Bible. What's yours based in?
Answer: There's a big difference between the capital G God of the Bible, and a more generic lower case g god or higher power. The generic higher power is more difficult to 'disprove', and it's in this sense that many atheists admit there's still a small possibility of a god existing. But the capital G God of the Bible? Well, we've got the Bible itself to look at, along with archaeology. I've written about such things many times on Quora, and it would be easy to turn this into a Gish Gallop. In fact, I've already written such a 'Gish Gallop' type answer, which itself includes many links to other answers and articles: The introduction to that question is as good a summary as any: In short, the Bible seems exactly like the type of collection of stories that would develop organically over generations within a bronze age to iron age culture, and nothing at all like an inerrant work inspired by an actual God. There are all types of indications and clues within the Bible itself of how it developed over the generations, including the people’s changing concept of Yahweh. The early parts in Genesis seem like just-so stories that obviously don't match history on a literal level, and later parts like Exodus and the conquest of the Holy Land don't match archaeological evidence. And on top of all that, there are some stories that are just absurd at face value. To list just one example here, I'll go with the Kuntillet Ajrud inscriptions*. The Kuntillet Ajrud archaeological site dates to some time around the 8th century, B.C. It was most likely "an Israelite state-sponsored enterprise" (source: The Inscriptions of Kuntillet ‛Ajrud Through the Lens of Historical Research). Among the findings there are inscriptions and drawings mentioning El, Yahweh, Ba'al, and Yahweh's wife, Asherah. For example, one of these inscriptions (on Pithos A) includes: I have blessed you by YHWH of Samaria and to [his†] Asherata. While another (on Pithos B) includes: I have blessed you by YHWH of Teman and [his†] Asherata. ABOVE: A projection drawing of Pithos A, which includes the wording, "I have blessed you by YHWH of Samaria and to [his†] Asherata." SOURCE: https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Projection-drawing-of-Pithos-A-Meshel-et-al-2012-87-Fig-524-147-Fig-65-tags_fig1_318275592 So, right off the bat, we have a depiction of Yahweh that predates the composition of much of the the Bible‡, and shows the belief that he had a wife. (And note that these weren't the only two such inscriptions from the site.) This shows that the precursor to monotheistic Judaism was a polytheistic religion, where Yahweh wasn't the only god or goddess. It's also significant that there were separate mentions of a Yahweh of Samaria and a Yahweh of Teman. At the very least, these types of localized centers of worship contradict the Biblical narrative that the worship of Yahweh had been centralized to the Temple of Jerusalem by that point. But, according to that paper I already linked to, the author believes these different Yahwehs actually represent different regional deities with "distinct cultic vessels, rituals and ceremonies". The Yahweh of Samaria was only concerned with Samaria, while the Yahweh of Teman was concerned only with Teman. And further, a certain amount of the Deuteronomistic influence§ in the Bible was trying to bring these disparate religions and customs together into a unified religion for all of Israel and Judah. As one more quick note, another inscription from the site contains what may be a version of the story of Moses and the Exodus, but, according to that same paper, with "marked differences compared to the canonical biblical story, confirming the assumption of scholars that biblical traditions developed gradually over many years." So, from the archaeological findings at Kuntillet Ajrud, we have evidence showing one of the steps in the development of Yahweh, as a local deity with a goddess for a wife, before he developed into the monotheistic God of all creation that most people are familiar with, now. We also have details showing that the Biblical narrative isn't completely trustworthy, since worship of Yahweh hadn't yet been centralized to the Temple at Jerusalem like the story claims. And as I said, that's just from one archaeological site. That other answer that I already linked to provides many, many more examples. If you don't feel like scrolling back up to the top of this answer, here's that link again for easy reference: Even More Info: If you want a really, really detailed explanation, I wrote a short book that I self-published, that you can download for free from my personal website (since it is available as a free download, I trust this isn't spam according to Quora's policies): Footnotes: * Portions of this section were adapted from a prior answer: † I included the 'his' in brackets in those quotes because some researchers think there's a possessive suffix attaching Asherat to Yahweh, while others think the suffix is actually just part of the name, Asherata. ‡ The composition of the Bible is a whole topic in itself, that I did cover in the previously linked 'Gish Gallop' answer. § That 'Deuteronomistic influence' is part of the same topic of the composition of the Bible.

Question: Is it true that Americans from the South are friendly?
Answer: It depends on the context. I just finished reading Malcom Gladwell's book, Outliers. In one portion, he described an interesting series of experiments that took place in the 1990s at the University of Michigan. Young men were asked to enter a classroom to fill out a questionnaire, and then drop it off down the hallway before returning for some follow up. For half of the participants, the trip to drop off the questionnaire and return were uneventful. For the other half, a plant (as in an actor) got in their way in the narrow hallway trying to access a filing cabinet, acting annoyed when the student tried to get past, then slamming the filing cabinet drawer shut and calling the student an asshole. Upon returning to the original classroom, the researchers "shook the young men's hands to see if their grip was firmer than usual. They took saliva samples from the students, both before and after the insult, to see if being called an asshole caused their levels of testosterone and cortisol... to go up." They also had them provide a conclusion to a story about a hypothetical situation of a couple, Jill and Steve, going to a party, and another guy, Larry, hitting on Jill. The researchers looked at all types of different characteristics of their study subjects, but found the biggest predictor of their reactions to the hallway incident was where they were from. For northerners, "They laughed it off. Their handshakes were unchanged. Their levels of cortisol actually went down, as if they were unconsciously trying to defuse their own anger. Only a few of them had Steve get violent with Larry." On the other hand, "But the Southerners? Oh, my. The were angry. Their cortisol and testosterone jumped. Their handshakes got firm. Steve was all over Larry." They did follow up studies with similar scenarios, always finding that southerners typically reacted much more aggressively than did northerners. The difference is that the Southern United States has a "culture of honor", partly inherited from the immigrants who settled there (for historical reasons I won't delve into here – see Culture of honor (Southern United States) - Wikipedia ), and partly maintained throughout history. The scenarios in the above experiments were anything but 'friendly'. The southern students were much more likely to react aggressively. But in other situations, a culture of honor can lead to more formal politeness, or going out of your way to establish your reputation. The use of 'sir' and 'ma'am' is a pretty obvious one. In my experience, I've also seen many more people here in Texas stop to help a stranger stranded on the side of the road than I did growing up in Pennsylvania and Maryland. So, it depends. In some ways, the culture of honor can lead southerners to be friendly. In other ways, it can lead them to being more aggressive. It really just depends on the situation. But overall, I definitely wouldn’t say that they’re more friendly than me and my fellow Yankees. There are just different cultural norms and expectations.

Question: Scientists dabble and meddle in the genome with the intent to make life better, but are they really, intentionally or unintentionally, redefining or redesigning life? If so, how?
Answer: People have been 'redesigning' life since the advent of domestication and selective breeding of crops and livestock. The big difference between that and intentional genetic engineering is that the old methods were haphazard, relying on willy nilly random mutations that nobody understood at all. It wasn't even until the last century or so that people even knew about genetics. So in the past, if somebody wanted to know if a new strain of crop that improved yield was also safe to eat, the only recourse was to eat enough of it to see what happened. Nowadays, we have enough of an understanding of the underlying genetics to already have an a priori idea of whether certain genetic changes will be safe or not. And we have more rigorous testing protocols for genetically engineered crops. Do I think such intentional genetic engineering can make life better? It certainly has the potential to do so. Take golden rice, for example. This is a new strain of rice engineering to have beta-carotene, a precursor to vitamin A, which can help drastically reduce Vitamin A deficiency in certain regions of the world where malnutrition is a problem. Or take Bt crops, so named for incorporating genes from the Bacillus thuringiensis bacteria, making proteins that are toxic to insects. This allows farmers to reduce the amount of insecticides they spray on their crops, with a secondary effect of reducing the greenhouse gas emissions from the equipment that does the spraying (FWIW, organic famers often spray a solution with the live bacteria onto their crops, since bacteria are 'organic'). ABOVE: A conventional rice variety on left compared to the more nutritious golden rice on right SOURCE: GM golden rice gets landmark safety approval in the Philippines So yes, genetic engineering is redesigning life, just like we’ve done for millennia, but in a much more controlled and less haphazard manner than traditional selective breeding. And yes, it certainly does have the potential to make life better. And if you were asking about the human genome, just ask anybody with a genetic disease if they'd like to be able to be cured. I lost a few childhood friends to cystic fibrosis. Genetic therapy would have been a literal life saver.

Question: What are the scientific odds of human existence? What conditions are necessary for life to exist?
Answer: That's a very interesting question (the first one). The late Stephen Jay Gould came up with a thought experiment of 'rewinding' the history of life and starting over. Would you get the same results? How much of evolution is driven by randomness and chance, how much is driven by contingency, and how much is driven by more general principles? Here's how Gould himself put it: Suppose that ten of a hundred designs will survive and diversify. If the ten survivors are predictable by superiority of anatomy (Interpretation 1), then they will win each time – and Burgess eliminations do not challenge our comforting view of life. But if the ten survivors are protégés of Lady Luck or fortunate beneficiaries of odd historical contingencies (Interpretation 2), then each replay of the tape will yield a different set of survivors and a radically different history. And if you recall from high-school algebra how to calculate permutations and combinations, you will realize that the total number of combinations for 10 items from a pool of 100 yields more than 17 trillion potential outcomes. There's one particular experiment that comes as close as I can think of to replaying the tape of life, in the small scale, at least*. Back in 1988, Richard Lenski started out with one strain of E. coli, and split it into 12 different populations. He grew each population in identical conditions (well, as close to identical as experimentally possible) which were actually somewhat harsh for E. coli. He used a particular growth medium named DM25, which has a limited amount of glucose that the E. coli need to feed on. Lenski wanted to see how the E. coli would evolve due to this limited food supply. Every day, he would transfer 1% of the previous day's populations to new flasks with a fresh supply of DM25, periodically freezing samples to maintain as a kind of 'fossil record', and also periodically measuring attributes of the populations to see how they were evolving. The experiment is still ongoing today, making it one of the longest running (and supremely well documented) evolutionary experiments. Here's how one particular trait evolved in each of these populations, cell size: ABOVE SOURCE: E. coli long-term evolution experiment - Wikipedia While there's a general trend of increasing cell size in all 12 populations, they didn't all follow the exact same trend. In fact, the largest lineage evolved to be nearly twice as big as the smallest lineage. One particular adaptation was so rare that it only occurred in one of Lenski's populations.* The DM25 growth medium also happened to contain a large amount of citrate, which E. coli usually can't digest in anaerobic conditions, but which was included in the DM25 formulation way back when it was first developed for antibiotic experiments because it improved the efficiency of penicillin. Well, in this single lineage of Lenski's twelve E. coli populations, they did evolve the ability to digest citrate in anaerobic conditions. This adaptation is so profound for E. coli that some have proposed it actually represents a new species. So, starting from identical genetics, and subjecting populations to as identical of conditions as experimentally possible, each of the 12 populations took their own different evolutionary paths, from cell size, to the ability to digest citrate, to other traits I didn't mention here. There wasn't simply one optimum set of adaptations that natural selection drove towards in each population. This really does seem to indicate that chance† and contingency are major factors in the evolution of populations. And Lenski's experiment only had 12 isolated populations. What if he'd had 100? Would there be 100 unique strains by now? What about 1000? Or a million? Or to put it into the terminology of this question, what are the scientific odds of any particular strain of E. coli evolving in any particular flask? Based on Lenski's experiment, we can say it's no greater than 1 out of 12, but the reality could be a much, much smaller probability. So, let that play out in every population that's ever existed, and it seems that every particular species has a very low probability of existing‡. That goes for everything from ocelots to dandelions to Humboldt's squid to portabella mushrooms. And yes, it goes for us humans, as well. To add one more thing, it does seem like some body plans or adaptations are more common than others, implying that there are general principles that drive these adaptations. Levers to propel an organism on the seafloor or land, aka legs, have evolved in animals as diverse as insects, tetrapods, and starfish. Free swimming organisms evolved streamlined hydrodynamic bodies. Flying animals evolve wings. Etc. But other adaptations appear to be quite rare, like Lenski's citrate digesting E. coli. If elephants were to go extinct, I'm not sure we'd ever see another animal with that kind of trunk. And I can only hope that when aye-ayes go extinct, that particular combination of nightmare fuel never reappears. I rather suspect that we humans are kind of like elephants in that respect. You simply don't see many other animals similar to us outside our closest evolutionary cousins. We have a weird combination of an upright bipedal posture, complex social groups, extremely high intelligence with a penchant for technology combined with hands that are really good at manipulating our environments to effect that technology, along with several other unique characteristics. So, outside the general principle of all particular species being highly improbable, I'd say that even a species along the lines of us humans is highly improbable. Play the tape of life 1000 times, and while you might get lots of critters superficially resembling a crab, you might not get another elephant or another human. While I'm not sure anybody can give the precise odds, I think it's safe to say that the odds of human existence were quite low. So much of evolution is driven by chance and contingency, and we seem to be a rather odd combination of traits on top of that. That's all the more reason we need to get our acts together and make sure we don't screw up our planet (whether through things like climate change or good old fashioned global thermonuclear war). Because if we do go extinct, the odds are decent that nothing with our ability for science and understanding will ever evolve on this planet, again. *Both of these paragraphs are mostly copied from a previous answer of mine: †Chance could be things like Genetic drift or even the raw material of random mutation. ‡Don't confuse low probabilities of a particular species with low probabilities of life in general. A common analogy is shuffling a deck of cards. With 52 unique cards, the odds of any particular order for an entire deck is 1 in 10^68, an astronomically tiny probability. But, you're essentially guaranteed some order of 52 cards. That's the way it is with evolution and species – the odds of any particular species may be infinitesimally small, but the evolution of species in general is pretty much guaranteed. Argh. Once again, I failed to ensure I was answering an actual human before typing up my answer. You got me again, QPG. Oh well, I guess that means that at least some QPG questions aren’t trash.

Question: Why are non-professional cyclists drawn to road bikes?
Answer: Back when I was in college, I bought a somewhat decent mountain bike* to get around. I didn't give a whole lot of thought to mountain bike vs. road bike at the time. I mean, mountain bikes just sounded cooler, and it seemed that a mountain bike would be more robust to the abuse of daily riding, jumping curbs, hitting potholes, and the like. It was fine, got me to and from campus, and I even took it on a nearby trail a handful of times. Riding a bike daily like that for over 2 years got me pretty accustomed to cycling. Fast forward a few years to living in Wichita Falls, Texas, and we have a huge cycling event known as the Hotter'n Hell Hundred, so named for a 100 mile route in potentially 100°F weather (though it now takes place in the morning and so isn't usually quite that hot). A group of us decided to participate one year just to say we did it, but sticking with a shorter 25 mile route. One friend was really into cycling, so he offered to go down to a place in Dallas to pick up good road bike rentals for the weekend – bikes up in the several thousand dollar range if we were going to buy them. ABOVE: The Mass Start at the Hotter'n Hell Hundred SOURCE: 40th Hotter 'N Hell Hundred event photos When I first got up on that road bike and pressed down on the pedal... Wow! The bike just glided across the pavement like it was nothing. And when I stopped pedaling, the bike didn't stop. It just kept on coasting and coasting seemingly forever. There was just no comparison between that road bike and the mountain bike that I'd ridden back in college. The road bike was supremely optimized to be low friction for riding on pavement. Now, I'm still not sure a road bike would have been the best option for me in college with the amount I abused my bike. And there's no way I would have been able to shell out several thousands of dollars for a road bike comparable to that one I rented. But after riding a good road bike when all I was used to before was a mountain bike, I can definitely understand why people opt for road bikes. I mean, it’s in the name. That’s what they’re designed for. *My bike in college was a Raleigh M50 - looked just like this: 2000 Raleigh M50 Front Suspension Mountain Bike for Sale in Mechanicsburg, PA - OfferUp. If memory serves, it cost somewhere around $300 back in the 90s, which would be the equivalent of around $600 today. So not a world class bike, but definitely better than what you find in a typical Walmart.

Question: I have responded to a fare number of Christian trolls on here as a Christian myself, so this is an honest question. Regardless of which theistic religion, would there be anything that could convince you of the existence of a god(s)? If so, wouldn’t that make you more agnostic that truly atheist? (I believe the wisest amongst us are the agnostics)
Answer: All knowledge is provisional. Pretty much everything I think I know could be a mistaken belief. For an example, let's take something extreme like the roughly spherical shape of the Earth. In everyday language, I would say that I know that to be a fact. But, I can also imagine scenarios where I might be wrong. These might seem like absurd scenarios, but I can't rule them out entirely. Perhaps I'm living in something like The Truman Show, where I've been misled my entire life merely for the entertainment of some viewing audience, and what I think is the real world is merely a very, very elaborate set. Maybe 'real' society is much more advanced than my simulated society, and I'm living in something like a Star Trek holodeck, with advanced AI generating the bredth and depth of this deception (e.g. why I can google convincing evidence for a spherical planet). If you could produce and show me sufficient evidence along these lines, then you could convince me that the Earth really was flat. But, in everyday conversation, I'm not going to say I'm agnostic over the shape of the Earth because of that. It's the same way with gods. I think they're very, very unlikely, on par with me living in The Truman Show. But, that slim chance still exists, and sufficient evidence could change my mind. But why treat this one question differently from all other knowledge questions? Why use a special word to denote that I might possibly be wrong about the issue of gods, when that same possibility also exists for everything else? No, in common usage (as opposed to some corners of the Internet who try to define the term differently), 'agnostic' means someone who's unsure about the existence of gods, not merely somebody who could be convinced with sufficient evidence. So going by the common usage, 'atheist' really does describe me better, as I really am quite sure that gods don’t exist.

Question: I'm not convinced any non-theistic worldview is true because non-theists haven't provided any evidence. I can't make myself believe something without evidence, so can any non-theist please provide evidence that any non-theistic worldview is true?
Answer: You've got a weird way of approaching this question. Take fairies, for example. As you said, if you "can't make [your]self believe something without evidence", and there's no compelling evidence for the existence of fairies, the default position is to lack belief in fairies, or to take a non-fairiest worldview. If you needed some type of positive evidence for the non-existence of fairies, you'd be stuck in some weird ontological limbo. With no evidence for the existence of fairies, you couldn't believe in fairies, but with no evidence against the existence of fairies, you couldn't believe in their non-existence. But it's not just fairies. This goes for anything. You can build up positive evidence for the existence of something. It's much, much harder to build up evidence for the non-existence of something. That's why the burden of proof has developed the way it has. In general, it's up to the person claiming that something exists to prove their case. The rest of us have no need to take their claims seriously until they have such evidence. To borrow a somewhat silly example from the Internet, do you have any evidence against the existence of Eric The God-Eating Magic Penguin? Wouldn't it seem a bit ridiculous to say that just because you can't find any evidence against Eric, that you're not going to take the non-Ericist position? I hope you see where this is going. If gods exist, the burden of proof is on the people claiming that they exist. Until they can provide compelling evidence, the rest of us are under no obligation to take their claims seriously. Just like with fairies, the lack of evidence makes the default position a non-theistic worldview.

Question: What is the atheist position on respect for other people's beliefs (especially religious ones)?
Answer: The problem is that 'respect' has multiple meanings. Quoting Google, here are the three most relevant (for a verb, the meanings for a noun are similar): Nobody's beliefs are entitled to respect in that first sense merely for holding them. Not all beliefs are equal. Some people, for example, believe the earth is flat. That's not an admirable belief, at all, and in the sense of the first definition, I don't respect such beliefs. However, the second two definitions are much more in a sense of tolerance. You don't have to admire somebody's beliefs to respect their right to hold such beliefs. If someone wants to believe in a flat earth, that's their right, and I 'respect' that. Religious beliefs can vary quite widely, from Unitarian Universalists or Buddhists (who might actually be atheists) to Methodists to hard core young earth creationist Southern Baptists, and plenty of others. To reiterate what I already said, none of those beliefs are entitled to respect in that first sense merely for existing. If you want me to respect your beliefs in the sense of admiration, then those beliefs better be worthy of admiration. But religious beliefs that contradict reality, or that preach intolerance, definitely don't fit the bill. However, everybody has the right to believe whatever they want (within reason), even if it is something that I find rather silly or absurd. If you want to believe the entire universe was created just a few thousand years ago, that's your right. Where things start to get messy is when your beliefs harm others, or when you try to impose your beliefs on others, such as the recent and infamous draconian abortion laws in states like Texas. When your beliefs in opposition to abortion begin to affect other people, then there's an issue. You have the right to have such beliefs, but absent a compelling secular purpose, you shouldn't be able to force those beliefs on others. If someone doesn't want to consider abortion as an option for themselves, I respect that. If someone wants to take away that option for others, they've crossed a line. Per the third definition up above, tolerating such beliefs wouldn't actually be "avoid harming or interfering with" others, since those beliefs are doing that, already. So really, it depends on which particular sense of 'belief' your referring to, and which particular religious beliefs you're referring to. And depending on which combination, the answer can range from respecting certain beliefs, to not respecting other beliefs, to being vehemently opposed to yet others.

Question: Are atheists truly correct if everything has to have a creator? The Earth can't come out of nothingness. It had to be created by something.
Answer: If everything has to have a creator, then who created the creator? Some higher level creator? And who created that higher level creator? An even higher level creator above that one? Does this chain keep going and going for infinity? That's not mere snark. That's the exact same existential angst inducing thought process I had when I was still a Christian which left me laying awake in bed plenty of nights. It's not philosophically satisfying to say that a god created everything. You still have to explain why that particular god exists and has the properties it does (as opposed to somebody else's god from some other religion). And, perhaps most importantly, you have to explain how a god makes more sense than other ideas about how the universe got started. Trying to figure out how the universe got started is mind bending with or without invoking a god. But invoking a god doesn't really offer a more satisfying answer than non-religious explanations. If anything, trying to saddle the 'uncaused cause' with personality, feelings, and though processes just seems even more implausible. And to be clear, we have a pretty good idea of the history of the universe from the Big Bang on. But in the spirit of your question, I’m answering about the universe as a whole, since we know more or less how the Earth formed as part of our solar system from a nebula.

Question: Why has Quora devolved into a toxic cesspool?
Answer: For just about any question that starts with, "Why has Quora...", the answer is almost always money. I didn't get started on Quora back at the very beginning, but I still got on early enough to get a taste of what it was at its best. I mean, you still got people like Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton contributing answers when I first started using the site. But as great as Quora was back then, it was operating at a loss. It was living off of the cash from investors, trying to build up its userbase and reputation so that it would eventually become profitable. Those investors weren't putting their money into Quora just for fun. They want to see a return on their investment. And operating a social media site is expensive. Googling it just now, it has something like 400 million active monthly users. That takes tons of hardware and bandwidth, which costs tons of money. So, if Quora wants to start turning a profit, they have to find ways to reduce costs and increase the things that bring in money. And bringing in money mostly boils down to advertising, which means getting people to 'engage' with the platform. So, the questions Quora's management asks aren't how changes will affect the user experience, but how they'll affect the bottom line. And cutting down on moderation is an easy way to cut costs. Can a negative user experience drive some people away from the site? Sure. But you're still here asking questions, and I'm still here answering them. And according to Semrush.com, it looks like Quora's traffic has just continued growing over the past 6 months, despite all of us users complaining about the decline in the user experience (accessing stats going beyond 6 months cost money that I'm not going to spend just to answer this question): In short, the user experience on Quora has declined because it saves Quora money by not having to pay as much for moderation, while it doesn’t seem to have had a big impact on the engagement which brings in the ad revenue.

Question: How is it possible that every little detail required for life and the human species to exist on Earth just happened to happen naturally?
Answer: There's probably somewhere on the order of 100 billion planets in the Milky Way galaxy, with all types of varying conditions. Just by chance, some of those planets will be conducive to life, while others won't. But guess where the intelligent life is going to be, wondering why their planets just so happen to be so well suited for their evolution. Just say that "every little detail required for life and the human species to exist" on a planet is a one in a million chance. With 100 billion planets, that still means 100,000 planets in our galaxy with those conditions. Even if it's a one in a billion chance, that's still 100 such planets. We don't yet know enough about planets outside our own solar system to say how rare it is for such conditions to exist. But even if it is extremely rare, it just stands to reason that the organisms pondering such things will be on the life supporting planets. And of course, we evolved to fit our planet, not the other way around. If other planets harbor life but with slightly different conditions, that life will almost certainly follow a different evolutionary path, producing creatures that don't resemble us humans. Also, this is an extremely self-centered question. You might as well ask how Earth is so conducive to tapeworms, or mushrooms, or oak trees. I rather like humans myself, but we're not the end-all, be-all of life on this planet. Heck, by biomass, the Earth really is a planet optimized for microbes, with us multicellular creatures just adding a bit of variety to the fringes.

Question: Young Earth creationists like to use Bishop Ussher's calculated date for when the Earth was created. Who else has done the calculations to confirm it?
Answer: I've gone through a portion of the estimate, myself*. You can read a good summary of Ussher's estimate on Wikipedia. Basically, he broke it down into three portions (note that the timespans are the ones that Ussher calculated, not mine): Ussher then used other sources outside the Bible to determine the enthronement of the Babylonian king Amel-Marduk to have occurred in 562 BC, which was tied in to the end of the Babylonian Captivity through 2 Kings 25:27. From there, it was just a matter of going backwards by all the years previously calculated, putting creation at 4004 BC. Since the first two portions of the estimate are so straightforward, they were easy enough to double check. Creation to Exodus Like I said, this part is easy enough to look up yourself in Genesis 5 and Genesis 11. The only real minor cases of uncertainty in there are when Noah had Shem, and when Nahor had Terah, since the wording used is a tad ambiguous. In the first case, per Genesis 5:32: After Noah was five hundred years old, Noah became the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth. In the latter case, per Genesis 11:26: When Terah had lived seventy years, he became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Those sons weren't triplets, so you have to decide whether those ages are when those guys started having kids, or when they'd finally had all three. Folks who care more about this than I do (like Ussher) have tried to get to the bottom of it. I just used those numbers as is, since it's still in the ballpark. Anyway, here's my table of going from Adam to the birth of Abraham: So, it comes out to 1949 years. Next, take a look at Genesis 12:4: So Abram went, as the Lord had told him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran. So, Abraham was 75 years old at the start of the events in Exodus. Add those two numbers together, and you get 2024 years from the creation of Adam to the start of the events in Exodus. Ussher came up with 2082. Maybe that's to do with the aforementioned issues around Noah and Terah, or the time between the start of the events of in Exodus and actually escaping, or maybe even which source of the Bible he was using (they don't all have the same ages in Genesis 5 and Genesis 11), but those numbers are certainly in the same ballpark. Exodus to Solomon's Temple The next part is really easy. Per 1 Kings 6:1: In the four hundred eightieth year after the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv, which is the second month, he began to build the house of the Lord. So, you've got 480 years from the Exodus until the building of Solomon's Temple. Solomon's Temple to the Babylonian Captivity After that, it takes more effort than I was willing to put into it to trace the reigns of all the kings of Israel and Judah. But just to give a taste, here's 2 Kings 3:1: In the eighteenth year of King Jehoshaphat of Judah, Jehoram son of Ahab became king over Israel in Samaria; he reigned twelve years. So go searching for all those types of verses, and you can work out how long it was until the crowning of king Amel-Marduk. Ussher apparently made some judgment calls on overlapping periods, working out his estimate of 424 years. Somewhat independently, but not nearly as precisely, there are unbroken genealogies in the Gospels from Adam all the way to Jesus. Granted, they do contradict each other, but we'll just look past that. Matthew lists 42 generations from Adam to Jesus, while Luke lists 77. In either case, those give ballpark estimates on the order of thousands of years, even with the unrealistically high generation times in the early books of the Bible. So, the first two portions of that estimate are really pretty straight forward. And they rely on what seem to be matter of fact, boring ancestral lists, not fables, parables, or allegorical moral tales. Sure, it might seem unbelievalbe for a guy to be having kids at 500 years old, but is it really more unbelievable than the Plagues of Egypt or other Bible stories? And the third part, while I didn't go through the numbers, is from the part of the Bible that's actually probably more historically reliable. Even with just the portions I did for myself, if you take those ancestry lists at more or less face value, they get you all the way to Solomon's Temple, going through Egyptian Pharaohs along the way. In the grand scheme of things, that's not that long ago. Assuming for the sake of argument that Solomon and the First Temple really existed, you're looking at a Bronze Age civlization, so somewhere on the order of 1000 BC. So going back 2500 years from that gets you to 3500 BC. So once again, we're in the same ballpark as Ussher. My takeaway after going through all this, is that Ussher was a lot more reasonable than certain quarters of the Internet give him credit for. Sure, you have to accept the Bible as more or less true in the first place. But once you do, his estimate just follows from simple statements of 'fact' within the Bible. Even the slight uncertainties and judgment calls are only on the order of decades (at least for a particular Bible with given numbers) and aren't going to push the dates around all that much. Basically, if you accept Genesis 5 and Genesis 11 as factual, you’ll end up with an estimate somewhere on par with Ussher’s. If you want to reconcile the Bible with the true age of the Earth, you have to explain why Genesis 5 and Genesis 11 aren’t meant to be taken at their word.** *Parts of this answer were adapted and/or copied from a previous answer along similar lines: **And yes. Plenty of Christians do say that Genesis 5 and Genesis 11 aren’t meant to be taken at their word. I’m just pointing out that Ussher was merely following the text.

Question: WHEN does the real future of radical improvement like safe flying cars for the masses, holographic movies, massive building structures like seen in Judge Dredd etc actually start? Are we trapped in the present nightmare of potholes, jammed roads etc?
Answer: I think you might want to consider what travel was like just a century ago before calling the present state a nightmare. I wrote an answer once about travel in the 1800s and early 1900s (Jeff Lewis's answer to Before the industrial revolution when there were no cars or planes how did people travel and how far would they typically go?). A 30 mile trip would have been an all day affair back then. Now I can do that in around half an hour. It took Wilbur Wright a week to travel from Dayton, Ohio to Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. Google tells me I could make that drive in a little over 10 hrs, which is within reason for a single long day. Automobiles and the Interstate Highway System (or equivalent freeways in other countries) make relatively high speed long distance travel accessible to common people. As far as common sci-fi tropes like flying cars and holographic movies, you can't invent something physically impossible. As far as we know, there's no way to create levitating vehicles, except by already understood physics like magnets, which limits your altitude to something like a maglev train, or aerodynamics, which is basically just an aircraft, and we already have those. You're never going to see something like the cars in Blade Runner that just seem to float in midair with no visibile means of propulsion. Of course, there's more than one use of the term, flying car. If you mean an aircraft with folding wings or a folding rotor, people have already built prototypes of those. The big issue is that the compromises make them subpar aircraft and subpar ground transportation – the worst of both worlds. If you mean a dedicated aircraft that doesn't drive on the road, the issue comes down to physics and hover efficiency. Helicopters look the way they do for a reason. And even the new batch of eVTOL aircraft still have a large amount of total area for their lifting devices to have any type of reasonable efficiency. ABOVE: Various eVTOL Concepts – I don't think this is what most people think of when they hear the term 'flying car'. SOURCE: eVTOL is Almost Here: What About Pilot Training? The way holograms are portrayed in movies is somewhere between very, very difficult to impossible. Keep in mind that what we see is light heading towards our eyes coming from specific locations in space. You can't just make light originate from points in space from nothing. You need something to reflect it off of, or some medium that you can make glow at certain points to generate that light. Here's one of the approaches I've seen that comes closest to what people think of as sci-fi holograms, but just imagine the engineering difficulty of scaling this up to something that could generate an entire full color screen, without the particles interfering with each other, and with opacity (instead of just see through 'wireframes'). And other than the gee whiz factor, how useful would it even be? We've already got the ability to make 3D movies, and they only come and go as brief fads. People seem perfectly content with regular movies. And movie makers use that medium to frame shots and show things from specific perspectives. Horror movies would lose their jumps scares if you had a holographic representation of the entire scene and could see the monster hiding behind the bushes. So yeah, within our lifetimes, we probably are limited to only incremental improvements beyond our current technology. But our current technology is anything but a nightmare. It really is pretty amazing when you stop and think about it, and would have seemed like a technological marvel to people from just a century ago.

Question: Does driving a manual transmission get annoying?
Answer: It certainly can. Okak, let me establish my 'bona fides' before criticizing stick shifts. From high school through my first car after college, all I drove were stick shifts, including a year's worth of daily commuting in Washington, D.C. And that first car I bought for myself was a sports car, no less, because I really did enjoy driving for driving's sake. All that's to say that I was plenty comfortable and proficient driving a manual transmission. As so many people have said, under ideal conditions, you hardly notice the mechanics of shifting. It becomes second nature. There are even situations where it's especially handy, like choosing your gear on hills, push starting a car with a dead battery, or that time my brakes went out on me in a hand-me-down beater and I was able to nurse it home with downshifting and the emergency brake. But there are plenty of situations where stick shifts are decidedly less convenient. I injured my acromioclavicular (AC) joint in high school, and had to spend a few weeks with my arm in a sling. That would have been a non-issue with an automatic, but was a PITA with a stick. Then there are all the road trips where you swing through the drive thru to grab something to eat on the road – again, not ideal when you need one hand for shifting. My RX-7 made this problem even worse. In their quest to create a pure driver's experience, they didn't include cup holders. Running to Subway on your lunch break to grab something to take back to the office is a pain when you have to try to hold your drink while operating the clutch and gear shift. And while I got buy with a stick shift in D.C. rush hour traffic, my experiences later in life with automatics were definitely easier. When I got married, the vehicles we wanted for family vehicles tended to be available only as automatics. So, I've spent the last 20 or so years driving mostly automatic vehicles (minus an RX-8 that replaced my RX-7 as a more 'family friendly' sports car). And in all honesty, I don't miss the stick shift much at all. I thought I did, so I was excited when we got an automatic with paddle shifters that did give you control over exactly what gear you were in. But I only used those for about a week until the novelty wore off, and haven't really touched them since. As an engineer, I've also taken on a different mindset regarding manual transmissions. First off, they're a band-aid because of the crappy torque/power bands of internal combustion engines. Electric motors are showing that you don't need multi-speed transmissions if you have a better power source to begin with. Second, we engineers try to automate as much as practical to reduce the workload on operators. Early cars had manual timing advance, manual chokes, and all types of controls that just distracted the driver from their primary task of controlling the speed and path of the vehicle. The fact that stick shifts survived so long is not an endorsement of manual control of gear ratios, but a condemnation on us engineers that it took us so long to come up with better automatic transmissions. So yes, manual transmissions can get annoying. I'm not saying I'll never buy a stick shift again (I keep telling my wife that a 3rd gen RX-7 is going to be my midlife crisis car). But for my typical daily driver, I'll stick with automatics, and eventually something electric with a single speed gearbox that doesn't shift at all.

Question: What is the biggest flying vertebrate of all time?
Answer: Given the incompleteness of the fossil record in general, the fragmentary remains of certain species in particular, and the vagaries of trying to reconstruct an entire animal based solely on fossil skeletal remains, the best answer can only be an estimate, not definitive. There are still a few standouts worth discussing, all of them pterosaurs, and all within one particular family, the Azhdarchidae. ABOVE: From left to right – a typical person for comparison, Quetzalcoatlus northropi, Arambourgiania philadelphiae, Hatzegopteryx thambema, and Cryodrakon boreas; note that these reconstructions are not based on the most complete of remains CREDIT: Gabriel Ugueto SOURCE: https://malibestsk.xyz/product_details/22449788.html Quetzalcoatlus northropi Q. northropi may be the most well known of these. When I was growing up, Quetzalcoatlus was the undisputed king of flying vertebrates before those other fossils had been discovered (or at least properly identified – Cryodrakon was originally misidentified as a Quetzalcoatlus species). Unfortunately, as Mark Witton put it in the article, Quetzalcoatlus: the media concept vs. the science, "It's also only known from bits and pieces of a gigantic left wing and cannot be regarded as a well known animal." Reconstructions of Q. northropi are instead based on comparisons to its smaller cousin, Q. lawsoni (referred to as Q. sp in older literature before it was finally named in 2021) – we have found much more complete remains of that species. As such, many estimates are based on scaling up Q. lawsoni to the size of the wing bones found for Q. northropi. ABOVE: Doug Lawson holding the massive humerus of Q. northropi SOURCE: The Quetz Monograph Lives and Other News on Azhdarchid Pterosaurs — Tetrapod Zoology Anyway, referring to that same Mark Witton article, "recent estimates of its wingspan being in the region of 10 m [32.8 ft] and predicted body masses of 200-260 kg [440-575 lbs]." Arambourgiania philadelphiae There are only very fragmentary remains of this animal. Here's a diagram from Mark Witton to show just how little. Only the parts in white are known from actual remains – one neck vertebrae and a few fragments from the wing. The parts in gray are conjecture. Note that A. philadelphiae is the creature on the right, while Q. lawsoni (the smaller Quetzalcoatlus species) is shown on the left for comparison: ABOVE: Q. lawsoni on left, A. philadelphia on right SOURCE: Why the giant azhdarchid Arambourgiania philadelphiae needs a fanclub If you look at the Wikipedia description of the animal, you find winspan estimates anywhere from 7-13 m (23-43 ft), though many pterosaur experts feel the higher side is an overestimate. In that same article from Mark Witton that I pulled the above figure from, he made a casual comment of a body mass in the range of 200-250 kg (440-550 lbs). Hatzegopteryx thambema Hatzegopteryx is know from a bit more fossil material. Here's a similar figure to the one above, which includes this species. It includes Q. lawsoni on the left, A. philadelphiae on the right, and H. thambema front and center. The figure uses the same conventions of white for known material, and gray for conjecture. 2BNaish%2Band%2BWitton%2B2016.jpg ABOVE: Q. lawsoni on the left, A. philadelphiae on the right, and H. thambema front and center SOURCE: New paper: when the short-necked, giant azhdarchid pterosaur Hatzegopteryx ruled Late Cretaceous Romania These bones show Hatzegopteryx to have been much more robust than the other known Azhdarchids, with a much wider skull than other known Azhdarchid skulls. Combined with the fact that no large theropods are known from the sediments where the Hatzegopteryx fossils were found, this has led to the idea that it might have been an apex predator in its environment. Wingspan estimates for this creature range from 10-12 m (33-39 ft). Relying on Wikipedia for another weight estimate, it might have been somewhere between 180-250 kg (400-550 lbs). Cryodrakon boreas From the little I've been able to find about this animal, the fossil remains come from a few different individuals, including (but not limited to) a neck vertebrae from a juvenile, and another neck vertebrae from an adult comparable in size to Quetzalcoatlus northropi. The Wikipedia description does state that it appears to have been slightly more robust thatn Q. northropi, so perhaps a bit heavier. ABOVE SOURCE: Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology (@RoyalTyrrell) on X So, which one of these species was actually the biggest? Who can say? The fossil remains just aren’t complete enough to say anything definitive about even the individual animals they’re from, let alone variation within each species. But it is interesting that all of them seem to be bumping up against the same limits on wingspan and bodyweight, of somewhere in the neighborhood of 10 m (33 ft) and 225 kg (500 lbs). That seems to suggest that that's approaching the limit of how big pterosaurs could get and still be able to fly. So perhaps, even if we do find more giant pterosaurs in the future, they'll still be in the same ballpark. Most of the links provided in the above answer are worth reading if you want more details. Question: Are atheist countries happier?
Answer: Yes, although that doesn't tell you the direction of causation. But first, let's look at the data showing the correlation. For this first graph, the data comes from the UN’s 2013 World Happiness Report and the 2013 Pew Survey of Religious Importance. The blue line is the linear regression, and the grey band is the 95% confidence interval. This is a pretty robust correlation between religiosity and happiness. ABOVE SOURCE: Religiosity versus happiness: among nations, the first doesn’t bring the second Here's another graph. This one plots two things – the religiosity of the country, and the belief in God within the country. You can see that the correlation with belief is even steeper than the correlation with religiosity. ABOVE SOURCE: Happiness and Religion: Does Belief Make You Happy Or Does Unhappiness Make You Believe? As far as the direction of causation, there was an interesting study back in 2011 that looked at year by year income inequality and year by year religiosity. You can ready a layman's summary here: I don't have a pretty graph for this next part, but quoting that summary, here are two interesting findings: I'm not a Marxist by any stretch of the imagination, but old Karl really did capture this in his famous 'opium of the people' passage: Religious suffering is, at one and the same time, the expression of real suffering and a protest against real suffering. Religion is the sigh of the oppressed creature, the heart of a heartless world, and the soul of soulless conditions. It is the opium of the people. The abolition of religion as the illusory happiness of the people is the demand for their real happiness. To call on them to give up their illusions about their condition is to call on them to give up a condition that requires illusions. The criticism of religion is, therefore, in embryo, the criticism of that vale of tears of which religion is the halo. Now, I'm not sure the causation goes solely in one direction. A single study on income inequality only goes so far. Real life is very complex, and there's certainly a possibility for reinforcing feedback, where religion isn't solely a reaction to bad circumstances, but that it can also exacerbate them. But, at least per this particular study, it seems that the bad circumanstances drive religion more than the other way around. So if you're like me and want to see religion lose its grip on so much of the world and its harmful influences in American politics, the long term solution is to improve people's living conditions. Once people have a high quality of life, they won't feel the need to turn to religion for solace. FWIW, this is where Stalin and the Soviets got it wrong regarding state imposed atheism (well, this and the fact that they were ruthless authoritarians who saw the church as competition). Religion was a symptom of bad living conditions. You can't try to get rid of a symptom without first addressing the cause.
