Question: What hasn't natural selection eliminated criminals and selfishness? Do we need a few more billion years?
Answer: While evolution is a mindless process without any conscious intent, sometimes anthropomorphizing can help to explain things. And in that sense, the 'goal' of evolution is to produce more offspring. And in a social animal like us, that sets up conflicting imperatives. Depending on the conditions and the niche, social groups and cooperation can offer animals synergistic benefits greater than the sum of the individuals. If you've ever tried working on DIY projects by yourself, you've probably found times where two people working together can get the job done in less than half the time of one person working alone. So, for example, if I help my neighbor build a shed, and then he helps me build mine, we'll get two sheds built in less time than it would have taken either of us to try to build our own. It's a win-win. So, you see various levels of social cooperation in all types of packs, herds, tribes, troops, pods, etc., with ants and bees being some of the most extreme examples. Individuals living in such social environments need social instincts, not just to make the group successful, but so that they're accepted into the group so that they can take advantage of the group benefits for themselves. If I was the cantakerous neighbor that nobody liked, I'd never get anybody to help me on projects. But, there are also conflicting instincts to not be too selfless to the group, lest they sacrifice their own reproductive success. I don't want to go around only helping out neighbors, but never get around to my own projects. Similarly, all members of the group have an interest in identifying and punishing freeloaders and cheats, since they would drag down the success of the group as a whole, and conversely, individuals will have an interest in not being identified as cheats, themselves, to avoid punishment. So, social animals evolve a whole range of complex and sometimes conflicting impulses to maximize their success in such settings. Even actions that go against their own short term self interest may be important in maintaining long term acceptance within the group. I'll give up my own time to help my neighbor move with no expectation of reward other than the obligatory pizza and beer, but it cements my standing in the community as a 'good guy'. Of course, most of us aren't so Machiavellian and calculating in our own behavior, but, anthropomorphizing a bit more, natural selection was. And so, we've evolved all these instincts for noble and selfish impulses. As long as our species survives and we continue to live in these types of social groups, selfishness will unfortunately persist alongside our more noble impulses. It's the way natural selection ensures that we take care of propagating our own genes. Question: As a non-Christian, do you have any questions or anything I can clarify with you about Christianity/the Bible?
Answer: Skimming over your profile and responses to other questions, you seem to have asked this question in good faith, so I'll respond in kind. Starting at the beginning, the first creation account in Genesis does not match the actual history of the universe and our planet that we've learned through geology, astronomy, paleontology, etc. Now, I've heard some folks argue for a day-age interpretation to try to reconcile the creation story with reality, but that still has issues with things not being created in the right order (e.g. day, night, and plants all being created before the Sun, birds being created before land animals, etc.) So how do you reconcile the first creation account in Genesis with reality (or do you)? And assuming the story is divinely inspired, why would a god inspire such a misleading story in the first place? Related to that, the two creation accounts in Genesis contradict each other, with the 7 day creation account telling a different story than the Garden of Eden story. It appears nearly certain that's because they come from different traditions, the Priestly source for the former, and the Yahwist source for the latter. In fact, there are at least four sources for the Pentateuch, the two already mentioned, along with the Elohist source and the Deuteronomist source, not to mention the Redactor who edited them all around the time of the Babylonian Exile (more info: How Was the Bible Formed? - Bible Odyssey and What Is Source Criticism? - Bible Odyssey). While the discrepancies between sources are clear in the two different creation accounts, there are plenty of other discrepancies throughout the books. Even for a common story told in two prior traditions like Noah's flood, you get interweaving of details, like different durations for the flood, and different numbers of animals to take on board. So again assuming that the Bible is divinely inspired, why would a god take such a tortuous route to assemble it from all these various prior sources, and why leave so many contradictory details? What about the polytheistic origins of Yahweh and the Bible? You said questions about the Bible, so I'll leave out archaeological questions (like the Kuntillet Ajrud Inscriptions). But what about Deuteronomy 32:8–9: 8 When the Most High[b] apportioned the nations, when he divided humankind, he fixed the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the gods;[c] 9 the Lord’s own portion was his people, Jacob his allotted share. This seems very much to come from a prior tradition where Yahweh was still considered one of many gods. There's also the story in 2 Kings 3, where it seems very much that King Mesha's sacrifice of his firstborn son to his god (unnamed in that particular story, but it was Chemosh) granted the Moabites favor to win the battle: Then he took his firstborn son who was to succeed him and offered him as a burnt offering on the wall. And great wrath came upon Israel, so they withdrew from him and returned to their own land. How do these polytheistic passages fit into a conception of Yahweh as the one and only God? And echoing the prior question, why assemble a divinely inspired book from such prior traditions that didn't agree with the final message in the now canonical Bible? Anyway, that'll do for now. I've got plenty more questions, but this is long enough.

Question: How does an atheist explain 1 cor 15 appearance to the 12 stated by Paul, who investigated and interacted with them directly?
Answer: First, as far as I'm aware, Paul never met all 12 disciples. I know Wikipedia's not a 'scholarly' source, but it states, "In Paul's account of his visit to Jerusalem in Galatians 1:18-19, he states that he stayed with Cephas (better known as Peter) and James, the brother of the Lord, was the only other apostle he met." (See also Dick Harfield's answer to What was the proof of Paul's meeting with the Apostles?). So we can't really say that Paul "interacted with them directly", let alone that he "investigated" the claims. I mean, Paul had already had his own vision (whatever that entailed), so he was going in as a true believer, not a skeptic looking to poke holes into Christianity. Moving on, let's look at a more recent holy man. There was an Indian guru man named Shri Sai Baba* who died in 1918. Here are some excerpts from the online biography maintained by some of his followers, from Chapter 12 of The Saint of Shirdi. On the very next day after his death Baba, appeared to one of his devotees in a dream-vision, saying, “Jog thinks I am dead, I am alive. Go and perform my morning arati.” Soon, other devotees also began to get unmistakable signs of the Master’s deathless presence until almost each disciple was able to claim with conviction -- “The Master is come again, he cannot die.” The Master manifests himself in different ways to different devotees. His voice is not hushed. Nor is his physical presence lost to his devotees. Testimonials come pouring in from all quarters of the tangible reappearance of Sai Baba. In many cases the Master gives darshan in actual flesh and blood, not only to those who had been his close disciples during his life time, but also to many others who had not even seen him or heard of him. This deliberate choosing of fresh disciples and devotees by vouchsafing to them some kind of mystical experience is very characteristic of the Saint of Shirdi. [emphasis mine] You can find modern examples right here on Quora of people who've claimed to have been visited by Shri Sai Baba, whether in dreams or in waking hours: I suppose that if we were being super open minded, we might believe that certain people actually can come back from the dead to visit the living, and that Jesus was just one of those people, like Shri Sai Baba. Although I would point out that if more people than Jesus can do this, then it it would seem Jesus wasn’t all that unique. But I'm going to go out on a limb and assume you doubt the stories about Shri Sai Baba. So basically, just think of all the explanations you can think of for people's visions of Shri Sai Baba, and apply them to the visions of Jesus – things like dreams, altered states of consciousness, grief hallucinations, other types of hallucinations, memories becoming a bit skewed over the years, second hand stories growing in the retelling, and possibly even just outright lying. If I had to guess, I'd chalk up the original visions of Jesus to grief hallucinations**, and that by the time Paul heard the stories, it was a combination of skewed memories and exagerrated second hand stories, with Paul maybe twisting things a bit to fit his own preconceptions. But we're talking about things that happened 2000 years ago with very little in the way of surviving evidence or independent accounts, so there's really no way to be certain of all the details. *Note that this is a different holy man from the one I've written about previously, Sathya Sai Baba: **For details on grief hallucinations being the possible inspiration for the resurrection stories, see here:

Question: Who was the first ancestor of ours who walked on four legs?
Answer: It depends on what you mean by 'walking'. It's also a bit cloudy because of the incompleteness of the fossil record. Let's address the definition of 'walking', first. Take a look at this video of a modern day creature (i.e. not our ancestor, and not even particularly closely related): I think it’s reasonable to say that it's walking along the coral reef, using its fins much like legs. And the truth is, walking underwater is a useful form of locomotion. Handfish and frogfish are also quite well known for walking underwater. And it seems that in our own ancestors, walking underwater came first, before any of them ever tried to crawl up onto a mud bank. I found an article that goes into great detail on the origin of tetrapods, The Fish–Tetrapod Transition: New Fossils and Interpretations. Here's a figure from that article, showing the relationships of species know from fossils, along with the general timeframe of when tetrapods evolved: ABOVE: Stratigraphic table of Late Devonian and Early Carboniferous with cladogram of tetrapodomorphs superimposed to show distribution in time. Broad bars show known range, narrow bars show possible range where exact dating is not available. Based on Ahlberg et al. (2008) SOURCE: The Fish–Tetrapod Transition: New Fossils and Interpretations Note that most of those are side branches, not our direct ancestors, so they're really only giving us a general idea of what our ancestors would have been like, not precise snapshots. Still, the first creatures to walk would have been along those lines. Here's another figure, with less animals, but with pictures of the ones that were included, including diagrams of their forelimbs: SOURCE: The origin of tetrapods - Understanding Evolution So, the first of our ancestors to walk underwater probably would have been something along the lines of Panderichthys. The first of our ancestors to spend an appreciable amount of time walking on land would have been something along the lines of Acanthostega. Though keep in mind the timeframes from the earlier figure, and that Acanthostega was living well after the actual first creatures to become so terrestrial. With recent finds over the past few decades, the current fossil record actually already is a lot more complete than when I was a kid. But there are still plenty of transitional species left to be found. I'm excited for scientists to find them so that I can learn about them.

Question: Some worry that the United States is in an unusually anti-intellectual period right now. Is this really the case? Haven't societies always been composed mostly of people who are rather unthinking and just want "bread and circuses"?
Answer: Like so many things in the modern day U.S., it's a partisan issue. Here's one graph with poll results going back to the mid '70s (note that the y-axis is compressed): SOURCE: Why Being Anti-Science Is Now Part Of Many Rural Americans’ Identity Historically, Democrats, Republicans, and Independents all hovered around close to the same trust in science at somewhere around 40%. In fact, for most of that period, Republicans had greater trust in science than Democrats, which is what you'd expect from the stereotypes of the parties when I was growing up (i.e. that the Republicans were the mature adults in the room, tempering the wide eyed enthusiasm of the idealistic but naive Democrats). But starting some time around the '90s, those historical positions began to reverse, with trust in science dropping among Republicans, while growing among Democrats. Today's Republicans have a historically low level of trust in science, while Democrats have an unprecedented level of support*. To those of us following the scientific side of the 'Culture Wars', the Republican collapse of trust in science isn't at all surprising. Folks were raising alarm bells around this issue back in the 2000s. Chris Mooney even wrote an entire book about the issue: ABOVE SOURCE: Amazon You saw it in global issues like climate change and local issues like evolution vs. creationism in the public schools. One very emblematic example came from our State Board of Education (SBOE) here in Texas, where the former chairman of the SBOE somewhat famously said, "Somebody's got to to stand up to the experts" (source: NCSE - McLeroy booted in Texas). Stop and let that sink in for a minute. The board of education thought it was their duty to go against the experts in the fields they wanted students to learn about. In more recent times, we saw the way this played out with the public response to COVID-19, in everything from how seriously people took the threat, to how willing they were to follow expert advice on mitigating the risks. And sadly, this had the follow on effect of a noticeable difference in death rates by party: SOURCE: Tomas Pueyo (@tomaspueyo) on X While there has always been a strain of anti-intellectualism within the U.S., the current trends are towards a sharper divide along political lines, with the Republican party becoming the anti-intellectual party. I wish this wasn’t a partisan issue. There's nothing inherent in conservative vs. liberal policies that makes this inevitable. It's just the unfortunate reality we live in right now. *I'm a bit cynical about the Democratic support of science. While I'd love for it to be authentic, I suspect it's mostly virtue signaling in opposition to the Republican distrust of science. But at least lip service in support of science is still better than organized opposition.

Name: Jeff Lewis
Question: If you have a Bible at hand, can you open it up to a random page and see what it says? Maybe it will change your life.
Answer: Okay. I decided to give this a try, and I really did open up to random pages rather than cherry picking verses that I knew were problematic just to make a point. And to up the odds that I’d get something good, I actually tried it three times, not just once. Here’s what I got: First Attempt – Joshua 14 and Joshua 15 Well, there's nothing really profound or life changing here. It was mostly just details of how the conquered areas of the Promised Land were divied out to the various Jewish people. Just to give a taste of how tedious it is: And their south boundary ran from the end of the Dead Sea, from the bay that faces southward; it goes out southward of the ascent of Akrabbim, passes along to Zin, and goes up south of Kadesh-barnea, along by Hezron, up to Addar, makes a turn to Karka, passes along to Azmon, goes out by the Wadi of Egypt, and comes to its end at the sea. This shall be your south boundary. If you wanted to be less charitable, you could point out that the Israelites were the evil conquerors who went in and subjugated or displaced the people already living there, but that kind of thing is so common throughout history that it's just par for the course. I mean, look at how many times the lands that would become England were invaded and conquered by outsiders, or basically the entire history of Rome. (Also, somewhat thankfully, these stories about conquering the Promised Land probably aren’t true – Frans du Plessis's answer to Do we have extra-biblical evidence for the origins of the Israelites?) Second Attempt – 2 Chronicles 1 and 2 Chronicles 2 Well, at least we get one of the classic Bible stories, here, with God offering Solomon anything he wanted, and Solomon asking for wisdom. But it all reads as just typical ancient literature, so still nothing life changing. I'll note the the final couple verses, though: Then Solomon took a census of all the aliens who were residing in the land of Israel, after the census that his father David had taken, and there were found to be one hundred fifty-three thousand six hundred. Seventy thousand of them he assigned as laborers, eighty thousand as stonecutters in the hill country, and three thousand six hundred as overseers to make the people work. Huh. No calls to send them back across the border where they came from, or complaints that the immigrants were stealing Israelite jobs. Just a pragmatic approach of putting them to work. I feel like there might be a lesson there for certain modern day folks who claim to follow the Bible. Third Attempt – Job 30 and Job 31 These were the chapters where Job wrapped up his defense to his friends who insisted that he must have done something wrong to have incurred God's wrath, while Job insisted that he'd done nothing wrong and had lived a good life. It's really just a reminder of how unfair and cruel God can be. As I've said elsewhere, the lesson one takes away from Job is that might makes right, and God is the mightiest of all. So I actually gave it three shots. None of the chapters I came across offered anything particularly profound or life changing. And actually, that is an important point that I don't think a lot of folks really understand. You so often hear people say that, even if you're not religious, at least the Bible is great literature, or carries profound moral lessons. But on the whole, it isn't, really. There may be certain sections of the Bible that are good (e.g. Ecclesiastes). But when you look at the entire Bible, it's a very mixed bag, with the tedious and mundane parts outnumbering the good parts.

Question: Is it true that ex-Christians and Muslims still hold some kind of belief in a god for a long time after deconverting, they are just pretty sure it isn’t real?
Answer: It depends on the person, and it depends on what you mean by a long time. Speaking for myself, because I've written so much on my personal website and was pretty meticulous about documenting updates, I can actually go and look back over things I've written over the years to trace my development. I think I can say that round about 2004 is when I first started on the road that would lead me towards to atheism. This was right around the time that Intelligent Design was at the peak of its influence, and the voices of so many creationists / Intelligent Design advocates insisting that evolution went against Christianity made me question if I was being a good Christian by accepting evolution. Needless to say, after researching evolution vs. creationism in more depth than what I'd learned in my high school biology class, there's a reason why evolution is so overwhelmingly accepted by the scientific community. That's when I wrote my first article on my personal website touching on the subject of evolution, back in December of 2004, Evolution Rant (it's not a terribly great essay, to be honest). Another issue that was perhaps important was the debate around legalizing gay marriage. I wrote an essay on that, as well, just a bit earlier in April of 2004, Legality of Homosexual Marriage. I was arguing more from a perspective of separation of church and state, insisting that as a Christian, I still personally saw homosexuality as immoral, but couldn’t see any reason for a secular government to ban gay marriage. In hindsight, I think this was another important point in making me question my religion. Over the next year or so, I wrote a few more essays on such topics, but the one I think really marks my departure from mainstream Christianity came in August of 2005 in the essay, How to Interpret the Bible, where I argued that the Bible wasn't divinely inspired, but merely the work of men doing their best to try to document their interactions with the divine. While I remained a Christian at the time, that was a huge turning point. By April of 2006, in an email correspondence that I later posted online (How to Handle Religion with Your Children When You Don’t Believe in the Religion), I admitted to someone that I no longer accepted Christianity, but I didn't yet consider myself an outright atheist, because I wasn't so sure that there was no 'higher power' at all. Then, by July of 2007, in an essay titled Am I Religious?, I finally referred to myself as an atheist. Around the same time in September of 2007, I posted a blog entry announcing my atheism, My Hundredth Blog Entry & An Announcement. Thinking back, that's when I became comfortable with the idea that there probably weren't any gods at all. I was still hedging my bets a bit (“I leave open the slight possibility that gods could possibly exist, but I base my worldview on the idea that they probably don't”), but barely more than you hedge your bets on all knowledge claims. And in the 17 years since, I’ve only grown more confident that gods aren’t real. So, from my first inklings of doubt in 2004, I went through a transition period of roughly 3 years where I began to question Christianity, with somewhere around a year of that going from recognizing Christianity wasn’t true to becoming an atheist about all gods. Whether or not you think those periods are a long time is down to your perspective.

Name: Jeff Lewis
Question: Do atheists think that theists are unintelligent?
Answer: It's complicated. So, let's get the provocative part out of the way, first. Numerous studies have found a negative correlation between intelligence and being religious. In other words, the less intelligent a person is, the more likely they are to be religious. And the more intelligent a person is, the more likely they are to be an atheist or agnostic. For example, one study that surveyed 432 people (The Relationship Between Religiousness/Spirituality and Psychometric Intelligence in the United States) found Christians to have an average IQ of 96.7, compared to 104.9 for atheists and 107.5 for agnostics. There was also a meta analysis (The Negative Intelligence–Religiosity Relation: New and Confirming Evidence) that synthesized the results of 83 prior studies, finding a negative correlation that ranged from -0.20 to -0.23. But, it's important to keep in mind that these are only averages, and that a correlation of -0.2 isn't very strong. Here are some examples of correlations, to give you an idea of what -0.2 looks like: SOURCE: https://quizlet.com/514729056/statistics-flash-cards/ As you might expect from the above, there's also quite a bit of overlap between religious and non-religious folks. If you were to plot bell curves of the IQs of those two groups, it would look something like this: SOURCE: Unwarranted Assumption There is lots of overlap, with plenty of religious folks among the most intelligent people, and plenty of non-religious folks that aren't the sharpest knives in the drawer. It's trivial to find examples of intelligent Christians (e.g. List of Christians in science and technology - Wikipedia). I follow plenty of intelligent Christians, myself, here on Quora. And, of course, there's plenty of discussion on just exactly what it means for non-believers to do better on IQ tests. Obviously, researchers try their best to account for confounding factors, but have they properly accounted for all of them? Is it general intelligence that makes the difference, specific types of intelligence, or even learned skillsets that allow some people to do better on these types of tests? But overall, there have been enough studies with similar results, that it's safe to say that non-believers are on average slightly more intelligent than believers. Still, the correlation is so small that it doesn't tell you much about individual believers or non-believers.

Question: When did the celebration of Christmas begin to shift away from its religious origins?
Answer: Sadly, some time around the Middle Ages, or perhaps a bit later at the Protestant Reformation. Prior to that, the pagan religious origins of some Christmas celebrations were still in full swing, and let me tell you, they sound fun. To be clear, the source of Christmas traditions is a bit mixed. While certain Internet sources would have you believe that it's entirely based on pagan traditions, the truth is more nuanced. But that's not really what I want to write about in this answer, so here's a link, if you're interested: However, it is true that when Christmas was first getting started and Roman pagans were converting to Christianity, they brought over a lot of their old traditions with them, particularly traditions related to Saturnalia, since it was celebrated around the same time of year. And these were fairly rowdy traditions, more in line with Mardi Gras than spending quality time with the family by the fireplace. There were costumes, props, heavy drinking, singing, gambling, and a Lord of Misrule, where one commoner was elected by the people to be the temporary 'leader' for the day. I read one description of Christmas as “like a nightmarish cross between Halloween and a particularly violent, rowdy Mardi Gras." (source) Here's one of my favorite pictures of this Christmas tradition. You've got the whole rabble entering into the church to confront the clergy and nobleman to assert the Lord of Misrule’s leadership. And look at that assemblage. You've got the Lord of Misrule himself (they guy wearing the pointy cap), a jester, fake knights on fake horses, and even somebody dressed up like a dragon. ABOVE: The Abbot of Unreasons by Cruikshank SOURCE: Lord of Misrule - Wikipedia Here are a couple more of these illustrations that I like to get across the feel of ‘traditional’ Christmas celebrations. ABOVE: This one’s got a fish man, if you look close enough. SOURCE: Lord of Misrule ABOVE: Lots of interesting costumes SOURCE: Bodleian Library MS. Bodl. 264, pt. I Christmas caroling also grew out of this. It didn't start as a bunch of folks going around singing songs just to make people happy. The carols were more like drinking songs, and the carolers were demanding food and drink from the houses of the rick folks that they visited. You can see this in a few Christmas carols that people still sing, like We Wish You a Merry Christmas (in the verses where they demand the figgy pudding) or Here We Come a-Wassailing (i.e. everybody drinking alcohol out of the communal Waissail bowl). ABOVE: Everybody Getting Sloshed Off the Wassail Bowl SOURCE: The Centuries-Old History of Wassail - Tales of the Cocktail Foundation Starting in the Middle Ages, stodgy old holier-than-thou types tamped down on these traditions, probably simply because they didn’t want people to have fun, but justifying it by saying that they wanted to focus more on the Christian aspects of Christmas. So that’s when “Christmas begin to shift away from its [pagan] religious origins”. Anyway, now we’re left with a much more anodyne Christmas celebration. Oh sure, you might have the office Christmas party were somebody has a few too many Jack & Cokes. But nobody’s wandering around the neighborhood in drunken groups dressed up in costumes while demanding that their rich neighbors treat them to food and even more alcohol. But it still sounds like fun. Here are a few articles with more details on these traditional Christmas celebrations, if you’re interested:

Question: Food and supplies are air dropped from a plane which is flying at a constant speed of 238 m/s at an altitude of 6.7 km. How far horizontally will the supplies travel after they are released?
Answer: I'm not going to do your homework for you, but I will say that you need a lot more information to answer this question. While I am an aerospace engineer, airdrops aren't my particular area of expertise. However, I can say that nearly all airdrops I'm aware of use parachutes. The ones that don't are for things that usually fall slowly anyway, like leaflets. Also, 6.7 km is pretty high up, and 238 m/s is pretty fast. To put it into more typical aeronautical terms, that's basically 22k ft high at a speed of 463 kts, or somewhere on the order of Mach 0.75. So, you really can't solve this assuming a simple ballistic path in a vacuum like a lot of homework problems tell you to. At 463 kts, with or without a parachute, air resistance won't be negligible, so you’ll need to understand the aerodynamics of the package. And assuming that your cargo likely will have a parachute, wind patterns will complicate the path all the more. ETA: Okay, I decided to go back and do a few calculations to make this answer a little more informative. I kept it simple, ignoring parachutes and wind, and just looked at a spherical ‘package’ in freefall, comparing a scenario that ignored drag to one that included drag. I set up a simple simulation in a spreadsheet, breaking the fall down into 0.1 second time segments (i.e. not an exact answer, but close enough for engineering). I’ll save you all the formulas, but I assumed a 5 ft diameter and a 500 lb total weight, using the drag vs. Mach estimate from this paper, Constraining the Drag Coefficients of Meteors in Dark Flight. Here are the graphs of the results. The first graph is the trajectories in space. The next two graphs break it down into vertical and horizontal components (note that I left everything in more typical engineering units of ft and ft/s): As you can see, you get wildly different results. Dropping from such a high altitude, there’s plenty of time for the object to reach terminal velocity, so the freefall speed levels off at around 200 mph, which makes it take a lot longer to fall all the way to the ground. Also, the horizontal velocity drops very quickly because of how high the drag is initially. So even though the scenario including drag takes so much longer to hit the ground, the slow horizontal speed means that the ‘package’ travels a lot less distance horizontally than the no-drag scenario. There may be scenarios where the no-drag assumption is a close enough approximation, like say dropping balls from relatively low heights. But when you’re talking about objects close to the speed of sound, and altitudes on the order of 4 miles, that’s no longer a good assumption. You really do need to consider aerodynamic effects. And keep in mind that this was still a super simple analysis. Different shapes, whether they’re spinning or not, Reynolds number effects, winds, etc. will all affect the results.

Question: What grade did you learn Darwin’s theory of evolution?
Answer: Just going with the flow on "Darwin's theory" vs. the Modern Synthesis, I learned about evolution in earnest in my high school biology class. There was a bit of flexibility to when you took certain classes, but if memory serves, most of us typically took Biology in 10th grade (you could later take A.P. Biology if so inclined – I honestly can't remember if I did or not). Prior to that, most of my exposure to evolution had been brief comments here and there, whether in school or watching nature documentaries, but no actual in depth explanations of mutation and selection. In other words, there were enough matter of fact statements about evolution that I accepted it as the default history of life, but I didn't really understand it. My ideas on evolution were a mix of teleological views and Lamarckian style use and disuse. That high school biology class truly was a revelation. I mean, when you think of evolution in Lamarckian terms, you'll understandably have some questions about how various traits could evolve. I remember one particular example from a documentary I'd seen, of a type of plant that provided food and shelter to ants, in exchange for the ants protecting the plants from more harmful herbivores. And, in my pre-Darwinian mindset, I was dumbfounded as to how something like that could have evolved. How did the plants 'know' to provide anything to the ants? How can use and disuse apply to plants, when plants don't 'try' to do anything? IMAGE SOURCE: Myrmecophytic Plants and Their Ants But as soon as you put it in terms of random mutations and natural selection, it all just falls into place. Of course plants didn't need to consciously plan anything, nor did the ants benefitting from the plants. It was all a mindless process, and whatever by chance happened to work better simply became more common than things that by chance didn't work as well. Growing up in a fairly well educated family and going to pretty good schools, I was never exposed to any creationists arguments that tried to cast doubt on evolution. But at the same time, for most of my childhood, I never actually received any type of proper education on how evolution actually works. It was that sophomore biology class that finally gave me a proper explanation of mutation and natural selection.

Question: How long were dinosaurs on Earth compared to humans?
Answer: These comparisons always strike me as really strange. 'Dinosaurs' are an entire group of many, many different species. Humans are a single species. Of course dinosaurs as a group have existed much, much longer than humans as a species. But by the same token, dinosaurs as a group existed much, much longer than T. rex as a species. If you want to compare group to group, which group do you pick? The first dinosaurs evolved some time around 240 million years ago, give or take (which is also the total time dinosaurs have been around, since birds are still living). The first cynodonts, which is a group we belong to, evolved around 260 million years ago. So, cynodonts are older than dinosaurs. But the first mammals, another, slightly smaller group that we belong to, only evolved around 225 million years ago, so mammals are younger than the dinosaurs. So it's somewhat arbitrary which group to pick to do the comparison. Anyway, Homo sapiens first evolved around 200,000 years ago. So our particular species is much, much younger than dinosaurs as a group. But if you want to start going back to our ancestors, well, then it's arbitrary again where to draw that line. The oldest member of our particular genus, Homo, evolved around 2 million years ago. Older ancestors like Australopithecus evolved around 4 million years ago. Apes have been around roughly 25 million years. Primates have been around roughly 55 million years. And of course, you can trace our ancestors (and dinosaurs) all the way back to the first life billions of years ago.

Question: Atheists, isn't your Darwinian theory a little far-fetched when you think about it? The theory states that all living things have a common ancestor. An elephant and a mosquito share a common ancestor? Really?
Answer: When I've talked to people about this, part of the misconception seems to be expecting something like a mosquito evolving into something like an elephant, or vice versa. But that's not the way evolution works. Both mosquitos and elephants are highly evolved, complex creatures. But their common ancestor wasn't anywhere near as complex as either of them. Here's the oldest known bilaterian animal (i.e. the group that includes elephants and mosquitos). This likely isn’t the actual, specific common ancestor, but it would have been fairly similar. SOURCE: Oldest “bilaterian” found: wormlike creature discovered along with its tracks From our modern point of view, that's a pretty simple, worm-like animal (though in its own time, it was one of the more complex creatures yet to evolve). But from that worm-like form, as it's descendants carried on and diversified, each separate lineage was free to 'add on' to that body plan, evolving into more complex forms as time went by. But since they were separate lineages, they couldn't share mutations between them. Each lineage went its own way, so that the types of complexity that evolved in each lineage was different from their cousin lineages. SOURCE: ResearchGate.net - Origin and Evolution of Nervous Systems As far as insects in particular, you can trace their evolutionary history, and see how various traits evolved generation by generation, eventually resulting in the complexity of modern day mosquitos: SOURCE: Fossils, genes and the evolution of animal limbs - Nature Likewise, you can trace the independent evolutionary history of vertebrates, which followed a different path, resulting in a different type of complex body plan: SOURCE: Fossils, genes and the evolution of animal limbs - Nature In fact, you can do this for the whole tree of life. The organisms we see today are the tips of the branches. The tips didn't evolve into the other tips. Instead, you have to trace the branches back in time to find the common ancestors that the branches evolved from. SOURCE: Researchgate.net - Informational Ecological and System Approaches for Complete Genome Analysis So, that’s how mosquitos and elephants evolved from a common ancestors. That ancient ancestor wasn’t yet very mosquito-like nor very elephant-like. It was really much more worm-like. It’s only as time went on, and each of those lineages went their separate ways, that one particular lineage evolved into mosquitos, while a different lineage evolved into elephants. As an aside, all the normal caveats go here. Most Christians and other religious folks accept evolution, so this isn’t an atheist vs. religious issue. And most folks only use ‘Darwinian’ in a more historical context, and specifically in reference to natural selection, to contrast with other ideas on evolution (like Lamarckian use and disuses). The modern day theory is the Modern Synthesis, which includes many more concepts and principles than Darwin ever knew about.

Question: Do atheists believe Jesus was a person but no God?
Answer: Yeah, sure. Probably. I know that there are a decent number of atheists who doubt that Jesus was a real person and think he was probably entirely legendary. But, while I don't think there's enough evidence to say anything conclusive, I do think it's more likely than not that he did exist. For one, it's a rather mundane claim. Charismatic leaders starting religious cults are a dime a dozen throughout history. We've got plenty in modern times and recent history, like Joseph Smith, L. Ron Hubbard, Jim Jones, David Koresh, Marshall Applewhite, Sun Myung Moon, Sathya Sai Babe, etc. Plenty even have stories of miracles they've performed. So the claim that a guy named Jesus (or the ancient equivalent of that name) founded a cult around 2000 years ago is not an extraordinary claim requiring extraordinary evidence. For another, unlike other mythical characters like Romulus and Remus, Robin Hood, or King Arthur, we've got Jesus pinpointed a lot more closely. Especially with the authentic letters of Paul, we've got a guy writing about this cult within living memory of Jesus, claiming to interact with folks who knew Jesus personally. We've also got the Gospels and a few extra-Biblical references from a few years later. And while the Gospels have plenty of problems around just how historically accurate they might be, it still seems reasonable that they'd be based on a real person, especially considering 'difficulties' that make more sense in light of trying to accommodate known details about a real person (the Nativity, Jesus's baptism, and the crucifixion itself). Sure, there's no eye witness or contemporary evidence, but how much of this type of evidence would you expect? If Jesus and his followers were illiterate peasants, they wouldn't have been writing much of anything themselves, so you wouldn't start to get things like Paul's letters or the Gospels until the popularity of the cult spread to more educated folks. And while some folks protest the lack of Roman records for things like the crucifixion, the fact is that we just don't have that many surviving records of anything like that from ancient Rome. Such records were written on perishable materials, so unless someone made an effort to save them, they didn't survive. We don't actually have records of any specific crucifixions from Rome, let alone Jesus's. So yeah. I think it's more likely than not that Jesus was a real cult leader 2000 years ago. As I already said, such cult leaders aren't exactly rare. The interesting thing about this cult is the way it struck a chord with so many people and rose in prominence. But that’s bound to happen from time to time, such as with later religions like Islam, Mormons, etc. For much more detail on the historicity of Jesus, here's one of the best answers I've ever come across on Quora. Question: Why do so many people hate the self checkouts?
Answer: Actually, I tend to prefer it. But it really depends on the implementation, and what the store was like before they brought in the self checkouts. Let me take my local Walmart as an example. Back in the days before self checkouts, they never had enough cashiers for the number of customers. There was no such thing as a quick trip to Walmart, because you inevitably got stuck in a long line waiting to check out. Then, when they did bring in self checkouts, they brought in dozens of them. So now, there's almost always at least one self-checkout open. And even if there is a line, it's more like a bank line, where everybody waits in one line, and then just goes to the next open checkout. So it doesn't matter if there are a few folks with full carts, because they're only tying up that one particular checkout, not the entire line. Now it really is possible to be in and out of Walmart in 5 minutes if I only need one thing. I've been to other stores, though, where they've only installed a limited number of self checkouts. And the worst offenders don't even go with the bank-style lines, but have separate lines for each self checkout. Those are annoying, where you may end up waiting longer than the pre-self-checkout days. My favorite modern checkout is Sam's Club (I'd imagine the other warehouse stores have this as well, but Wichita Falls, TX doesn't give you many options). You just download an app to your phone to scan the items as you shop, swipe a button to pay with a credit card on file, and then just briefly show your phone to the receipt checker on your way out the door. It's hard to get much quicker and convenient than that. But my second favorite checkout is at a small grocery chain called United Market Street, which has a good compromise between self checkouts and old school people. They do employ plenty of real life cashiers to scan your groceries, so the lines are rarely very long. And they even still have baggers, who take your groceries out to your car for you. They also have about half a dozen self checkouts, largely to replace the express checkout. So even the express line folks don't get all that inconvenienced by somebody cheating with a cart full of 50 things. Of course, you pay for it. Their prices aren't horrible, but they're definitely higher than Walmart or Aldi. As far as a few other answers I've seen about taking away low skill jobs, meh. The recent trend of online shopping seems to have taken care of that, with employees running around to fill all those online orders. My daughter did that for a bit at the aforementioned Market Street, and I see plenty of folks with that job at my local Walmart. So, until robots take over that, those jobs offset the loss of cashiers. So as long as it's done right, and considering that stores were skimping on cashiers even before self-checkouts were a thing, I've found self-checkouts to make shopping more convenient.

Question: Atheists, if a 10-year-old child asks you why you don't believe in God, do you feel guilty for crushing their innocent beliefs?
Answer: I have to admit, this has always seemed like a weird concept to me. It's not just religion. You see it in other types of children's stories, like Santa Claus, fairies, magic, etc. It's this idea that, not just are we supposed to indulge children in believing obvious nonsense that we as adults know isn't true, but that we're actually supposed to encourage it, because, well, I'm not entirely sure why. It never seems to be explained other than holding belief in itself as a virtue (some might say gullibility). I think a lot of adults don't give kids enough credit. By somewhere around 3 to 5 years old, children are able to distinguish reality from fantasy (Young Children Learn to Distinguish Between Fact and Fiction, Research at University of Texas at Austin Finds). That doesn't mean their imagination withers away after they turn 5, or that they quit playing make believe. They're just mature enough to know, for example, that all the ghost and goblin stories around Halloween are just fun stories we tell to scare ourselves a bit, not real things that we need to fear in real life. So, while I was still a recent 'convert' to atheism when my own daughter was young, so that I still thought of religion as a bit of a taboo subject, and I did give in a bit to societal pressure on Santa Claus and the Easter Bunny, I didn't shy away from telling her the truth about other mythical ideas like fairies or the Loch Ness monster*. (Of course, like dad's everywhere, I did take a few cues from the dad in Calvin and Hobbes, leading her on with obvious nonsense from time to time just to keep her on her toes.) It didn't stunt her imagination, because we still invented plenty of games where we had to create entire worlds that didn't actually exist inside our living room or back yard. And it's not like the real world is boring. Try teaching a seven year old about deep time and evolution, or the vastness of the universe, the sheer power of supernovae, or the incomprehensibility of quantum mechanics. Obviously, I wasn't giving my daughter super deep lessons in any of those things. But when she went through her stage of asking why, why, why, I always tried to give her as accurate of an answer as I could, tailored to something she could understand at her age. And sometimes, the answer ended with an "I don't know," which left it open as a mystery and something that she might be able to figure out. And of course, there were practical lessons, too, from the typical kitchen science experiments, to the time we dissected a squirrel that the cat had killed (my wife wasn’t exactly thrilled about that one, but since she’s a nurse and had studied anatomy, we still called her out to the back yard to help us identify everything we were seeing). It gets a bit touchy when it's somebody else's kid and not your own – not so much because I'm worried about the kid, but because I'm worried about respecting the parents and not interfering in how they're raising their own children. Even if I don't agree with them on that particular subject, it's still a touchy thing to undermine parents. But overall, I don't understand this idea that we should actively encourage children to literally believe in things that we adults know aren't true. Past around 5 years old, kids are perfectly capable of separating fact from fiction, and realizing that the worlds they create in their imaginations are fantasy, not reality. But that doesn't stop them from creating those fantasy worlds. If anything, the scenario proposed in this question is an indictment on the kid's parents, for letting the kid believe in a fantasy to such a late age. By 10 years old, kids should already have a decent idea of what's real and what's pretend, so there shouldn't be any possibility of 'crushing' their beliefs. *If I had it to do over again, I wouldn't have pussy-footed around religion. And I would have treated Santa like Halloween – a game of make believe that we'd all participate in, not something to lie to her about or mislead her.

Question: Why did some monkeys stop evolving when other monkeys evolved to be humans?
Answer: The general trend of evolution is diversification. You start off with one ancestor species. It somehow splits into two populations, who go their own ways and develop into two different species. Those two new species split themselves, becoming more species. For the lineages that survive and don't go extinct, this splitting just goes on and on and on. You can see this in something like the dinosaur family tree. I never hear anybody ask why other dinosaurs didn't all evolve to become triceratops. It actually seems odd to even write it out. People just seem to assume that it's perfectly natural that there are lots and lots of different types of dinosaurs. But for some reason, when it comes to monkeys and apes, some people don't expect this same type of diversity. ABOVE SOURCE: Rates of Dinosaur Body Mass Evolution Indicate 170 Million Years of Sustained Ecological Innovation on the Avian Stem Lineage If you want to get more technical about it, it comes down to niche partitioning. Different organisms specialize in different diets and ecological niches. In the diagram below, you can see how different antelope species all specialize in slightly different niches, leading to the diversity among those species. It wouldn't do any good, for example, for a reedbuck to 'try' to evolve to become more like a nyala. The reedbuck already has a niche where it survives and that it's well adapted to, while the nyala are already well adapted to their niche. Any reedbuck that tried to push into the Nyala's niche wouldn't be able to compete. ABOVE: Niche partitioning slide from a good presentation - follow the link below to watch the whole thing SOURCE: Niche Partitioning It's the same way with monkeys and apes. If you go far enough back, there is a single common ancestor that we all evolved from. But evolution followed the same pattern in primates as in any other group – splitting and diversifying to take advantage of various different ecological niches. ABOVE: Primate family tree SOURCE: Nelson, Gilbert, Wong, Miller, Price (2012) Every monkey and ape still alive is just as evolved as any other. We just took different evolutionary paths to take advantage of different niches.

Question: Did you hate Trump before he decided to become president?
Answer: As someone who grew up in the '80s and '90s, I tried to think of an analogy for Trump's early fame to help put it in perspective for younger folks who only knew about Trump after he began his political career. Think of somewhere in between the Kardashians or Paris Hilton and Elon Musk or Jeff Bezos. He had the reputation of a rich playboy, largely famous for being famous. He was a perennial feature of the tabloids for his gaudy lifestyle and scandalous relationships, especially his affair with Marla Maples. He was famous enough to make a cameo in Home Alone, for example, but he wasn't exactly well thought of or respected by the majority of the public. My own hometown had a prestigious private boarding school, The Hill School, and the fact the Donald Trump Jr. went there was enough that people talked about it, but not something we were exactly proud of. And when Trump first ran for president way back in the year 2000, everybody just chalked it up to a guy who loved the limelight trying to get more public attention, but nobody really took it seriously. Think about when Kanye West announced that he was going to run for president. ABOVE: This photo kind of encapsulates the smarmy, gaudy reputation of Trump from that era SOURCE: Donald Trump’s Lavish Homes Are Gaudy Behemoths Then in the early 2000s, he got cast for a reality TV show, the Apprentice. He even had a catch phrase. And while reality TV certainly generates ratings, it's definitely not the kind of thing that earns respect. He was in the same category as Flavor Flav, an aging celebrity reduced to a caricature trying to stay in the public eye through a low budget TV show. ABOVE: Trump being reduced to a meme SOURCE: https://www.trump.com/lifestyle/the-apprentice * Unfortunately, this was also around the time that Trump began his birtherism campaign against Obama. Most people I know recognized it for the nonsense it was, but it found a receptive audience among the political right, pushing Trump from a harmless attention whore to a bit more dangerous to the nation. He hadn't graduated to deserving hate, just yet, but he was on the way there. And then, of course, he ran for President in 2016. Once he secured the Republican nomination, I thought a Democratic presidency was a sure thing. Obviously, nobody would vote for a washed up, former playboy, reality TV show host. And with the extra scrutiny his political aspirations brought, a lot of us who'd only vaguely paid attention to Trump's tabloid appearances in the past learned just how unscrupulous, unethical, and corrupt he truly was. It's not that people who paid attention didn't already know all this. It's just that most of us didn't actually pay that much attention to Trump. So no, outside the folks who had business dealings with him, or perhaps the folks in New York and Atlantic City who had to deal with all his shenanigans, I didn't know many people who actually hated Trump prior to his campaign for the presidency. He simply didn't occupy enough mental real estate to merit that level of emotion. But yeah, once he did run for president, and especially after he won and sowed so much division and brought so much shame on our country, I think it's safe to say that he earned a much stronger emotional reaction. *Wow – that Apprentice image is from Trump's own website. I'm surprised he'd allow something that shows him in that light. Then again, he made an appearance on professional wrestling, so ‘shame’ may not be in his vocabulary.

Question: Why is there a theory to evolution?
Answer: Because that’s how science works. Theories are the high level frameworks we use to study things. In my own field of aerospace engineering, for example, let’s say I wanted to analyze a propeller. For a back of the envelope type analysis, I could use momentum theory. If I want to dig a little deeper, I could use blade element theory. If I want to go even further, I could use computational fluid dynamics. So, I’ve got at least three different theories I can use to analyze the same thing (with many different levels of implementation even within each of those theories). Evolution’s the same way. We know it happens, but there are different ways of looking at it and different theories you can use to study it. The over-arching high level theory is the modern synthesis or the extended synthesis, but there are sub-parts to that, many of which could be considered theories in their own right: ABOVE SOURCE: Epigenetic opportunities for Evolutionary Computation And off the top of my head, even that figure is leaving out lower level concepts like genetic drift, neutral theory, Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, etc. Basically, there are theories to evolution, because evolution is science, and science uses theories.

Question: What is the science behind a ouija board? Has anyone ever had an experience that made them question reality?
Answer: Ouija boards rely on a phenomenon know as the ideomotor effect. Here's how it's described in the article, What's The Spooky Science Behind The Ouija Board?: Basically, the ideomotor effect is subconscious, involuntary movement; scientists first documented it in 1852. "You often accidentally move a little bit if you think about a movement," says Marc Andersen, an assistant professor at the Interacting Minds Centre at Denmark's Aarhus University. "If you think about kissing your partner, for instance, you're inclined to just lean a little bit forward without really thinking about it." The same force is at work with Ouija boards: Participants think about the planchette moving, so they subconsciously move it themselves. But the movement of the planchette is only part of the Ouija board's mystery. What about the message? Our subconscious minds are responsible for those too. "Once it starts to spell something, inevitably, you're trying to guess, even if you're not doing it consciously," says [Chris] French. "If you ask, 'What's your name?' and it goes to the letter p, and then e, you're automatically thinking 'Peter.' Probably everybody else around the board is also thinking 'Peter.' And that's what is likely to be then spelt out." There have been multiple studies on people using Ouija boards, and probably unsurprisingly, it comes down to the vision of the people using the planchette. In one study by Dr. Andersen (from the quote above), participants wore goggles to track their eye movements. In a control case, when asked to spell out BALTIMORE, the participants all looked at each of the letters before moving the planchette there. If you only had the eye tracking data, you could have easily predicted that they were spelling BALTIMORE. When they went to open ended questions more typical of Ouija board use, at least one person in the group looked at each letter of the word that was eventually spelled out. In fact, what mostly happened was that one person would subconsciously 'select' the first letter. Then, per the quote above about how people would start to guess the final word, more and more people in the group would also start looking at the subsequent letters as the word was spelled out. The researchers found that they were still able to predict the word that was spelled out just by looking at the eye tracking data. Somewhat related experiments have looked at blindfolded participants. As you might have guessed, when the participants couldn't see the board, the resulting answers were far less informative. Here's a short video of an informal demonstration along these lines: I used a Ouija board once many years ago with one of my best friends growing up. And I can attest to the fact that it does feel very convincing, with the planchette moving about without any conscious control. But just because it's not under conscious control doesn't mean it's anything supernatural. It's our subconscious minds that drive the motion.

Question: Do you believe that atheism will become the dominant belief system in America during our lifetime? If so, how long do you think it will take for this to occur?
Answer: Almost certainly not. In recent years, the term ‘nones’ was coined to describe the group containing atheists, agnostics, and people who describe their religion as “nothing in particular.” The ‘nones’ as a whole have been increasing, and are projected to approach the majority by 2070 if current trends continue, perhaps even becoming the majority by one scenario: ABOVE SOURCE: Pew Research Center - Modeling the Future of Religion in America [pdf] However, atheists are only a portion of this group. This next table doesn’t include the projection, but it does show the trend over the past 14 years: ABOVE SOURCE: About Three-in-Ten U.S. Adults Are Now Religiously Unaffiliated In 2021, atheists were only around 4% of the total population. If you lump agnostics and atheists together as non-believers, it’s still only around 9%. If atheists and agnostics made up the same proportion of ‘nones’ in 2070 as they do now, then even under the most optimistic scenario, atheists would only be around 7% of the population in 2070, while atheists and agnostics combined would only be around 16% of the population. That’s far from being a dominant belief system.

Question: If Adam and Eve were indeed the 1st humans on Earth, theoretically, what’s the fastest they could populate the Earth to today's level?
Answer: Theoretically in what sense? If you account for enough factors, then certainly no faster than we actually achieved our current population, and probably quite a bit slower. Basically, if you use realistic assumptions for fertility rates and mortality rates for various eras based on the conditions and medical knowledge of the times, then starting with the same initial conditions, your theoretical population growth will match the actual historical population growth. But those initial conditions are where the differences come in between reality and Biblical literalists. Here's an estimate of the global population going back several thousand years: ABOVE SOURCE: Global population 10,000BCE-2100 | Statista Per Biblical literalists, Adam and Eve would have been alive around 4000 BC. The estimates I've seen for the actual population back then range from around 7 million to 50 million. So, to get to our current population in 6000 years with realistic assumptions on fertility and mortality rates, you need a starting population in the millions. Adam and Eve were only two people. That's, well, a magnitude of around a million times less than reality. Now maybe mortality rates wouldn't be quite as bad with less people. Maybe pandemics wouldn't be as common with lower population densities. Maybe there would have been fewer famines with different environments not being pushed to their carrying capacities. Maybe there would have been less wars because of reduced conflicts over resources. So just maybe, an initial population of two people (with no genetic defects) could grow faster on a percentage basis than a population of several million and eventually catch up to the historical reality. But there's no way they could get there faster. And once the Adam and Eve hypothetical line does catch up to reality, then they'd have all the same limits on growth and causes of mortality as real historical populations. If by 'theoretical', you're ignoring realistic mortality rates, and wondering how quickly a population could grow if unconstrained by such considerations, well, that would be exponential growth, so the answer is pretty quick. For a rough calculation, if you assume that each couple has 4 surviving children that go on to have children of their own, and that generation times average 20 years, then population would double every 20 years. So, population can be calculated as 2^n, where n is the number of generations. It would take 22 generations to reach 8.6 billion people, or 440 years. But that's really more 'hypothetical' than 'theoretical', since the calculation is based on poor assumptions. So 'theoretically', as long as you're using good assumptions in your theory, if you start from a population of just 2 people 6 thousand years ago, then the population in that scenario would certainly lag the real world population for at least some period of time. Most likely, this lag would mean that it would take longer to get to our current population. But even if a reduced population allowed for reduced mortality rates, once the hypothetical population did catch up to reality, then mortality rates would be the same, and population growth would play out the same way as reality from then on out.

Question: Why do most Americans prefer processed food and artificial over fresh and natural food?
Answer: Because ‘processing’ isn’t the boogey man you think it is. Processed foods are delicious. And in many cases, the processing actually makes the foods safer and more nutritious. ABOVE SOURCE: The Truth About Eating Processed Foods — The Bodybuilding Dietitians Let me give an example. I like milk and dairy products. Only one time in my life have I I tried unprocessed milk, right after milking it from the cow. It was even still warm. But most of the time, I buy my milk from the grocery store, so I want it pasteurized to make sure it's safe from pathogens. I also like cheese and butter, which are both also processed foods (they're no longer simply raw milk). And for a lot of folks, the processing to make cheese or yogurt can reduce the lactose for people who have issues with that. Same thing with bread. I could eat bread all day. Raw, unprocessed wheat? Not so much. The grinding and cooking even make the nutrients easier to digest. And meat? Now, don't get me wrong. There's nothing wrong with a steak that's only minimally processed (butchering, seasoning, and cooking). But sausages, ham, and bacon? Oh man. A world without bacon would be a sad world indeed. And maybe you think I'm being a smartass, but I'm not. I'm going to guess that you weren't considering bread to be a processed food, but it is. Some foods may be processed more than others, but it's hard to draw any clear dividing line between what's too processed and what isn't. I mean, how does extra chopping or mixing magically make foods unhealthy? I've got the same pet peeves over 'artificial' ingredients. We don't have Star Trek replicators that can create molecules from scratch from energy. Everything we put into our food came from nature at some point. Where do you draw the line between natural and artificial ingredients? And even if you do have some threshold of chemistry that you'll use to designate 'artificial' ingredients, what does that have to do with health or safety? (As an example from medicine, we synthesize acetylsalicylic acid for aspirin, because it actually has less side effects than the naturally occurring salicylic acid found in willow bark that inspired the medicine.) And don't get me started on the silly saying that if you can't pronounce an ingredient, don't eat it. Have you ever seen all the chemical constituents of an egg? Practically all food is a complex mix of lots and lots of hard to pronounce chemicals. Most of those chemicals are safe. Some aren't. But whether or not they're safe has no correlation to how easy they are to pronounce. ABOVE SOURCE: Ingredients of an All-Natural Egg So yeah. I like sausage and bread and ham and pasteurized milk and all types of other processed foods I can buy from the grocery store. I eat processed food because I'm not a wild animal. While I was looking for images for processed foods, I came across many figures where people try to add an extra category, of ‘ultra processed’. Here’s one that was especially silly: ABOVE SOURCE: ABOVE SOURCE: MailOnline's guide to tell ultra-processed food apart They called French fries ultra processed. Sliced potatoes fried in oil. I’m not sure how much less processing you can do to a cooked food. And they’ve got ice cream on there. My family had a hand cranked ice cream maker when I was growing up, and we used it quite a bit for extended family get togethers. It’s just milk, cream, sugar, and a little vanilla, mixed up in a container surrounded by ice and rock salt. What’s ‘ultra processed’ about that? Now, I’m not saying an excess of fries and ice cream would make a healthy diet, but it’s got nothing to do with the amount of processing that went into making them.

Question: Where does the concept of the Earth being six thousand years old come from? Is it from the Bible?
Answer: It really does come from the Bible, if a bit indirectly. There are several passages in the Bible that give information on such things as how old people were when they had children or how long certain periods lasted, that if accepted at face value, can give a very close approximation of when Adam and Eve were created (according to the stories, at least). There are a few places where things get somewhat murky, but not enough to change things by more than a few decades* – nothing on the order of millions or billions of years. This was a fairly well accepted interpretation for generations, and many scholars made their own estimates of when creation would have taken place, including Johannes Kepler. Arguably the most respected of these was the estimate done by James Ussher, who put much effort into sorting out the murky periods. It's because Ussher's chronology was so well respected that it was included in the introductory material to several printed Bibles, including the famed Scofield Bible. Wikipedia gives a good summary of how Ussher made his estimate (Ussher chronology - Wikipedia). He broke it down into three periods: Using other sources outside the Bible, Ussher determined the enthronement of the Babylonian king Amel-Marduk to have occurred in 562 BC, which was tied in to the end of the Babylonian Captivity through 2 Kings 25:27. From there, it was just a matter of going backwards by all the years previously calculated, putting creation at 4004 BC. Creation to Exodus You can easily look up Genesis 5 and Genesis 11 for yourself, but to give an idea, here's the start of Genesis 5: This is the list of the descendants of Adam. When God created humans,[a] he made them[b] in the likeness of God. 2 Male and female he created them, and he blessed them and called them humans[c] when they were created. 3 When Adam had lived one hundred thirty years, he became the father of a son in his likeness, according to his image, and named him Seth. 4 The days of Adam after he became the father of Seth were eight hundred years, and he had other sons and daughters. 5 Thus all the days that Adam lived were nine hundred thirty years, and he died. 6 When Seth had lived one hundred five years, he became the father of Enosh. 7 Seth lived after the birth of Enosh eight hundred seven years and had other sons and daughters. 8 Thus all the days of Seth were nine hundred twelve years, and he died. It goes on and on like that. So, as long as you accept these statements as true, it's mostly a simple matter of adding up how old each man was when he begat his heir. The only real hiccups are between Noah and Shem, and between Nahor and Terah. Both of these are somewhat ambiguous. In the former, the passage states, "After Noah was five hundred years old, Noah became the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth." In the latter, the passage is, "When Terah had lived seventy years, he became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran." People who care about this issue more than I do have gone into detail to try to pinpoint those ages (e.g. Contradictions: Noah’s Three Sons). You also need to know how old Abraham was when the Exodus occurred. His age at the start of all those events comes from Genesis 12:4, "So Abram went, as the Lord had told him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran." I ran the math myself with a spreadsheet, and came up with 2049 years from the creation of Adam to the birth of Abraham, plus another 75 years until the Exodus, for 2124 years total (a bit different from Ussher because I didn't put in the effort to figure out the ambiguity around Noah/Shem and Nahor/Terah). I suppose there's one other hiccup, depending on which particular version of the Bible you're using. Since we don't have an 'original' version of Genesis, we have to rely on copies of that version, most notably the Masoretic text and the Septuagint (though those aren't the only two). And those copies differ on certain details, including all those ages in Genesis 5 and Genesis 11. Exodus to Solomon's Temple Like I said, this one comes straight from a single verse, 1 Kings 6:1: In the four hundred eightieth year after the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv, which is the second month, he began to build the house of the Lord. Solomon's Temple to the Babylonian Captivity This is the period where things purportedly get a bit more complicated. I haven't gone through this period in detail, yet, myself, but to give just one example, you have this verse from 2 Kings 3:1: In the eighteenth year of King Jehoshaphat of Judah, Jehoram son of Ahab became king over Israel in Samaria; he reigned twelve years. Go through finding all those verses and work out the years, and you come up a little over 4 centuries of history. In a somewhat independent path, other books in the Bible also give more genealogies, such that you can trace each and every claimed descendant from Adam all the way to Jesus. Granted, there aren't ages associated with all of those genealogies, but these also give a ballpark range in the thousands of years. So, if you accept the claims of the Bible at more or less face value, and assume all those genealogies represent real people and not just imaginary people made up out of thin air, and that all the events in Egypt, Israel, and Judah all really happened, you'll end up at an estimate for the date of creation somewhere around 4000 BC. As a side note, while it seems to be somewhat fashionable to dismiss exercises like these because some parts of the Bible were ‘obviously’ meant to be taken more metaphorically or allegorically, I don’t see such figurative interpretations as obvious at all. The crux of this argument would be the genealogies in Genesis 5 and Genesis 11 – after that, you’re already into Egyptian pharaohs, so nothing that’s going to be a major difference from real history (at least as far as timelines). But these genealogies aren’t fables with moral lessons or some type of simplified explanation of complex concepts for a pre-scientific society. They’re boring, dry lists of ancestry. It’s about as close to a conventional history section as you’ll find in Genesis – the part least likely to be metaphorical or allegorical (though there’s certainly a reason to ‘invent’ such lists to provide legitimacy for the rulers of Israel and Judah). *As I already touched upon, that difference of only a few decades is using a specific version of the Bible, such as the Masoretic text or the Septuagint. The differences between those different versions can add up to a couple millennia, though still not anywhere near on the magnitude of real history.

Question: How do you feel about the resurgence of vinyl records?
Answer: The nostalgic nerd in me really likes it. Don't get me wrong, the music quality is worse than digital formats, but that's not the only reason we own things. I have a couple movie projectors that I found at garage sales, along with old adding machines that can’t hold a candle to my graphing calculator, let alone Excel. I don’t use the movie projectors to watch any types of new movies, and I certainly don’t use the adding machines in my day job as an engineer, but they’re still interesting curiosities. I see record players and vinyl records the same way – a reminder of an older, more physical method of audio recording. It’s worth having a turntable and a handful of records for that reason. My parents actually own a hand-cranked Victrola, which takes it up even another level (you control the volume with doors on the resonance chamber). And to top it off, it’s then just fun to be able to play new music on this old technology, kind of like if somebody actually did release Marvel movies on 8 mm, or turning a video into a flip book. ABOVE SOURCE: How to Make a Flipbook Animation Machine From Cardboard Listening to vinyl is kind of like that. I'm not going to watch an entire episode of the Simpsons as a flipbook, but that flipbook machine is still pretty cool. Likewise, I'm still going to listen to most music in some digital format, but record players are fun to use on occasion. Heh. I just found this while writing this answer. Question: Do evolutionary biologists typically hold atheistic beliefs due to their understanding of human evolution?
Answer: To a degree, yes. It's hard to find recent polling data on precisely this question, but there is enough related data to give a good impression. First, here's a poll on scientists’ belief in a higher power. It's from 2009, which is 15 years ago, and quite a decent time considering how quickly U.S. religious demographics have changed over the past two decades. It also just looks at scientists as a group, rather than looking at biologists in particular. However, it's still informative: ABOVE SOURCE: Scientists and Belief As you can see, only 33% of scientists believed in the capital G God, while another 18% believed in a more vague "universal spirit or higher power". On the other end, 41% didn't believe in either – a much, much higher percentage than the general public. The survey doesn't get into distinctions between atheists, agnostics, or other terms, but for the sake of this question, we'll count those 41% as some level of "atheistic beliefs". While I admittedly didn't do exhaustive searching for this, the polls I did find that broke down the responses by type of scientist were more limited to elite scientific societies such as the National Academy of Sciences or the Royal Society, rather than all practicing scientists. A correspondence to Nature from 1998, Leading scientists still reject God, polled the National Academy of Sciences and had this to say: Biological scientists had the lowest rate of belief (5.5% in God, 7.1% in immortality), with physicists and astronomers slightly higher (7.5% in God, 7.5% in immortality). The correspondence had a related figure, though unfortunately not breaking it down by field of study: ABOVE SOURCE: Table 1 Comparison of survey answers among “greater” scientists Another study, Eminent scientists reject the supernatural, surveyed the Royal Society, with similar findings, and I'll throw in results about 'consciousness surviving' as a bonus (note that the y-axis is number of respondents, not percentages): ABOVE SOURCE: Eminent scientists reject the supernatural: a survey of the Fellows of the Royal Society - Evolution: Education and Outreach Finally, let me just highlight the general shift of religious beliefs among the U.S. public over the past two decades: ABOVE SOURCE: In U.S., roughly three-in-ten adults now religiously unaffiliated Keep in mind that 'No religion' doesn't necessarily mean atheist. There are plenty of folks who are 'spiritual but not religious' who fall into that category, such that actual self-professed atheists and agnostics are only a fraction of that group. But it's still a pretty clear trend of Americans shedding faith in traditional religions. So, putting all that together, I think we can confidently say that disbelief in God or a higher power is much more prevalent among scientists than the general public, and becomes even more pronounced as you move up the ranks to more elite scientists. Also, I think we can say that biologists are even more likely to be non-believers than those in the physical sciences. As to the specific question asked here, whether "biologists typically hold atheistic beliefs", if I had to guess, I'd say probably. It was already pretty close back in 2009, and I'd guess that given the overall shift since then, that by now, the majority of biologists probably hold “atheistic beliefs”. Though whether they'd self-identify as atheists, agnostics, or something else is a bit of a different question.
