Question: Why does my keyboard have a caps lock key? It must have some purpose, right?
Answer: This is a good question. Is there really a need for a caps lock key on modern keyboards? How many times do most people use it intentionally, vs. eNDING UP WITH SENTENCES UNINTENTIONALLY WRITTEN IN ALL CAPS? The obvious function is that it lets you write in all caps, LIKE THIS, without having to hold down the shift key. This stems from old, mechanical typewriters, where the shift key actually did mechanically shift the typing mechanism to switch between lower case and upper case letters, which required a decent amount of force on the key. So, for prolonged all caps typing, a shift-lock locked the mechanism in the shifted position, easing the load on your pinky fingers. But shift-lock shifted all the keys, including the symbols on numbers, so a slightly later innovation was caps-lock that only shifted the letters, not the entire keyboard. Once electric typewriters, word processors, and early computers came around, the effort to hold down shift wasn’t nearly so hard, but it was still nice to have a caps-lock key. Remember that typewriters and early printers (like Daisy wheels) still didn’t allow for much formatting or different font sizes, so all-caps was still a convenient way to distinguish things like titles and headings. But on modern day computers? Just about any serious project that needs to be in all-caps can be handled by software, and in many cases, it’s even preferable to do it that way. For example, for headings in a paper, you should type them out in normal mixed case, e.g. Heading Example. Then, if you want it in all caps, just change the heading style to all caps, and the word processing software will take care of it for you. But if you decide later to switch back to mixed case, it’s just a quick change of the style rather than re-typing everything. In my own field, technical drawings use all caps as the standard for drawing annotations, but this can also be handled through software settings instead of using caps-lock (e.g. Displaying Annotation Notes in Uppercase). Even typing here on Quora, there are already a basic text formatting options. Adding an all-caps to that would be simple. There may be some niche applications, like programming, where caps-lock still has a bit of use, but I imagine a lot of that’s driven by complacency. Remove the caps-lock key from the keyboard, and programming software would pretty quickly include software features*. The more I think about it, the more I’d like to see the caps-lock key done away with, to free up that space on the keyboard for something more useful. Maybe replace it with a keyboard shortcut to enable all caps (like alt-shift-c), or at least relegate it to a far corner of the keyboard where you’re less likely to hit it by accident. Here’s something related I found doing a bit of googling: *I’m only a novice programmer, with most of my experience in Visual Basic (which just earned me several snorts of derision from the real programmers). But even back in VB 6, I only worried about capitalization when I declared my variables. After that, I typed them in all lower case, and VB would automatically convert them to the capitalization from when they were declared. Not only did it save me the effort of pressing the shift key, it was a nice, quick double check that I typed in the correct variable name (if it didn’t update capitalization, I’d made a typo).

Question: Do pro-choice people at least think we should reduce the number of abortions?
Answer: That's a weird question. It's about like asking if we should reduce the number of bypass surgeries for clogged arteries. On the one hand, as the old saying goes, an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. It would be great if we could get people to live healthier lifestyles to avoid clogged arteries and the need for bypass surgeries in the first place. But as long as people do have clogged arteries, I very much want bypass surgery to be available. I don't want to reduce the number of bypass surgeries if the need still remains. And it still remains a fact of life that clogged arteries will happen regardless, so some amount of bypass surgeries will always be necessary. It's similar for abortion. It would be great if everybody had comprehensive sex education and easily available contraception and birth control to reduce the number of accidental pregnancies. And it would be great to have generally good living conditions for all families, easily affordable and accesible prenatal care, or at least adequate social safety nets, so that nobody was worried about having the means to raise a child with a good quality of life and opportunities. And it would be really great if there were no more rapes, developmental abnormalities, or other complications with pregnancies. So of course it would be nice to reduce all the reasons for abortions in the first place. But I don't want to reduce access to abortions while the need remains. And it's still a fact of life that some amount of abortions will always be necessary, because we never will fully eliminate all those reasons. So yes, like with any other healthcare issue, it would be best to reduce the causes that lead to needing medical intervention. But as long as the need's still there, you still provide the healthcare. And it's just a weird way to phrase a question, asking if we want to reduce a specific medical procedure, rather than addressing the causes that lead to that procedure.

Question: Why do people go to so-called fancy restaurants that serve small average portions with insanely high prices?
Answer: My wife and I have done this a handful of times for special occasions, and we really enjoyed it. My guess is you're probably thinking of dishes like these, where everything is put on the plate with an eye to detail and presentation, but the portion sizes are pretty small: ABOVE SOURCE: Sidart Introduce New Set Menu - Restaurant & Café And you may also be thinking that that's just a publicity photo of dishes at that restaurant, and that you'd only get to pick one of those plates for your meal. But these dishes are usually part of a 'tasting menu' or 'set menu', which works a bit differently than the normal restaurant routine. If you ordered the set menu at that particular restaurant that made the food in the above photo (Sidart), you'd get all of those dishes brought out to you in succession. In this case, that's 6 food courses plus a drink (probably as a palate cleanser somewhere in there), but I've heard of tasting menus with over a dozen courses. Add on your wine, and it's a decently filling meal. Sometimes they'll even offer a glass of a different wine with each course to complement each particular dish. You may not be stuffed the same way you would be after an all you can eat buffet, but it's enough food to be satisfying. And man oh man does the food taste good (at least the ones we've tried). The restaurant is really focused on attention to detail, and packing as much flavor as they can into those small portions. Think about Thanksgiving dinner, and how there are so many different dishes that you can only take a little bit of each thing – just enough to get a taste. But now, imagine that with actual chefs, preparing dishes far more involved than cheesy potato casserole, bringing each dish out to you one at a time so that each course is still freshly prepared when you take your first bite (and not having to do any of the cooking or cleaning up afterwards). On top of all that, it's an experience. The portions may be small, but going through that many individual courses still takes time. This isn't your typical hour-ish restaurant meal. Depending on exactly how many courses you're getting, expect somewhere in the 2 to 3 hour range, relaxing and enjoying the company of whoever you're with. But realize that this means the restaurant only gets your party at that table for those 2 to 3 hours, not the 2 to 3 parties they could have gotten with a more typical meal, which is part of the reason the prices are higher. It's not an everyday thing, or even a once a month thing (unless you're a lot better off than we are). But for a rare treat for a special occasion, these types of meals are very nice. Question: What do you think about TV Land's warnings for 1960-70s episodes of "Bonanza" and "Gunsmoke" that say "this program contains outdated cultural depictions. Viewer discretion is advised." Do you think this is necessary?
Answer: First off, this question hits one of my pet peeves – using the word 'necessary' without any context, implying that 'necessary' is some intrinsic property all on its own. It isn't. Just about every time this word is used, it's in relation to a specific outcome. For example, are fermentable sugar and yeast necessary ingredients? Yes if you're making beer or bread. Not so much if you're grilling a steak. Considering that TV itself isn't a necessity, hardly anything around the medium is necessary in any universal sense. It all depends on what outcomes you want. So, if you're asking if these disclaimers are necessary – necessary for what? If you wanted to be cynical, you could say that the purpose of these disclaimers is merely a way to silence the busybodies with a token message that only lasts a few seconds, that most viewers will forget about almost as soon as the action starts. The network can still show controversial or 'problematic' content essentially unaltered, retaining most of the audience that enjoys those shows (and their associated advertising dollars). The networks have balanced the conflicting influences of alienating more politically correct viewers to losing more old fashioned viewers, and figured these disclaimers were the best compromise. It's the free market at work. If you want to be more charitable about their motivations, such disclaimers do play at least a small part in consciousness raising. It may only be a short message, but at least it's putting it in people's heads that these depictions may not be so benign. And so when they do watch these shows, they're not just uncritically accepting such depictions as right or normal. I think this is especially true when it comes to kids watching TV. I know, some folks like to say that parents should be aware of all the media their children are consuming. That's a bit unrealistic, not to mention a bit questionable advice in its own right. Such constant supervision has taken on its own derogatory term these days – helicopter parenting. On the other extreme, you have folks fondly remembering the 'good old days', when kids roamed their neighborhoods unsupervised for hours on end (and believe me, even back then, we found parents' stashes of 'questionable' media hidden in boxes in the attic). Ideal parenting is somewhere in between – a balance of oversight and child independence, where parents have a general idea of what their kids are up to, but not necessarily screening each and every TV show their kids are going to watch. And in this context, such disclaimers are important in the consciousness raising of children, who don't have the background and experience to fully understand such shows like adults. So yes. I think these disclaimers serve a purpose. They help in the consciousness raising of both nostalgic older viewers and younger first time viewers. And considering that it's such a short message and that the shows themselves are unaltered, it seems that it's only the most easily offended who get worked up about these disclaimers, anyway.

Question: Is it possible to be both an atheist and a believer simultaneously? Have you ever met someone who identifies as both an atheist and a believer?
Answer: Going strictly by the definitions of the words, no. An atheist, by definition, is someone who lacks a belief in deities. So you can't logically be both an atheist and a believer in deities. However, people aren't always logical, nor do they always use words by their dictionary definitions. I've met one person in real life (and only one) who called themself an atheist, yet went on to describe how evil God was for allowing so much suffering in the world – and not in the way that someone like me treats God as a hypothetical or fictional character in a story, but actually stating it all as reality. While people like that are rare, they're not completely unheard of. Here are the results of a poll on atheists' beliefs in evolution: SOURCE: Religious Landscape Study Probably unsurprisingly, the vast majority of atheists accept evolution due to natural processes. But 2% of self-proclaimed atheists thought that evolution was due to God's design. So, while I don't want to pull a No True Scotsman, that guy and other folks like him aren't really atheists per the definition of the word, even if they do describe themselves as such. But, at least as far as self-identification, you can find people who call themselves atheists yet are nevertheless believers.

Question: Have you ever met an intelligent creationist?
Answer: I've met intelligent creationists, but never any creationists in person who actually understood evolution. Every time I talked to an intelligent creationist about how they thought evolution worked, I invariably found that they didn't actually understand. Their views tend to be a mish-mash of Lamarckism, teleological thinking, evolution being progression towards a goal, and human exceptionalism, along with a lack of knowledge of how evolution works, and even a lack of knowledge of modern day organisms. These types of misconceptions drive such questions as wondering why there are still monkeys if we evolved from monkeys (though it's never why there are still birds if penguins evolved from birds), or wondering whether the first fish to crawl onto land would have had either gills or lungs (totally ignoring all the existing fish that have both). You can browse through the Index to Creationist Claims to get an idea of the types of arguments creationists might use. I don't wholly blame these folks, either. They were raised in an environment where creationism was the default, from their parents to their preachers, to possibly even their school teachers (my daughter's high school biology teacher made an announcement at the start of the lesson on evolution that, as a Christian, she didn't believe in it, herself, but it was just part of the curriculum that they had to get through). They were taught all these misleading creationist arguments from people they trusted from a very young age. So the smartest kids were actually the best at absorbing those lessons. And since it takes a while for people to fully develop critical thinking skills, and a fair amount of discipline to go back and apply that to things you think you already know, it's hardly a surprise that those bright kids brought up within a creationist environment carried that belief into their adulthood. (And to be fair, ask yourself how you know that matter is composed of atoms and that atoms are composed of even smaller particles – do you really understand the evidence, or is it just common knowledge that you were taught back when you were younger?) I will say, though, that the number of intelligent, well-educated creationists I've met is rather small. You can definitely see a correlation vs. education level (note that graph is a bit old from 2005): SOURCE: Americans Weigh In on Evolution vs. Creationism in Schools So yes, I've met otherwise intelligent folks who were also creationists. But once you talk with them, it almost invariably turns out that, for whatever reason, they don't actually understand evolution. I have yet to meet a single person in real life who could accurately explain evolution yet still rejected it.

Question: If the urge to reproduce in humans is set biologically, how come that many people don't want to have kids?
Answer: Because evolution is a mindless process with random mutation as the raw material for natural selection, it only gives the illusion of design. You don't necessarily end up with traits or features the same way you would as from thoughtful, intentional design. Traits and instincts don't necessarily need to match up directly with the corresponding selection pressure as long as they still end up there eventually. In the context of this question, it means evolution doesn't necessarily instill animals with an instinct to want to reproduce*. Instead, instilling an instinctual desire for sex is good enough, since having sex is what does eventually lead to reproduction. But when you get a species smart enough to put two and two together, and who realizes that birth control can break this causal chain, then you can understand why the instinctual desire for sex is only a proxy for reproduction. That instinct that served evolution's 'purpose'** for so many millions of years of our prior ancestry is no longer quite as effective as it used to be. If this current set of circumstances were to persist for long enough, you probably would see a rise in instinctual desires for actual reproduction, not just sex, since the people with the strongest instincts for reproduction would have more kids. * I'm not saying there's no instinct for reproduction for its own sake, but it's a separate instinct from that for sex. And we have plenty of other aspects of human nature that were optimized for our pre-industrial lifestyles, that aren't necessarily the best evolutionary fit to our current lifestyles (see next footnote, as well), along with our big brains and abstract thought processes and culture. So, it's easy to see how these conflicting influences could lead to someone not wanting kids of their own. ** Of course, there's no actual evolutionary purpose. That's just metaphorical language to help understand the process. Traits evolving because they help an organism to be more plentiful than other organisms is no more a purpose or success than water flowing downhill to collect in a river. It's simply what happens. This also means that we don't need to feel any allegiance to evolutionary 'purpose' or success. We're free to live our lives how we want to.

Question: Why would you disable comments on a Quora answer that has engagement? That seems like a missed opportunity for engagement which creates more views.
Answer: I have mixed views about people disabling comments on their Quora answers. First of all, Quora is not a debate site. It's a question and answer site. And it's been structured to give answer writers control over the comments section of their own answers. So, answer writers are well within their rights to disable comments. But, in ideal situations, at least, I tend to think of Quora like a presentation at a conference. At the technical conferences I go to, a typical format is 20 minutes for the speaker to give their presentation, followed by 10 minutes of Q&A. This Q&A can range from asking for clarifications or additional explanation, to offering advice from an audience member's own experience, to critiquing an aspect of the speaker's presentation (lest less informed audience members come away with misconceptions). i.e. While the format is more biased to allowing a speaker to present their own case, there's still a portion for feedback. So in my mind, that's the archetype I hold for Quora. The platform is mainly for answer writers to present their own case, but the comments section serves the role of Q&A. And in such ideal situations, that's my issue with writers who disable comments. There's no other good mechanism for feedback. I'll sometimes see very popular answers that I know are factually wrong. Writing my own answer that doesn't gain any traction isn't going to have anywhere near the same reach as a comment to that answer. Same thing with differing points of view. And the person who originally wrote that answer is much less likely to see a separate answer that I write rather than a comment to their own answer, so they're more likely to continue spreading their mistaken views elsewhere. Dismissing comments by telling someone to go write their own answer is akin to a speaker at a technical conference telling an audience member to go give their own presentation. But, online interactions aren't always ideal, and Quora is not, in fact, a well moderated technical conference. When the audience of a presentation is mostly fellow experts in a field, you can expect a certain level of quality to most of the Q&A, even the critiques. And when the Q&A period is limited to 10 minutes, there's simply not much time for arguments to escalate too too much. But on a platform open to the entirety of the world, and when the comments section can be left open indefinitely, there's lots of opportunity for abuse and for things to go sideways. Doubly so if you're one of the very popular Quorans. I'm not super popular here, but I've had answers go viral to where it's difficult to police the entirety of the comments section. I can't imagine that task if all of my answers had that type of popularity, especially keeping in mind that Quora is just a hobby to pass the time. So, that's why I have mixed views. Even as a Q&A site, ideally there would still be an appropriate level of discussion and critiquing for any answer. But the Internet is what it is, so I can understand why some people don't want to deal with the trolls and shit posters.

Question: What do atheists think the evolution of atheism will be like in the year 2050?
Answer: Dan Bradbury has written along similar lines in regards to gay counterculture (e.g. Dan Bradbury's answer to As it's Pride Month, what is something you would like to share with others about the LGBTQ community that could help spread awareness and just share knowledge to help open other people's eyes? and Dan Bradbury's answer to Are gay bars disappearing?). These types of countercultures exist when you're an ostracized minority, but as you become more and more accepted into the mainstream, there's no need for a counterculture because you just become an accepted part of the overall culture. I'm not saying that atheists have faced the same issues in my lifetime as the LGBTQ+ community. Since atheism isn't so outwardly apparent, it's pretty easy to blend in and just get along. But, especially 20 years ago when I first became an atheist, the social stigma was pretty strong. Here's just one example, using a polling question Gallup has been asking for decades, whether people would be willing to vote for an otherwise well qualified candidate who happened to be [insert characteristic]: ABOVE SOURCE: Socialism and Atheism Still U.S. Political Liabilities As you can see, atheists have always been either at the very bottom of the list or close to it. Back when I became an atheist in the early 2000s, less than half of Americans would have voted for an atheist. But, you can also see that things are getting better. By 2020, even if the number is still depressingly low, it's at least a majority of Americans that would now vote for an atheist. And I suspect that public opinions towards atheists will continue to improve, especially as more and more Americans are leaving behind Christianity. Back when I became an atheist, something like 85% of Americans were Christians. Now it's down to somewhere around 60%. And when you look at public attitudes towards atheists by age group, you can see that the younger generations are much more accepting of atheists than the older generations. ABOVE SOURCE: Americans Express Increasingly Warm Feelings Toward Religious Groups So, I suspect that the combined effects of atheism becoming more accepted and more mainstream, more people growing up as atheists rather than 'converting' to atheism from organized religion, and Christianity losing its influence over society, will all translate to less need for organized atheism. It's not like atheism is all that organized right now, but even things like atheism themed forums here on Quora will go by the wayside as there simply won't be much audience. Atheism will become as normal as not believing in Bigfoot, and by 2050, only nerds and skeptics (like me) will still be interested in debating the issue.

Question: As a native-English-language-speaker, is there ever situation in which you actually should not speak perfectly accurate English as defined by most academically approved English grammar and vocabulary books?
Answer: I do it all the time, especially depending on how pedantic of a book you’re thinking of. In fact, I did it just there in that sentence, by ending it with a preposition. Sure, most modern style guides don’t include that rule, but it was something I was taught back in grade school. Ending sentences with prepositions often just flows better than other constructions. There’s also the old rule about not splitting infinitives. It’s another one that’s growing outdated, but you can still find style guides recommending against it, such as here: But again, sentences often flow better when you split the infinitive, so I’ve got no qualms with doing so. There are also times were ‘proper’ grammar sounds stilted or pompous. For example, I know when to use ‘whom’ vs. ‘who’*, but I usually go with ‘who’, anyway, to avoid the appearance of being pretentious. In other cases, there are words or phrases that I simply avoid, because the technically accurate meaning is not the same as the common usage. So if you use it the technically accurate way, a large part of your audience won’t understand you. And if you use it the common way, the pedants will jump on you. A good example of this is ”begs the question” – it doesn’t mean what most people think it means**. There are also cases where the incorrect grammar carries a certain connotation or emotional aspect that you wouldn’t get from proper grammar. “Say it isn’t so” just doesn’t sound as good as “Say it ain’t so.” Related to that last one are informal contractions, where there actually are slightly different shades of meaning. If I ask somebody, “What are you doing?”, it carries a connotation of the actual, specific actions they’re currently engaged in. If I ask, “Whatcha doin’?”, it’s more of a general inquiry. I could go on, but hopefully that’s enough examples to make the point. You definitely don’t want to overdo it, but there are still plenty of occasions to use informal grammar that wouldn’t necessarily be approved of by your English teacher. As a note of caution from someone who’s semi-fluent in a second language, myself, you have to really know a language well before you understand the rules well enough to know when it’s appropriate to break them. If you’re learning English as a second language, it’s best to just try your best to speak it as properly as you can, at least until you’re really, really comfortable with the language and slang. (BTW – did you notice that split infinitive, there?) *The Oatmeal has a useful comic on this: ** Okay, as more of a descriptivist than a prescriptivist, ‘what it means’ is what most people think it means. But you’ll still get complaints from the pedants.

Answer: You’re right. It’s almost exactly like that. Anybody can write out a check purported to be worth $1 billion. And your bank might even charge you a fee for their inconvenience. You’ll have gotten your hopes up, only to be in the same financial situation or maybe even a little bit worse than before you received this check. If a random person offers you a $1 billion check, my advice is that you refuse to cash it. Of course, in the case of an afterlife, once you die and cease to exist, you won’t realize that it was an empty promise or a scam. But if there are strings attached (and with religions, there usually are), you’ll still have wasted at least some opportunities in the one life we actually do get.
